p.seg: 1.1 "On the First Discussion"
In the sixth year of Shǐyuán,
there was an imperial edict sending Chéngxiàng, Yùshǐ, along with the nominated xiánliáng and wénxué, to discuss matters.
They were to inquire into the hardships and sufferings among the people.
Wénxué replied:
"I have heard that the way to govern people
begins with preventing the sources of excess and dissipation,
broadening the beginnings of morality and virtue,
suppressing pursuit of profit and promoting benevolence and righteousness,
not displaying profit,
and only then can teaching and transformation be promoted
and folk customs be transformed.
Now, the commanderies and states have monopolies on salt, iron, wine,
and regulated transport,
competing for profit with the people.
This scatters the spirit of sincerity and honesty,
and produces a culture of greed and baseness.
Thus, few of the people pursue their basic occupation,
while many rush toward secondary pursuits.
When adornment flourishes, substance declines;
when the side branches flourish, the root is diminished.
If the side branches are promoted, the people become reckless;
if the root is cultivated, the people become honest.
When the people are honest, resources are sufficient;
when the people are extravagant, hunger and cold arise.
I respectfully request the abolition of the salt, iron, and wine monopolies, and the regulated transport,
to advance the root and reduce the side branches,
increase the benefit of agriculture—
this would be expedient."
The Dàfū said:
"The Xiōngnú have turned their backs and rebelled against us,
repeatedly invading and ravaging the border regions.
If we prepare defenses, it exhausts the soldiers of Zhōngguó;
if we do not, the raids and thefts will not cease.
The late Emperor, lamenting the long suffering of the border peoples
and their hardship from frequent captivity by the barbarians,
therefore repaired fortifications,
ordered beacons,
established garrisons for defense.
The border expenses are insufficient;
thus, the salt and iron monopolies were initiated,
the wine monopoly established,
and regulated transport instituted,
to enrich the public coffers and increase resources,
so as to assist with the border expenses.
Now those who propose to abolish these things
would empty the inner treasuries,
and make us want for what is needed outside for defense.
If we do this, the defenders at the passes and city walls will suffer hunger and cold at the borders;
how then will we provide for them?
To abolish these,
would not be expedient."
Wénxué said:
"Kǒngzǐ said:
'One who possesses a state or family
does not worry about scarcity, but about inequality;
does not worry about poverty, but about instability.'
Therefore, the Son of Heaven does not speak of abundance or scarcity;
the regional lords do not speak of profit or harm;
the Dàfū do not speak of gain or loss.
They preserve benevolence and righteousness to influence the people,
and broaden virtue to win their hearts;
thus those who are near draw close, and those far away are pleased and submit.
Therefore, the best conquerors do not go to war,
the best at war do not marshal armies,
the best marshals do not deploy in battle.
It is handled within the ancestral temples,
and so armies withdraw before combat.
When a true king practices benevolent government,
none can oppose him in the world,
so why would expenses be of concern?"
The Dàfū said:
"The Xiōngnú are violent and cunning,
presuming to enter our territory at will,
violating and endangering Zhōngguó,
killing officials in commanderies and counties, even the Duwei of Shuòfāng,
in great defiance and rebellion.
They ought to have been punished long ago.
Your Majesty extends great kindness,
in compassion for the masses who have not yet been provided for,
and cannot bear to let the warriors and officials die in the wilds;
even if it is difficult to send forth armored men,
yet there is still a resolve to subdue the Xiōngnú in the north;
and at the same time you wish to abolish salt, iron, and regulated transport,
thereby disturbing the border expenses,
weakening military strategy,
and showing no concern for the safety of the borders—
in this, it is not expedient."
Wénxué said:
"In ancient times,
virtue was valued and the use of arms was considered base.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'If those far away do not submit,
cultivate civil virtue to attract them;
when they arrive,
settle them in peace.'
Now you abandon morality and trust in arms,
raise armies to attack them,
station garrisons for defense,
expose soldiers to the harsh outdoors,
prolonging the conflict,
and endlessly shipping provisions;
thus the soldiers at the borders suffer hunger and cold,
the common people endure hardship within.
Establishing salt and iron,
and first setting up profit offices to supply them,
is not a long-term plan.
Thus, I believe abolishing them is expedient."
The Dàfū said:
"Those who founded states in ancient times
opened both the root and the branches,
connected the needs of those who have and those who have not,
standardized the marketplace for unified exchange,
attracting scholars and commoners,
gathering all kinds of goods,
so that farmers, merchants, artisans, and craftsmen could all obtain what they desired,
trade and then withdraw.
The Yìjīng says:
'Bring about change,
so the people do not grow weary.'
If artisans do not go out,
then farmers lack tools;
if merchants do not go forth,
then precious goods are cut off.
When farmers lack implements,
grain is not produced;
when precious goods are cut off,
resources become deficient.
Therefore, salt, iron, and regulated transport
are to circulate surplus goods and balance urgent needs.
To abolish them
would not be expedient."
Wénxué said:
"If the people are guided by virtue, then they return to honesty;
if they are shown profit,
their customs turn base.
When customs are base, they turn their backs on righteousness and pursue profit.
When they pursue profit, the people mingle on the roads and crowd the markets.
Lǎozǐ said:
'A poor nation seems to have surplus.
It is not because there is much wealth,
but because desires are many and the people are restless.'
Therefore, the true king extols the root and curtails the branches,
uses ritual and righteousness to restrain desires,
fills the stores with grain and wealth.
In the markets,
merchants do not circulate useless goods;
artisans do not make useless implements.
Thus, the role of merchants is to move what is stagnant,
the role of artisans is to prepare necessary tools—
these are not the main concerns of governing the state."
The Dàfū said:
"Guǎnzǐ said:
'If a state has abundant fertile fields but the people lack food,
it is because implements are insufficient.
If a state has mountain and sea products but the people lack wealth,
it is because merchants and craftsmen are lacking.'
The cinnabar, lacquer, feathers and banners from Lǒng and Shǔ,
the hides, ivory, and bone from Jīng and Yáng,
nanmu and catalpa, bamboo and arrows from the south of the Jiāng,
fish, salt, felt, and furs from Yān and Qí,
lacquer, silk, linen, and ramie from Yǎn and Yù—
these provide for needs in life and death,
requiring merchants for their exchange,
and craftsmen for their production.
Thus, the sages created boats and oars
to cross rivers and valleys,
harnessed oxen and horses
to traverse hills and plains;
reached the distant and plumbed the deep
to connect all things and benefit the people.
For this reason, the late Emperor established government ironworks to supply agricultural tools,
and opened regulated transport to enrich the people;
salt, iron, and regulated transport
are what the people rely upon and draw their sustenance from.
To abolish them
would not be expedient."
Wénxué said:
"If a state has abundant fertile fields but its people lack food,
it is because industry and commerce flourish while agriculture is neglected;
if it has mountain and sea products but the people lack wealth,
it is because public needs are disregarded and excessive cleverness abounds.
Thus, even source rivers cannot fill a leaky jar,
the mountains and sea cannot fill bottomless valleys.
Therefore, Pángēng gathered people together,
Shùn stored away gold,
Gāodì forbade merchants from serving as officials—
all to check the customs of greed and baseness
and cultivate a spirit of pure sincerity.
Even when the marketplaces were suppressed, profit-seeking blocked,
the people still committed wrongdoings—
how much more so when profit is promoted from above?
The Zhuàn says:
'When lords pursue profit, Dàfū become base;
when Dàfū are base, scholars become greedy;
when scholars are greedy, commoners become thieves.'
This opens a path to profit and becomes a ladder for crime among the people."
The dàfū said:
“In the past,
all the commanderies, kingdoms, and feudal lords each contributed tribute of their local products;
the comings and goings were complicated and troublesome,
and the goods were often poor and of inferior quality,
sometimes not worth the cost.
Therefore, the commanderies and kingdoms established transport offices to supply and deliver goods to one another,
making it convenient for distant regions to offer tribute;
hence it was called ‘equalized transport.’
Repositories were established in the capital,
to gather up all goods.
When prices were low, the government would buy;
when prices were high, it would sell.
By this, the prefectural offices do not lose out on actual value,
and merchants and traders have no avenue for excessive profit;
hence this is called ‘leveling the standards.’
With leveled standards, the people do not lose their proper occupations;
with equalized transport, the people equally share toil and rest.
Thus, leveling the standards and equalized transport
are methods to stabilize all things and benefit the common people,
not opening up profit channels as ladders to crime among the people.”
The literatus said:
“In ancient times, when taxes were levied on the people,
it was according to what they were skilled at;
not demanding what they lacked ability in.
Farmers would contribute what they had harvested,
and women their finished handiwork.
Now, they are made to relinquish what they have,
and are required to provide what they do not possess.
The people must sell their goods at low prices,
all to satisfy the demands from above.
In recent times,
the commanderies and kingdoms sometimes order people to make cloth and silk floss,
and the officials arbitrarily hold back and make trouble,
engaging in market dealings with them.
What the officials take in
is not only the fine silk from Qí and Ā,
or the cloth from Shǔ and Hàn,
but also what is produced by the common people.
They carry out fraudulent sales under the guise of fairness,
causing greater hardship for the farmers,
and subjecting the women’s labor to double taxation;
the equalization of transport is not yet seen.
When the local authorities suddenly issue demands,
closing off households and monopolizing the market,
all goods are collected together.
When all goods are collected together,
prices soar and leap.
When they leap,
merchants and traders reap equal profits.
When the market is monopolized,
the officials allow for corruption.
Powerful officials and wealthy merchants hoard goods in anticipation of urgent times,
petty traders and corrupt officials buy cheap to sell dear,
and as yet, the leveling of standards is not achieved.
In ancient times, equalized transport
was to balance toil and ease and to facilitate tribute and delivery,
not to profit and speculate in all things.”
1.2 "The Second: Strength in Plowing"
The dàfū said:
“The kingly ruler restricts Heaven’s wealth,
forbids border markets,
holds fast to the standards and keeps to seasons,
to regulate the people with lightness and heaviness.
In years of abundance and good harvest,
stores are stocked to prepare for times of shortage and want;
in years of disaster and bad harvest,
currency and goods are put into circulation;
to spread out surplus and balance deficiency.
In the past, when Yǔ faced floods and Tāng faced drought,
the people were destitute,
sometimes borrowing from one another just to get by with food and clothing.
Yǔ used gold from Lìshān,
Tāng used copper from Zhuāngshān,
to mint currency and ransom their people,
and the realm praised them as benevolent.
In the past, when resources were insufficient,
soldiers sometimes went without stipends,
and east of the mountains suffered disaster,
Qí and Zhào endured great famine,
but thanks to the stores gathered by equalized transport,
reserves in the granaries,
soldiers were supplied,
and the starving people given relief.
Thus, the goods of equalized transport,
and wealth in the treasuries,
are not only for trading with all the people or exclusively for supplying military use,
but also to bring relief to the destitute and prepare against the calamities of flood and drought.”
The literatus said:
“In ancient times,
one-tenth was collected as tax,
and fish and fowl from marshes and bridges entered at the proper season, with no prohibition;
every commoner tilled the southern fields and did not neglect their work.
Thus, after three years of cultivation, one had stores for an extra year;
after nine years of cultivation, there was reserve for three years.
This is how Yǔ and Tāng prepared against flood and drought and brought peace to the people.
If wild grass is not cleared,
arable fields are not managed,
then even possessing the riches of mountains and seas,
and commerce from every minor commodity,
still cannot support the people.
Therefore, in ancient times, emphasis was laid on strength, valuing the root, and planting many trees,
to personally farm at the right time and have ample food and clothing;
even amid successive bad years, the people did not suffer.
Thus, food and clothing are the people’s foundation,
and tilling and reaping are their vocation.
When both are cultivated,
the state is rich and the people at peace.
The Shījīng says:
'A hundred households abound and settle,
wives and children dwell in peace.'”
The dàfū said:
“The wise and sage manage a household not with a single treasure,
nor do they enrich a state by one way alone.
In ancient times, Guǎn Zhòng used craft and stratagem to achieve hegemony,
while the Jì family was overthrown despite a strong foundation.
If managing household and sustaining life must solely depend on farming,
then Shùn would not have made pottery nor Yī Yǐn served as cook.
Therefore, those skilled in statecraft,
when the world is low, I am high;
when the world is light, I am heavy.
With the nonessentials, they exchange for the essentials;
through the insubstantial, they exhaust the substantial.
Now, wealth from the mountains and marshes,
and the stores of equalized transport,
are means to regulate lightness and heaviness and command the feudal lords.
The gold from Rǔ and Hàn,
and the slender tributes,
are used to lure foreign countries and fish for the treasures of Qiang.
With a single bolt of silk from China,
we obtain from the Xīongnú quantities of gold,
thus depleting the resources of enemy states.
Thus, mules and donkeys, dromedaries and Bactrian camels,
come in lines, mouth to tail, into the pass;
fine horses of many breeds,
all become our livestock;
shrews, moles, foxes and raccoon dogs,
colored felts and patterned textiles,
fill our imperial storehouses;
while jade, coral, and lapis lazuli,
all become treasures of the state.
Thus, foreign goods flow inwards,
and the profits do not leak abroad.
With foreign goods flowing in, state resources abound;
when profits do not leak out, the people’s needs are met.
The Shījīng says:
'A hundred households abound and settle,
wives and children dwell in peace.'”
The literatus said:
“In ancient times,
merchants facilitated goods but did not accrue surplus,
artisans fashioned implements but did not fake them.
So the gentleman farmed, fished and raised crops,
always in reality.
Merchants, however, specialize in deceit;
artisans in disguised shoddy work;
secretly spying and picking holes while feeling no shame;
thus, the upright are cheated and the honest are slighted.
In the past, Jié filled his palace with female musicians,
and adorned himself in brocade,
so Yī Yǐn left the court and wandered afar,
while the female musicians finally brought ruin to the state.
Now, the use of mules and donkeys,
is not equal to the function of oxen and horses;
the hides and felts of moles and shrews,
do not increase the real worth of brocade and damask.
Beautiful jade and coral come from Kūnshān,
pearls and ivory from Guìlín,
places over ten thousand lǐ away from Hàn.
For the labor in farming and silkworms,
and the expense of capital,
this amounts to single items being sold for a hundred times their value,
a single bow earning grain enough to fill ten thousand storage bins.
When the ruler loves the strange and rare,
then extravagant habits spread below,
and if he prizes goods from afar,
then wealth flows outward.
Therefore, the king does not treasure what is useless to set limits for the people,
nor covet rare goods in order to enrich the state.
Thus, the way to govern the people
is to economize and value the essential,
partition the land and allot fields, and that is all.”
The dàfū said:
“From the capital in all directions—east, west, south, and north—
traversing mountains and rivers,
passing through commanderies and kingdoms,
all the densely populated and wealthy capitals,
none lack five intersecting avenues,
gathering places for merchants and traders,
and sites where myriad commodities are accumulated.
Thus, the sage rides the seasons of Heaven,
the wise exploit the local resources,
the superior man takes from others,
and the mediocre toil with their bodies.
Chángjū and Jié Nì,
have no store of a hundred gold pieces;
while those who stroll about idly
do not possess the wealth of Yī Dūn;
in Wǎn, Zhōu, Qí, and Lǔ,
commerce pervades the world.
Therefore, the wealth of merchants and traders,
some accumulate tens of thousands in gold,
is the result of pursuing profit and taking advantage of surplus.
Why must enriching the state necessarily depend on agriculture as the foundation,
and why must making the people sufficient require the well-field system?”
The scholar said:
“When the great flood covered the heavens,
there was Yǔ's achievement;
when the Yellow River overflowed,
there was the merit of Xuān Fáng.
When Shāng Zhòu was cruel and tyrannical,
there was the plan at Mèng Jīn.
When the world was troubled and chaotic,
there was the wealth from taking surplus.
In the most perfectly ruled times of antiquity,
the people were simple and esteemed the fundamental, were at ease and had few desires.
In those times,
travel on the roads was rare,
and grass grew in the markets and courts.
Thus, those who did not exert themselves at farming could not fill their needs,
and those who did not exert themselves at weaving could not cover their bodies.
Although there were essential points of exchange,
and the techniques of Táo and Wǎn,
there was nowhere to apply their skill.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one who receives reward without application,
or has merit without labor,
it has never occurred.”
1.3 “On Universal Possession, Chapter Three”
The senior official said:
“At Zhuō and Jì in Yān,
Hándān of Zhào,
Wēn and Zhǐ of Wèi,
Xíngyáng of Hán,
Línzī of Qí,
Wǎn and Chén of Chǔ,
Yángzhái of Zhèng,
the Two Zhōu in Sānchuān,
whose wealth leads all under heaven,
and all are famed capitals of the realm,
yet none has their fields tilled by assisting farmers,
but rather lies at the intersection of the five regions,
straddling the thoroughfares of streets and avenues.
Therefore, in places where goods are abundant, the people multiply,
and those whose homes are near the markets can be rich.
Wealth depends upon technique and calculation,
not toil of the body;
profit is found in advantageous locations,
not in strenuous farming.”
The scholar said:
“To the south of Jīng and Yáng are the riches of Guìlín,
within, they have the advantages of rivers and lakes,
to the left, the gold of Língyáng,
to the right, the timber of Shǔ and Hàn,
they cut wood and plant grain,
burn stubble and sow millet,
practice slash-and-burn and water-weeding,
the land is vast and rich in resources;
yet the people are lazy and idle, seeking only to live,
fond of fine clothing and rich food.
Even though their homes are plain cottages with thatched roofs,
they sing songs and play the qín,
provided for daily but lacking for the month,
rejoicing in the morning, grieving by evening.
Zhào and Zhōngshān border the great river,
joining the divine thoroughfares in all four directions,
situated in the paths of all under heaven,
where merchants and traders fill the roads,
and the feudal lords meet upon the ways;
yet the people indulge in frivolous pursuits,
extravagant and wasteful, neglecting the fundamental,
the fields and lands are not tended,
men and women adorn themselves,
the families lack even minuscule stores,
yet the sound of the qín fills their rooms.
Therefore, among the people of Chǔ and Zhào,
poverty is common and wealth is scarce.
As for Sòng, Wèi, Hán, and Liáng,
they love the fundamentals: sowing and reaping,
households are organized and people are orderly,
there is no family without abundance and supply.
Thus, profit is found in self-restraint,
not in situating oneself at the crossroads of streets and avenues;
wealth is in thrift, diligence, and seizing the right time,
not in overseeing flocks and wild birds each year.”
The senior official said:
“The Five Phases:
the east is wood,
yet Dān and Zhāng have mountains of gold and copper;
the south is fire,
yet Jiāozhǐ has the great rivers and seas;
the west is metal,
yet Shǔ and Lǒng have prized forests of timber;
the north is water,
yet Yōudū has land of piled sand.
It is by this that heaven and earth balance the presence and absence, and connect all things.
Now, the bamboo of Wú and Yuè,
the timber of Suí and Táng,
are inexhaustible in use,
yet Cáo, Wèi, Liáng, and Sòng,
resort to using coffins twice over.
The fish of rivers and lakes,
the cod of Lái and Huáng,
are inexhaustible in food,
yet Zōu, Lǔ, Zhōu, and Hán,
must subsist on wild herbs and coarse vegetables.
There is no resource under heaven and earth that is not abundant,
no product of mountain or sea that is not wealthy;
yet the people are impoverished,
materials are insufficient,
the distribution is unbalanced,
and wealth is not circulated under heaven.”
The scholar said:
“In ancient times,
rafters were gathered without being hewn,
thatch was not cut short,
people wore cloth and coarse wool,
ate food ground on earthen mills,
cast gold to make hoes,
molded clay to make vessels,
craftsmen did not produce curiosities,
and society did not value things that cannot be worn or eaten,
each was content with their home,
delighted in their customs,
enjoyed their food,
found their tools convenient.
Thus, goods from distant lands did not circulate,
and the jade of Kūnshān did not arrive.
Now customs are corrupted, and people compete in extravagance and luxury,
women seek ultimate delicacy,
craftsmen strive for extreme ingenuity,
carving away simplicity and preferring the rare and odd,
boring into mountains and rocks in search of gold and silver,
diving into the deepest pools for pearls and jewels,
setting traps for rhinoceros and elephant,
stretching nets to catch kingfisher and jadeite,
seeking exotic goods from southern and northern tribes to dazzle the Central States,
moving the products of Qióng and Zuó,
bringing them to the Eastern Sea,
trading for the wealth of ten thousand miles,
wasting days and labor,
all of no benefit to use.
Thus, the coarse-clad man and plain wife,
exhaust their strength with wearisome labor,
yet do not have enough to wear and eat.
Therefore, the kingly ruler restricts excess profits,
and curtails wasteful expenditures.
When excess profits are checked, people return to the root;
when waste is controlled, the people have what they need.
Thus, in life, there is no lack of resources,
and in death, there is no need to reuse coffins.”
The senior official said:
“In ancient times,
palaces and houses followed proper standards,
carriages and clothing suited their function;
gathering rafters and thatching with grass
was not the system of the former kings.
A gentleman regulates extravagance and prevents thrift from becoming meanness,
with thrift comes strength.
In the past, when Sūn Shū'áo served as minister in Chǔ,
his wife did not wear silk,
and his horses ate no grain.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘This cannot be,
for such excessive thrift becomes baseness.’
Thus was the song “Cicada” composed.
It is said in the Guǎnzi:
‘If palaces and houses are not adorned,
timber cannot be entirely used,
if kitchens are not filled,
birds and beasts are not reduced in lifespan.
Without secondary profits,
the primary occupation cannot grow,
without decoration,
women’s craft cannot be applied.’
Thus, craftsmen, merchants, woodworkers,
are the servants of state and society,
and the tools and implements they provide.
They have existed since ancient times,
not just now.
Xián Gāo sold cattle to Zhōu,
the Five Goat Cart rental entered Qín,
Gōng Shūzi used compasses and squares,
Ōu Yě smelted and cast metals.
It is said in the Analects:
‘Hundreds of artisans in their shops
complete their tasks.’
Farmers and merchants trade,
thus profiting both the fundamental and the peripheral.
Those living in mountains and marshes,
amidst weeds and waste ground,
resources circulate,
and there is a way to balance them.”
Therefore, where there is plenty, it does not flourish alone;
where there is scarcity, it does not suffer want alone.
If each were to dwell in its own place
and eat its own food,
then the jú and yòu would not be sold,
the salt of Qú Lǔ would not go out,
the zhān and jì would not be found in the market,
and the wealth of Wú and Táng would be of no use."
The Scholar said:
"Mèngzǐ said:
'If one does not go against the seasons for farming,
grain cannot be eaten up;
if silkworms and hemp are raised in their season,
there cannot be enough people to wear all the cloth and silk;
if axes and adzes enter the forests in season,
timber cannot be used up;
if fields and fisheries are worked in season,
fish and meat cannot be eaten up.'
If one then ornaments palaces and houses,
builds up towers and terraces,
carpenters and craftsmen cut the great into the small,
make the round into the square,
above form clouds,
below form mountains and forests,
then timber is not enough for use.
If men leave their roots for minor tasks,
even if they carve and engrave,
fashioning images of birds and beasts,
exhausting things and pursuing changes,
then grain is not enough for food.
If women devote themselves excessively to fine and delicate work,
producing intricate patterns,
pushing skill to its limits,
then silk and cloth are not enough for clothing.
If cooks slaughter embryo animals and eggs,
boil, roast, blend and harmonize,
exhausting the five flavors,
then fish and meat are not enough for food.
In the world today,
the problem is not that birds and beasts are not reduced,
nor that timber is inexhaustible,
but the endless extravagance and excess;
it is not that there are no zhān, jì, jú, and yòu,
but that there are no humble huts nor rice husks and bran."
1.4 "On the Mistaken Use of Currency, Chapter Four"
The Dàfū said:
"When currency is exchanged and benefits freely given,
the people's businesses cannot keep up,
things accumulate in some places.
By calculating resources and measuring allocations,
there will still be those among the people who are hungry,
and the grain will have places where it is stored.
The wise possess the achievements of a hundred men,
the foolish have affairs that never return to the root.
If the ruler does not regulate affairs,
there will be those among the people with wealth equal to ten thousand others.
Therefore, some have stores sufficient for a hundred years,
while others are not satisfied with husks and bran.
If the people are greatly wealthy,
they cannot be ordered by salary;
if greatly strong,
they cannot be subdued by punishment and authority.
If benefits are not spread and equalized, society will not be balanced.
Thus the ruler accumulates food,
guards its use,
controls the surplus,
balances what is lacking,
forbids excess,
blocks selfish profit,
and only then can every household be well-supplied and everyone have enough."
The Scholar said:
"In ancient times,
virtue was valued and profit made light,
righteousness was esteemed and wealth disregarded.
During the times of the Three Kings,
prosperity and decline alternated.
If weakened, they were aided;
if in danger of falling, they were stabilized.
Thus the loyalty of Xià, the reverence of Yīn, and the civil virtue of Zhōu,
the lessons of the xiángxù,
the rites of respect and yielding,
were all manifest and visible.
But afterwards,
ritual and righteousness decayed,
customs were lost and ceased.
So gentlemen who lived on stipends
departed from righteousness and contended for wealth,
the great and the small swallowed one another,
stirring conflict and causing mutual downfall.
Therefore, some had stores for a hundred years,
while others could not fill their emptiness nor cover their bodies.
In ancient times, those who held office did not farm,
farmers did not fish,
gatekeepers and watchmen
all had fixed stipends,
and were not allowed to combine interests and exhaust resources.
Thus,
the wise and foolish alike accomplished their duties,
without mutual harm.
The Shī says:
'There are abandoned sheaves for some,
there are lingering grains for others,
this is the gain of the widows.'
This speaks of not exhausting things."
The Dàfū said:
"Tāng and Wén followed times of decline,
the rise of Hàn followed after disorder.
The alternation of simplicity and formality
is not a matter of arbitrary changes.
When custom becomes corrupt, laws are changed;
not in pursuit of altering antiquity,
but also to rescue what is lost and support what is weak.
Thus teachings and customs change,
abuses change with the age.
Xià Hòu used black shells,
the Zhōu used purple stones,
later generations used coins of metal, knives and cloth.
Things, having reached their extreme, decline;
this is the cycle of beginnings and endings.
When mountains and lakes are untaxed,
then ruler and subject share the same interests;
when there is no prohibition on knife-money,
then honest and dishonest alike abound.
When officials are rich, they compete in extravagance;
when the lower castes monopolize profit, they undermine each other."
The Scholar said:
"In ancient times,
there was neither knife-money nor coins in the markets and courts;
each bartered what he had for what he lacked,
exchanging cloth for silk, nothing more.
Later, turtle shells, cowries, gold and coins appeared,
and exchanges expanded.
The more often currency changed, the more the people practiced deceit.
Fraud could be prevented by returning to plainness,
losses could be avoided by adhering to ritual.
Tāng and Wén followed times of decline,
and by reforming laws and changing customs,
the Dao of Yīn and Zhōu prospered.
At the founding of Hàn, they accepted the abuses,
yet did not change or reform,
accumulating profit and altering currency,
intending to return to the root,
which was like using boiling to stop burning,
or using fire to stop boiling.
When those above value ritual, the people busy themselves with ornament;
when those above value profit, those below strive for wealth with their lives."
The Dàfū said:
"In the time of Wén Dì,
the people were allowed to mint coins, smelt iron, and refine salt.
The King of Wú controlled the seas and lakes,
Dèng Tōng monopolized the Western Mountains.
In Shāndōng, the crafty and artful
were all gathered in the state of Wú,
Qín, Yǒng, Hàn, and Shǔ depended on the Dèng clan.
The coins of Wú and Dèng were circulated throughout All Under Heaven,
which is why restrictions were placed on coining.
Once laws for regulation were established,
deceit and falsehood were suppressed;
when deceit and falsehood were suppressed,
the people did not hope for unearned gain,
and each attended to his occupation;
why not then return to the root?
When there is unification from above,
the people have no division;
when currency comes from the top,
the lower people have no doubts."
The Scholar said:
"In the remote past,
when many currencies and commodities were circulating, the people rejoiced.
Afterwards,
old currencies were gradually abandoned,
and bái jīn, tortoise shells, and dragons were newly issued;
the people became ever more clever in making new coins.
As currency changed more frequently, the people grew increasingly suspicious.
Then all the currencies under heaven were abolished,
and only the Shuǐhéng Three Offices were charged with making currency.
Officials and craftsmen sought to profit for themselves,
sometimes not conforming to regulations,
causing differences in thickness, weight, lightness and heaviness.
Farmers were not skilled in this,
comparing by categories of goods,
trusting the old and doubting the new,
not knowing honesty from dishonesty.
Merchants exchanged the good for bad,
and half for double.
In buying, they failed to get reality;
in selling, they lost fairness;
their doubts grew ever deeper.
When counterfeit coins are cast with established laws,
the quality of the coins is no better or worse than before.
Picky coin selection causes goods to be held up,
and users suffer especially from it.
The Chūnqiū says:
'If calculations do not match those of the Mán and Yí, the system will not work.'
Thus, a true king does not shut off the seas and lakes outside to facilitate the people's use,
nor prohibit knife-money within, so as to facilitate the people's exchanges."
1.5 "On Prohibiting Farming, Chapter Five"
The Dàfū said:
"When a family has precious vessels,
they will still store them in boxes and cases;
how much more so the mountains and seas belonging to the ruler?
As for sources of power and profit,
they are always found deep in the mountains and remote marshes;
only influential families can realize those profits.
In former times,
before salt and iron were monopolized,
commoners had Qū Bǐng,
rulers had Wú Wáng,
all concerning the initial debates on salt and iron.
Wú Wáng alone enjoyed the abundance of mountains and marshes,
levying low taxes on his people,
relieving the poor and needy,
thereby establishing private power.
When private power accumulates, rebellious intent arises.
If the source is not cut off early, but one worries only about the consequences,
it is like breaching Lǚ Liáng;
the flood will pour forth,
and the harm caused will surely be great.
Tài Gōng said:
'One family harms a hundred families,
a hundred families harm the feudal lords,
the feudal lords harm all under Heaven,
thus royal laws prohibit them.'
Now, if the people are left free to pursue power and profit,
abolishing the salt and iron monopolies to supply the violent and powerful,
letting their greed run unchecked,
evil ones will gather,
private households will form factions,
then the power of the strong grows daily uncontrollable,
and the treacherous will form new cliques of annexation and usurpation."
The Scholar said:
"The people keep treasures in their homes,
the feudal lords store them in their states,
the Son of Heaven stores within the seas.
Thus, the people use walls as their safekeeping,
the Son of Heaven uses all within the seas as his chest and coffer.
When the Son of Heaven visits a feudal lord,
he enters by the eastern steps;
the feudal lord hands over the keys,
holding the register to await commands,
demonstrating that none but the king is master.
Thus, the king does not accumulate or amass,
but stores among the people below,
keeps distant from ill-gotten profit,
and devotes himself to what is right for the people;
when righteousness and ritual are established,
the people will emulate those above.
In such a case, even if Tāng and Wǔ were alive in this age,
they would have no cause for anxiety.
Affairs of merchants and craftsmen,
responsibilities like Ōu Yě’s,
— what evildoing could possibly succeed?
The Three Huán monopolized Lǔ,
the Six Qīng divided Jìn,
not because of salt and iron.
Thus the deepest sources of power and profit
are not in mountains and seas,
but at court;
one family's harm to a hundred families
is found within the palace walls,
not in Qū and Bǐng."
The Dàfū said:
"When mountains and seas are forbidden
the people are not destabilized;
when there is balance between noble and base
the people are not suspicious.
When the county office sets standards and scales,
each acts as they wish,
so that even a five-foot child sent to market
cannot be cheated.
Now if these standards are abolished,
then powerful families monopolize their functions and profits.
In the markets and alleyways,
prices rest on tongues and mouths,
value has no constancy,
and while sitting at ease, the powerful thrive among the people,
thus supporting the strong, suppressing the weak, while thieves hide their plunder.
If the strong are fostered and the weak oppressed,
commoners perish;
this is like an abundance of filth damaging the five grains.
When one family harms a hundred,
it is not in Qū and Bǐng;
how can this be?"
The Scholar said:
"Mountains and seas
are the precious avenues of resources.
Iron tools
are the deadly warriors of the farmer.
When deadly warriors are used,
enemies are destroyed;
when enemies are destroyed,
the fields are opened up;
fields opened and five grains ripen.
When the precious avenues are open,
the people are supplied, their needs met,
and the state enriched.
When the state is wealthy and guides with ritual,
then on the roads, people yield to one another;
the merchants and artisans do not interfere,
everyone connects with sincerity and plainness,
and none seeks to profit from another.
Now Qín, Chǔ, Yān, Qí —
their lands and strengths differ,
their natures hard or soft vary,
with various scales and utilities,
each has its needs according to circumstance,
their customs and dialects,
each has its convenience.
When the county office imposes uniformity,
iron tools lose their appropriateness,
farmers lose their convenience.
When tools are unsuitable,
farmers will wear themselves out in the fields and the wastelands will remain uncultivated.
When wastelands are not cleared,
the people become impoverished.
Thus, places of salt production,
salt ironworks all depend on the mountains and rivers,
near to iron and coal,
and their situation is always remote and work is hard.
Those drafted as laborers in the commandery
mostly cannot endure,
and buy substitutes to take their place.
Some districts assign iron levies by household population,
setting uniform prices cheaply.
Good families, following official routes,
hire transport for salt and iron — it is taxing,
the common people suffer for it.
I have secretly observed that one official's harm can reach a thousand miles,
but have never seen it occur at Qū and Bǐng."
1.6 'Return to Antiquity, Chapter Six'
The Dàfū said:
"Formerly, the Commandant of Shànshuǐ, Péng Zǔníng, returned
and said:
'The regulations for salt and iron
are exceedingly clear.
The troops are clothed and fed by the county offices,
work at casting iron implements,
which are supplied to many,
causing no harm to the people.
But, when officials are corrupt,
and prohibitions are unenforced,
the people then suffer hardship.'
The intent of the regulations is to unify salt and iron,
not solely for profit,
but chiefly to establish the root and restrain the tip,
dissolve factions,
prohibit luxury and excess,
and sever the path of annexation and monopolization.
In ancient times,
famous mountains and great marshes were not given as fiefs,
to prevent those below from monopolizing their profits.
The profits of mountains and seas,
the grazing of broad marshes,
the hidden stores of Heaven and Earth,
all ought to belong to the Minor Treasury;
Your Majesty does not privatize them,
but assigns them to the Minister of Finance,
to aid and assist the people.
Idle and eccentric folk,
desiring to seize mountain and sea goods,
in pursuit of wealth,
make use of petty people,
thus opposition to these measures is widespread.
Iron tools and weapons
are of great use to the whole empire,
and not what the masses ought to handle.
Previously,
when powerful great families
controlled the profits of mountains and seas,
they mined iron and smelted it,
boiled seawater for salt.
One family would gather a throng,
sometimes over a thousand people,
and in general these drew in exiles and wanderers.
Far from their home villages,
abandoning ancestral graves,
relying on great households,
they gathered in deep mountains and remote marshes,
forming enterprises of fraud and deceit,
and then wielding the power of factions.
Their lawlessness was truly great!
Now,
by broadening the path for able men,
and carefully selecting prefects and commandants,
there is no need to abolish salt
and iron monopolies in order to bring peace to the people."
The wénxué said:
"What Shàn Shuǐ Dūwèi says
pertains to the expedient powers
and all manner of techniques of that time;
these cannot be practiced long nor transmitted to later generations. This is not the way by which a sagely king governs the state and its people.
The *Shī* says:
'Alas for those who act in doubt,
they do not take the forebears as their pattern,
nor the great ones as their model;
rather, they listen only to what is near at hand.'
This poem censures those who do not comprehend the kingly way
but are adept at expedient power and profit.
Emperor Xiàowǔ repelled the Nine Yí,
pacified the Hundred Yuè,
and often raised armies;
yet supplies were lacking.
Therefore, he established agricultural officials,
set up the coinage,
created grain-tax offices,
and strove to give relief in emergencies and aid those in want.
Now Your Majesty continues the labor of great achievements,
nurturing a people fatigued by exertion;
at this time when surplus and scarcity fluctuate,
ministers and nobles ought to ponder how to pacify and gather the people,
to bring about benefit and eliminate harm,
to assist the enlightened ruler by means of humaneness and righteousness,
and to cultivate and enhance the grand enterprise.
Since the Enlightened Lord ascended the throne,
it has been six years;
not one court official has requested the reduction or elimination of unnecessary offices,
nor the dismissal of those skilled in opportunistic profit.
These expedient measures have lasted too long;
the good among the people look with hope to their superiors.
Your Majesty proclaims sagely virtue,
sheds bright illumination,
commands worthy and talented men of the commanderies and kingdoms,
to come by express messenger to the palace carriage,
to debate the ways of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
the spirit of the Six Arts,
to set forth a record distinguishing security and danger, benefit and harm,
with intentions made plain.
Now the ministers argue and debate,
but nothing is settled;
this is called holding fast to petty matters and neglecting the greater framework,
clinging to small gains but forgetting great profit."
The dàfū said:
"Within the rafters and beams,
swallows and sparrows do not know the height of Heaven and Earth;
the frog at the bottom of the well
does not know the vastness of rivers and seas;
a poor man or unlucky woman
does not know the concerns of state;
a porter or carrier
knows nothing of Yī Dùn's wealth.
The former emperor calculated the profits of foreign states,
assessed the arms of the tribes of Hú and Yuè;
when the enemy was weak and easy to control,
exerting little effort yielded great achievement.
Therefore, adapting to changing circumstances, he controlled the Four Barbarians,
holding land abutting mountains and sea,
connected to the Long Wall;
he advanced north beyond the Yellow River,
opening routes to the land of the Xiōngnú,
though the deeds were not yet complete.
King Wén received the Mandate and attacked Chóng,
establishing a city at Fēng;
King Wǔ continued his work,
moving ahead, carrying the corpses of his loyalists,
defeated Shāng and captured Zhòu,
and thus accomplished the kingly enterprise.
Cáo Mò cast aside the shame of losing the Three Northern Regions,
and took back invaded lands;
Guǎn Zhòng bore burdens of his age,
and established hegemonic merit.
Therefore, those of great ambition discard what is petty,
the expedient cut against convention.
The stewards thought upon Mèng Shīwàng's strategies,
continued the earlier emperor's works,
aiming to sever the threat of the Hú and Mò,
to capture Chányú;
hence, there has been no leisure to attend to the doctrine of 'closing the doors',
nor record the arguments of the restricted scholars."
The wénxué said:
"When swallows and sparrows leave the rafters and beams, they face the danger of hawks and falcons;
when the frog leaves the well, it faces the harm of snakes and rats;
how much more so those who soar a thousand fathoms and roam the Four Seas?
Such a calamity must be great indeed!
This is why Lǐ Sī had his wings broken
and Zhào Gāo was engulfed in the depths.
I have heard that Kings Wén and Wǔ received the Mandate,
attacked the unrighteous to bring peace to feudal lords and ministers;
I have not heard that they exhausted Zhūxià to make slaves of the foreign barbarians.
In past times, Qín would mobilize the might of the realm for the sake of the Hú and Yuè,
drain the wealth of the realm to supply them,
yet the people could not bear it all.
Deploying a million-man army
for the sake of one man's task—
this is heard throughout the world.
Moreover, frequent warfare wearies the people,
protracted campaigning ruins the troops;
this is what the people bitterly suffer,
and what concerns the constrained scholars."
2.1 "Against Shāng," Chapter Seven
The dàfū said:
"In former days, when Lord Shāng served as minister in Qín,
he established law and order domestically,
made punishments severe,
cleansed governance and teaching,
giving no quarter to treachery and deceit.
Externally, he set up hundredfold profit,
gathered taxation from mountains and lakes,
thus the state became rich and the people strong,
implements and armor were complete and fine,
and stores were abundant.
Therefore, when mobilizing for war and attacking states,
expanding territory and boundaries,
he required no taxes from the people to provide for the army;
thus, resources were never depleted and the people hardly knew it,
the land extended to the Western River and the people did not grow weary.
The profits of salt and iron
were to relieve the people's urgent needs,
cover the expenses of the army,
and accumulate reserves to prevent shortage or want.
What was supplied was great and numerous,
beneficial to the state
and harmless to the people.
Why, then, do the people suffer,
and why does the wénxué worry?"
The wénxué said:
"Back in the time of Emperor Wén,
though there were no state-run profits from salt and iron, the people were prosperous;
now that these exist, the people are poor and suffering.
I do not see where the benefit lies;
rather, I see the harm.
Moreover, profit does not come from Heaven,
nor does it spring from the earth,
but is always taken from among the people;
calling it hundredfold profit,
this is the error in calculation.
It is no different from a fool who turns his fur coat inside out to carry firewood,
cherishing the hair
without realizing that the hide is being worn away.
When the plum bears much fruit,
the following year it withers;
when the new grain ripens, the old stores are diminished.
Even Heaven and Earth cannot both be full at once—
how much less so human affairs?
Thus, gain here entails loss there,
just as yin and yang do not shine together,
or as day and night have different lengths.
Shāng Yāng emphasized harsh laws and profit,
so the people of Qín could scarcely live,
and together they wept for Duke Xiào.
Wú Qǐ relied on arms and conquest,
so the people of Chǔ were troubled,
and together mourned for King Dào.
After that, Chǔ became ever more precarious
and Qín grew ever weaker.
Thus, storing profit gather resentment,
broadening territory brings disaster;
so where is it that resources can be inexhaustible and the people unaware,
that the land reaches to the Western River and the people are not distressed?
Now with the policies of Shāng Yāng employed within,
and the military methods of Wú Qǐ used without,
those who travel are wearied on the road,
those at home are impoverished in their rooms;
old mothers wail and weep,
resentful maidens sigh.
Though the wénxué may wish not to worry,
how could that be possible?"
The dàfū said:
"Qín employed Lord Shāng,
and so the state became rich and strong.
Afterwards, it annexed the Six States and established empire.
By the time of the Second Emperor,
evil ministers usurped authority,
the public way was blocked,
the fief-holders rebelled,
and the ancestral temples were destroyed.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
'If one's last words are not wise,
then Zhai Zhòng perished.'
One who excels in song causes others to carry on his melody;
one who excels in work causes others to continue his merit.
The wheelwright's cicada-grasping,
derives from the teaching of carrying the child.
The completion of the Zhōu way
was due to Zhōu Gōng's effort.
Although Bī Chén opened up the design,
without Zǐchǎn's refinement,
although there were the compass and square of Kings Wén and Wǔ,
without the mortise and tenon of Zhōu and Lǚ,
the achievement could not be completed.
Now, to condemn Shāng Yāng because Qín perished at the hands of Zhào Gāo
is like blaming Yī Yǐn for Chóng Hǔ's violence that brought chaos to Shāng."
Wénxué said:
“A skilled mortiser can build a house whose pillars, once set, cannot be uprooted;
a master of foundations can raise heights that
never collapse.
Yī Yǐn used the way of Yáo and Shùn as the foundation of the Yīn state;
his descendants succeeded one another,
the line unbroken for a hundred generations.
Shāng Yāng made severe punishments and harsh laws the foundation of the Qín state;
thus, by the second generation, it was overthrown.
When punishments had become severe and harsh,
mutual-implication laws were instituted,
slanders fabricated,
mutilating punishments increased,
and the people trembled in fear,
taking no action nor knowing what to do.
When taxes and levies had already become frequent and burdensome,
restrictions were placed on the mountains and lakes outside,
excessive profits imposed within,
so the people had neither room for explanation nor freedom of speech.
Profit was esteemed while righteousness was ignored,
strength was prized and achievements revered;
though territory was widely annexed and lands advanced,
yet it was as with one stricken by dropsy—
the more water is added, the deeper the illness becomes.
Such men knew this as the foundation of Qín’s imperial enterprise,
but did not realize it was the path to Qín’s downfall.
In fox-burrow mortising,
even Gōngshū Zǐ could not fit the tenon well.
In building foundations with sand,
even a fine craftsman cannot make it high.
It is like autumn tumbleweed touched by frost—
when the wind comes, it scatters;
even if there were ten Zǐ Chǎn,
what could they do?
Thus Biǎn Què could not put flesh on bare bone,
and Wēi and Jī could not preserve a doomed state.”
The Dàfū said:
“Speaking is not difficult;
it is putting words into action that is hard.
So the worthy reside in reality and actualize results;
they do not simply emptyly declaim rhetoric.
In ancient times, Lord Shāng (Shāng Jūn) was clear in opening and sealing strategies,
made use of the authority of his age,
brought Qín profit and established its achievements,
and thus triumphed in war and captured territory,
annexed nearby states and destroyed those far away,
overwhelmed Yān and Zhào,
overawed Qí and Chǔ,
the various feudal lords stood with arms crossed,
turning west and looking up in awe.
Afterward,
Mèng Tián campaigned against the Hú,
expanding the territory by a thousand li,
crossing north of the Yellow River,
as if breaking down rotted wood.
Why was this?
It was due to Lord Shāng’s enduring strategies,
thoroughly prepared and long cultivated.
Thus, every undertaking brought profit,
every movement produced merit.
Accumulating resources and devising stratagems—
these are the sources of the strength of states.
So, letting go and neglecting these, returning power to the people,
is not to see major plans nor to tread the great Way.”
Wénxué said:
“The opening and sealing strategies of Shāng Yāng
certainly were implemented;
Mèng Tián’s expulsion of the Hú for a thousand li
certainly had merit;
their power shook all under Heaven,
their strength was unassailable;
the feudal lords turned west in submission,
certainly they complied.
Yet all this was exactly what brought Qín to ruin.
Shāng Yāng, by cunning and calculation, jeopardized the state of Qín;
Mèng Tián, by annexing a thousand li, brought ruin to Qín’s ancestral temple.
These two,
knew profit but not harm,
advance but not retreat,
so in the end, both perished and the multitude was defeated.
This is what is called the cleverness of clutching at a corner,
but the calculation of a fool;
where is there any great Way in it?
Thus it is said:
‘The petty man first conforms then opposes;
at first, though riding a horse,
he will, in the end, surely weep tears of blood.’
This is what is meant.”
The Dàfū said:
“A virtuous and comely woman
is envied by Qī Shī;
a worthy and wise official
is hated by Xì Róng.
Thus, Grand Master Shànguān slandered Qū Yuán to King Qǐng Xiāng;
Gōngbó Liáo accused Zǐ Lù before Jì Sūn.
Lord Shāng rose from humble origins,
entered Qín from Wèi,
became chancellor within a year,
reformed the laws and clarified instructions,
thus, the people of Qín were well governed.
Consequently, when the army moved, territory was annexed;
when the troops rested, the state grew rich.
Duke Xiào was greatly pleased,
and enfeoffed him at Shāng, giving him lands five hundred li square.
His achievements were like mountains,
his name passed down to later ages.
Yet people of the time could not emulate him,
so they banded together, envied his talent, and disparaged his merits.”
Wénxué said:
“The gentleman advances always by the Way,
retires without losing righteousness,
is high without arrogance,
toils without self-congratulation,
when holding high position, acts with humility,
when achieving great deeds, governs with order.
Therefore, the people do not begrudge his talents,
nor does the world envy his enterprise.
Yet Shāng Yāng abandoned the Way in favor of power,
discarded virtue and relied upon force,
cleared the laws and augmented punishments,
made cruelty the custom,
betrayed old friends for achievement,
punished his own clan to establish authority,
showed no kindness to the people,
no trust to feudal lords,
others bore him enmity,
households became his foes;
though thereby he gained merit and was enfeoffed,
it was like eating poisoned meat—enjoying fullness, yet suffering disaster.
Sū Qín united the vertical and horizontal alliances,
ruled the Six States;
his undertaking was not insignificant.
Jié and Zhòu are spoken of alongside Yáo and Shùn,
down to this day, their line endures;
their names are not short-lived.
Yet such things are not really worth esteeming.
Therefore, examples from the past should not be carelessly multiplied,
nor names passed down lightly.”
The Dàfū said:
“White silk cannot distinguish itself among black,
nor can sages and worthies maintain clarity amid a chaotic age.
Thus, Jī Zǐ was imprisoned,
Bǐ Gān was executed.
Wǔ Yuán served as prime minister to Hélǚ, bringing him to dominance;
but when Fū Chāi lost the Way,
he was driven out and killed.
Yuè Yì earned the trust of King Zhāo of Yān by his achievements,
and yet was suspected by King Huì.
Ministers exhaust their efforts in pursuit of fame,
and still suffer the neglect of their rulers.
Grandee Zhòng aided and supported King of Yuè,
devised profound strategies for him,
finally captured powerful Wú,
occupied the Eastern Barbarians,
yet in the end received only a death by sword.
An arrogant ruler turns his back on kindness,
listens to slanders,
and pays no heed to loyal service;
how is it the minister’s fault?”
Wénxué said:
“Bǐ Gān had his heart cut out,
Zǐ Xū’s body was cast into the river;
it was not that they lightly offended their lords and courted disaster,
but rather that, compelled by loyalty, they remonstrated and thus gained a name.
Such mournful sincerity
stirred their hearts within,
making them forget the disasters that would come from without;
their purpose was to correct their rulers and save the people,
so they died with no regret.
The gentleman may act rightly but cannot escape slander,
even should he perish under punishment,
it is not his own crime.
Thus, Bǐ Gān died and the people of Yīn resented it;
Zǐ Xū died and the people of Wú mourned.
Now the people of Qín hate Shāng Yāng’s laws
even more than a private enmity;
so, at the death of Duke Xiào,
the whole state attacked him,
and east, west, south, north—he had nowhere to flee.
Looking to Heaven, he sighed, saying:
‘Alas!
The abuses of governance
have come to this extreme!’
In the end, he was torn apart by chariots, his clan exterminated,
a laughingstock for all under Heaven.
This man caused his own death,
it was not done by others.”
2.2 "Cháo Cuò, Chapter Eight"
The Dàfū said:
“According to the law of the *Chūnqiū*,
neither a lord nor a parent shall lead troops;
if they do, they must be executed.
For a minister, no crime is heavier than slaying his lord;
for a son, none heavier than killing his father.
In recent days,
Huáinán and Héngshān cultivated learning and literature,
inviting wandering scholars from all directions.
The Confucians and Mohists of Shāndōng all gathered between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
engaging in lectures and discussions,
and composing dozens of treatises.
Yet in the end, they turned against righteousness and acted as disloyal subjects,
fomenting plots of rebellion,
bringing execution upon their whole clan.
Cháo Cuò reformed laws and altered the established norms,
disregarding proper systems,
pressuring and constraining the imperial clan,
encroaching upon and diminishing the various lords.
The feudal ministers did not submit,
kin were not on good terms,
Wú and Chǔ harbored deep resentment.
Cháo Cuò was beheaded at the eastern market,
to console the soldiers of the three armies and apologize to the feudal lords.
Who was it, then, that killed him?"
The Learned Scholar replied:
"Kǒngzǐ would not drink from the waters of the Thieves' Spring;
Zēngzǐ would not enter the lane of Shèngmǔ.
Their names alone abhorred it,
how much less would they be disloyal subjects or unfilial sons?
Thus Kǒngzǐ bathed and then went to court,
reporting this to Āigōng.
Chén Wénzǐ had ten teams of horses,
yet he abandoned them and left.
The *Tradition* says:
'A gentleman may be honored or humbled,
may be punished or put to death,
but must not be made to join in disorder.'
As for those who outwardly adorn their appearance but lack substance within,
reciting the texts by mouth but not acting in accordance with the Way,
these are thieves,
and with thieves cannot belong within the domain of gentlemen.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* do not endorse the few attacking the many;
the principle of executing and severing has its limits,
and does not extend to shared grievances or universal hatred.
Therefore, the one whom Shùn punished
was Gǔn;
the one he promoted
was Yǔ.
To reject the unblemished for a flaw in the jade,
and abandon the whole for a single defect,
to use the crime of one man
as grounds to punish the many,
then under Heaven there would be no precious treasures or trustworthy men.
Cháo Sheng says that the territories of the feudal lords are large,
so when rich they become arrogant and extravagant;
when threatened they quickly ally.
Thus, the error of Wú was taken as an excuse to reduce them to Kuàijī,
and the crime of Chǔ as cause to seize their lands by Dōnghǎi—
these were to balance the light and the heavy,
to divide their power,
and to provide for the concerns of the ages.
Xuán Gāo was born in Qín but trusted in Zhèng,
Cháo Sheng was loyal to Hàn but counted as a foe among the lords.
Each minister dies for his own lord,
serves his own country;
this is why Jiě Yáng was honored in Jìn and slighted in Jīng."
2.3 "On Criticizing Power, Chapter Nine"
The Dàfū said:
"Now as for Jùqū of Yuè,
Yúnmèng of Chǔ,
Jùyè of Sòng,
Mèngzhū of Qí—
they have the wealth of states and the resources of hegemons.
If the ruler unites and defends them, they are strong;
if he does not restrict them, they are lost.
Qí gave away its own innards,
so though its households were strong, they were out of control;
the branches grew large and snapped the trunk,
for they monopolized the resources of the Great Sea and controlled the profits from fish and salt.
Their power was sufficient to command the masses,
their benevolence enough to soothe the lower ranks—
thus, within Qí the population multiplied and abroad others joined.
Power shifted to the ministers,
government fell into the hands of families,
the royal house was humbled while the Tián clan grew strong.
There were as many as three thousand war-chariots rolling to the sea,
having lost control at the root so the branches could not be saved.
Now, the resources of mountains, rivers, seas, and marshes
are not limited only to Yúnmèng and Mèngzhū.
Wherever salt is boiled and metal worked,
those places are bound to be deep in remote valleys
where the people seldom go.
Rogues and traitors move to and from the borders between mountains and seas,
and great crimes may arise.
Seizing profits brings about arrogance and excess,
dispersion of the simple increases falseness,
so those who value the root are few.
The imperial officials in charge of salt and iron—Xiányáng, Kǒng Jǐn and others—submitted a proposal:
'Let us recruit the people to manage their own costs,
use the government’s implements,
so they may boil salt for our use,
thereby blocking the avenues of fraud.'
From this it can be seen:
the intentions of the law, though slight,
are well anticipated by the officials."
The Learned Scholar replied:
"Though the officials’ calculations are far-sighted,
the profit to the powerful families lies close at hand.
Though the law’s prohibitions are slight,
the ways of arrogance and luxury are manifest.
From the rise of profit and harm,
and the establishment of the three industries,
the noble houses,
move among the clouds in the thoroughfares,
their carriages collide on the roads,
they encroach on public laws,
expand their private benefits,
straddle mountain and marsh,
seize the government markets.
This is not only the fish and salt of the Great Sea;
they hold the levers of state,
and exercise power throughout the land—
not only the power of Tián Cháng or supporting ministers;
their authority outweighs the six ministers,
their wealth surpasses Táo
and Wèi; their vehicles and attire rival princes,
their mansions overflow regulations,
they swallow up contiguous estates,
cut off neighborhoods and lanes,
their towers and roads crisscross together
sufficient for pleasure outings,
their pools are dug and paths are winding
sufficient to gallop and chase;
fishing beside deep pools,
letting loose dogs and running hares,
nurturing ferocious animals and fighting cocks,
playing ball and holding cockfights,
fair Central Plains girls stroke the pipes atop the hall,
Ba and Yú drums sound below;
wives and concubines are clad in fine silk,
female servants trail long gauze and hemp;
sons and grandsons ride in carriages and process in ranks,
going in and out to hunt;
armored archers move swiftly and skillfully.
Thus the farmers lay down their plows and no longer toil,
the people’s hearts cool and they grow indolent.
Why is this?
They labor, but others profit;
arrogance and excess are imitated,
so extravagance rises without cease.
This is why the people increasingly turn to fraud and seldom return to their roots."
The Dàfū said:
"Those who hold high office have ample stipends,
just as trees with healthy roots have flourishing branches.
Thus King Wén possessed virtue and his descendants were enfeoffed,
the Duke of Zhōu was minister and Bóqín was wealthy.
Where water is broad, fish are big;
where the father is honored, the son is esteemed.
The *Tradition* says:
'The Yellow River and the sea moisten a thousand miles.'
Great virtue reaches across the four seas,
how much more so one’s wife and children?
Therefore, when a man is honored at court,
his wife is esteemed in the house;
the wealthy are called beautiful,
such was the Way of the ancients.
*Mencius* says:
'The princes' sons are like others,
yet those are made so
by where they reside.'
Those who dwell among the common households,
yet hope for the fortunes of ministers’ descendants,
is like a lame man wanting to reach the towers of Jī;
having no money but wishing for treasures worth a thousand pieces of gold
—is this not but empty longing?"
The Learned Scholar replied:
"Yǔ and Jì began as men of humble origins,
yet were concerned lest any under Heaven should fail to find their proper place,
as if they had pushed them into a ditch;
therefore, they arose to assist Yáo,
brought order to water and soil,
and taught the people to sow and reap.
Such was the weight they assigned themselves regarding all under Heaven;
could it be said they accepted emoluments merely to nourish their wives and children?
He who eats the strength of ten thousand men
bears their worries,
endures their labor.
If a single man fails in his duty,
if a single office is not well-administered,
all the ministers and nobles are at fault.
Thus, when a gentleman enters office,
he acts with righteousness,
not for the love of power.
He accepts salary to enrich the worthy,
not to monopolize the profit.
On meeting the worthy he does not hide them,
on receiving the stipend he does not claim it solely for himself—
thus, Gōngshū was called a man of letters,
and Lord Chéng of Wèi was called a worthy.
Therefore, only when King Wén’s virtue was completed were his descendants enfeoffed,
and all under Heaven did not call it partiality;
only when the Duke of Zhōu’s merit was complete did he receive reward,
and all under Heaven did not consider him greedy.
Now, however, it is not so.
Relatives promote one another,
factions raise each other up,
the father is honored in office,
the son is overflowing within the household,
the husband is esteemed at court,
the wife goes forth to seek favor outside.
They possess the wealth of Zhōu Gōng without his virtue,
the extravagance of Guǎn Zhòng without his achievements,
thus even crippled men among the common people are expected to walk swiftly.
2.4 “Satirical Rebuttal, Tenth Chapter”
The Dàfū, proud of his appearance yet uneasy at heart,
said:
“Those who merely dwell at ease do not know the toil of those who bear burdens,
and those who comment from the side are anxious in ways different from those directly involved.
Now, holding the position at the heart of the empire, presiding over a commandery,
with all the feudal lords gathering in attendance,
yet inside and outside are not at peace,
my heart is restless as if crossing a great river,
caught by the wind but not yet reaching the shore.
Therefore, I think of the needs of the state by day and night,
lying awake, forgetting to sleep,
hungry, forgetting to eat,
endless calculations remain before me,
ten thousand matters are sorted in my mind.
The subordinate clerks are small in ability,
not fit to join in planning,
I am left alone to bear the burden of the great Way,
yearning for talent and learning to appear,
as if awaiting Zhōu, Shào and hoping for worthy sons.
The censors inspect affairs in commanderies and principalities,
investigating honesty and recommending the worthy and talented,
so that there is no lack year by year.
Now, there are over sixty worthy and learned men assembled,
who possess the arts of the ‘Six Classics’,
give free rein to their minds and speak with utmost reasoning,
and it seems they should open light and dispel ignorance,
yet they faithfully speak of the past but are at odds with the present,
discuss antiquity but do not accord with contemporary affairs.
Is it that their intent is insufficient to know men of worth?
Or is it that many embellish their words and falsify their abilities to throw reality into confusion?
Why is it so hard to behold men of virtue?
Since Qiān Shèng and Ní Kuān, who governed the ‘Shàngshū’ and held rank above the Nine Ministers,
and those I have heard and seen chosen and recommended,
who were promoted and aided the constitution with great prominence,
yet have not seen a peerless equal,
and have established achievements for the state as outstanding officials.”
The learned scholar said:
“When the carpenter shapes wood,
he fixes his compasses and sets square, and fits tenons and mortises together.
When Master Kuǎng harmonized the five notes,
he tuned the six pitches and set the palace and commerce modes in harmony.
The craftsmen of the present age,
if they cannot fit the tenons and mortises,
then alter the compasses and squares;
if they cannot harmonize the sounds,
then change the old pitches.
Therefore, the tenons and mortises become awry and do not join,
and the notes sound discordant and lack harmony.
To uphold the compasses and squares and understand suitability,
to play the pitch flute and perceive the changes,
is the highest.
To follow custom and not act,
waiting for the right person,
is secondary.
Hence Prime Minister Cáo daily drank pure wine,
and Dàfū Ní kept his mouth closed and spoke not.
Thus, to govern great matters, one must not be overburdened,
for excess leads to chaos;
to govern small matters, one must not be negligent,
for negligence leads to failure.
The ‘Spring and Autumn Annals’ says:
‘His government is grand and outstanding,
— such can become a minister or chancellor.
His government is meticulous and exact,
— such can become a commoner.’
When the essential moral bond is not maintained,
and ritual and righteousness are not upheld,
it is the concern of the high ministers and nobles.
The documents on the desk,
the business of appointments and meetings,
are the duties of clerks and scribes.
The ‘Shàngshū’ says:
‘If the outstanding and intelligent are in office,
all officials mutually emulate,
the craftsmen labor in their seasons,
and the many magistrates are mutually harmonious.’
This means, if posts are filled with the right men,
and men are matched to their duties,
then offices are governed and not disorderly,
affairs arise and are not neglected,
scholars keep to their position,
Dàfū manage their offices,
ministers and nobles supervise and maintain the general order.
If one assigns the able, achievements come without toil;
if one relies on oneself alone, affairs fail and no merit is achieved.
When Duke Huán employed Guǎn Zhòng,
he listened and observed him closely.
Thus, the gentleman labors in seeking the worthy,
but finds ease in employing them,
how could this lead to danger?
In ancient times, when Zhōu Gōng served as chancellor,
he was modest and never haughty,
and toiled to attract the worthy of the world,
so that brilliant men filled the court,
and the talented filled his gate.
Confucius had neither rank nor title,
and yet as a commoner gathered over seventy talents,
all of them men fit to be ministers and nobles of feudal lords,
how much more one holding the dignity of the Three Dukes to nurture the scholars of the realm?
Now, with the high offices of ministers and nobles,
the fine glory and emolument,
yet failing to attract scholars,
there is as yet no means to advance the worthy.
When Yáo raised Shùn,
he honored him and gave him his daughter as wife.
When Duke Huán promoted Guǎn Zhòng,
he honored him and took him as teacher.
For the Son of Heaven to marry his daughter to a commoner,
can be called truly valuing virtue.
For a feudal lord to take a commoner as teacher,
can be called truly honoring the talented.
Therefore men of worth flocked to them as a river flows,
returning with no doubt.
Now, those in office today,
neither have the humility of Yān Zhāo before men of talent,
nor the joy in virtue as sung in ‘Lù Míng’,
but act with the mind of Zāng Wén and Zǐ Jiāo,
obstructing the able and envying talent,
exalting their own wisdom,
belittling the abilities of others,
satisfied with themselves and questioning nothing,
looking down on scholars and not befriending them,
valuing rank above merit,
being arrogant to scholars for their own sake,
yet seeking their service,
this is indeed difficult!”
The Dàfū was confounded and said nothing,
while the virtuous and good men present all sighed deeply.
The censor stepped forward and said:
“Tàigōng served Wén and Wǔ, thereby ruling the realm;
Guǎn Zhòng served Duke Huán and made him hegemon over the feudal lords.
Thus, when the worthy obtain office,
it is as dragons gaining water,
soaring serpents roaming through the mist.
Gōngsūn Chancellor persuaded the late Emperor with the ‘Spring and Autumn Annals’,
and was rapidly promoted to the Three Dukes,
holding the ranks of Zhōu and Shào,
commanding power over ten thousand li,
and set the standard for the whole world;
his garments did not have overlapping colors,
his food did not combine many flavors,
he placed the world first,
yet this brought no benefit to governance.
Scholars such as Chǔ Tài and Xú Yǎn,
in receipt of imperial orders,
established credentials and rushed by post,
making inspections in commanderies and principalities,
recommending the filial and honest,
exhorting the common people,
yet the customs below did not change.
They summoned and raised men of virtue, uprightness, and learning,
swiftly promoting them to office and rank,
some reaching the status of ministers and great officers,
but was this not like Yān Zhāo recommending talents,
or King Wén widely seeking the worthy?
Yet still achievements and success are unseen.
Surely it is because these are not men of dragon and serpent talent,
even though the ‘Lù Míng’ delighted in virtuous men.”
The learned scholar said:
“Ice and charcoal cannot be kept in the same vessel,
nor can sun and moon shine together.
In the time of Gōngsūn Hóng,
the ruler’s attention was set on planning strategies with thought of the four directions,
thus schemes of trickery and cunning advanced,
and men from Jīng and Chǔ were employed,
so that generals and marshals sometimes were enfeoffed and given fiefs,
and all who accomplished deeds of war received great rewards,
thus men of force and valor flourished thereby.
Thereafter,
war and strife did not cease,
armies were dispatched endlessly,
armored soldiers wore out and suffered,
state finances ran short,
so ministers who designed dangerous enterprises and sought profit emerged,
and men like the bears and tigers of Pánxī retired into obscurity.
The rivers Jīng and Wèi were channeled to facilitate grain transport,
Dōngguō Xiányáng and Kǒng Jǐn established the salt and iron monopolies,
setting up various profitable ventures,
so that the wealthy could buy rank and sell offices,
escape punishments and be absolved of crimes;
public offices multiplied and those within sought only their own interests,
those above and those below alike were in pursuit,
The common people cannot endure it,
so they root out abuses and follow the law;
thus ministers who are harsh and urgent rise to prominence,
and discriminatory, exclusionary laws are established.
Those like Dù Zhōu and Xián Xuān
value severe statutes and quick resolutions,
while followers of Wáng Wēnshū become infamous for striking and killing like hawks and falcons.
Those who would rely on benevolence and righteousness to serve their lord are few,
while those who deceitfully blend in to gain favor are many.
To depend on a single Gōngsūn Hóng alone,
what will become of it?”
2.5 “Discourse on the Ru, Chapter Eleven”
The Imperial Censor said:
“Scholars reverently emulate Zhòng Ní,
praising his virtue,
saying that from antiquity to today
there has never been his equal.
Yet Confucius cultivated the Way between Lǔ and Wèi,
teaching and transforming by the Zhū and Sì rivers.
His disciples did not bring change,
and his age was not governed well,
while the decline of the state of Lǔ only increased.
King Xuān of Qí promoted Ru scholars and esteemed learning,
and disciples like Mèng Kē and Chúnyú Kūn
received the salaries of senior ministers,
but held no office and merely debated state affairs.
There were over a thousand gentlemen of the Jìxià Academy in Qí at the time.
At such a time,
it was not just Gōngsūn Hóng alone.
Weak Yān attacked Qí,
driving straight on to Línzī,
where King Mǐn fled,
perishing at Jǔ and unable to save his country;
King Jiàn was captured by Qín,
taken prisoner along with the others and unable to survive.
Thus,
despite Ru scholars’ assertions of stabilizing the state and honoring the sovereign,
there has never in fact been any real effect.”
The Scholar said:
“Without whip and spur,
even Zào Fù could not control a team of four horses.
Without authority or position,
even Shùn or Yǔ could not govern ten thousand people.
Confucius said:
‘The phoenix does not come,
the Yellow River yields no chart:
I am done for!’
Therefore, with a fine chariot and good horses,
one cannot race without a road;
with sagely virtue, benevolence and righteousness,
there is nowhere to apply them.
In the times of Kings Wēi and Xuān of Qí,
the virtuous and worthy advanced,
the state grew rich and strong,
and its prestige reached enemy states.
By the time of King Mǐn,
he continued the last embers of former glory,
expanding south to Chǔ and Huái,
annexing great Sòng to the north,
embracing twelve states,
crushing the Three Jìn in the west,
holding back powerful Qín,
with five states coming as vassals,
while the rulers of Zōu and Lǔ,
and all the lords along the Sì River, became his ministers.
Yet boasting and not resting on merit,
the people could not bear it.
When the Ru remonstrated and were ignored,
each dispersed;
Shèn Dào and Jié Zǐ fled and departed;
Tián Pián went to Xuē,
and Sūn Qīng departed to Chǔ.
Without worthy ministers at home,
the feudal lords united in alliance and attacked.
King Jiàn listened to vagrant persuasion,
believed in spy reports,
adopted the queen’s stratagems,
did not join the lords in kinship,
and thus lost the state.
He was captured by Qín—
was this not to be expected?”
The Imperial Censor said:
“Yī Yǐn, by preparing sacrificial meat, served Tāng;
Bǎi Lǐ, by herding cattle, gained access to Duke Mù;
they might have begun with unworthy means,
but once trusted, truly joined with them to achieve overlordship.
Thus,
what words went unheeded?
What ways were untried?
Once Lord Shāng by royal ways advised Duke Xiào,
but when not accepted,
then by the way of strengthening the state,
ultimately achieved success.
Zōu Zǐ employed Ru doctrines to approach the rulers,
but when rejected,
he instead expounded views on the transformations of beginning and end,
ultimately winning renown.
A horse may run a thousand li,
yet need not come from Hú or Dài;
a scholar is valued for achievements,
not only for rhetoric.
Mèng Kē clung to old teachings,
not understanding the affairs of the world,
so he was troubled in Liáng and Sòng.
Confucius was upright but not accommodating,
so he starved at Líqiū.
If the Ru of today, despite their pursuit of virtue,
sometimes lack resources,
it is said their doctrines are wrong,
and so are not put into practice.
From the Zhōu house till now,
over a thousand years,
only Wén, Wǔ, Chéng, and Kāng
were models, as if one must always participate,
praising what is unreachable,
like a cripple speaking of distance yet unable to walk.
The sages may take different roads but reach the same goal,
sometimes advancing, sometimes holding back;
their aims are one.
Though Lord Shāng reformed the law and changed the teachings,
his intent was to strengthen the state and benefit the people.
Zōu Zǐ’s writings
