and doctrines of transformation
also ended in benevolence and righteousness.
Jì Zhòng, by self-deprecation, wielded authority
because of the times.
Therefore, a small wrong may secure a great right—
the gentleman does so.
Now, rigidly keeping to a single path
and taking inspiration from Wěi Shēng’s sincerity,
one may fault Duke Wén of Jìn for deceiving the feudal lords to honor the Zhou house, which is not worth discussing,
or blame Guǎn Zhòng for enduring humiliation to save the state, but this is not commendable.”
The Scholar said:
“When Yī Yǐn served Tāng,
he recognized a sagely king.
When Bǎi Lǐ went to Qín,
he recognized an enlightened ruler.
That these two could recognize a hegemon
was because they saw clear signs
and did not make decisions in darkness or confusion.
Confucius said:
‘If names are not correct, words are not appropriate;
if words are not appropriate, affairs are not accomplished.’
How could one form expedient unions and so achieve overlordship?
The gentleman upholds virtue and grasps righteousness in action,
thus, in haste he remains consistent,
and in distress he remains consistent.
Mencius said:
‘Dwelling at court in the present age,
without changing customs,
even having the power of a thousand chariots,
cannot secure even a morning’s place.’
It is better to be poor and hungry in a humble lane
than to alter oneself and follow vulgar ways.
When Hé Lú killed Liáo,
Prince Zhā withdrew to Yánlíng,
and never again entered the state of Wú for life.
When Duke of Lǔ killed Zǐchì,
Shū Miǎn retired in seclusion,
not accepting its stipend.
To compromise righteousness for honor,
to bend principle for acceptance—
devotion unto death would never do such a thing.
To hear the correct way is unheeded
and so withdraw from office—
I have yet to hear of one seeking acceptance by crooked ways.”
The Imperial Censor said:
“The Analects says:
‘If among relatives there are those who do wrong,
the gentleman does not enter their household.’
If that was said, then conduct can be inconsistent.
The Jì family governed without principle,
drove out their ruler,
usurped his power,
yet Rǎn Qiú and Zhòng Yóu served them.
The Rites says:
‘Men and women should not pass objects directly,
nor drink together from the same goblet.’
When Confucius visited Wèi,
he relied on the favorite Mí Zǐxiá to gain audience with Lady of Wèi,
and Zǐlù was displeased.
Mí Zǐxiá,
a flattery-seeking minister,
was used by the Master,
which was not correct.
Men and women should not mix,
yet Confucius met with Nánzǐ,
which was not in accord with propriety.
If rites and righteousness come from the house of Kǒng,
then even he made compromises to gain favor—
where, then, is evidence of resigning from office over principle?”
The Scholar said:
“When the world is unsettled,
and the feudal states disturbed,
that is the anxiety of a wise king.
Above there is no Son of Heaven,
below, no regional governors;
under Heaven all is in turmoil,
which is the sorrow of the worthy and sagely.
Therefore, Yáo worried about the great flood,
Yī Yǐn worried for the people,
Guǎn Zhòng was constrained,
Kǒngzǐ roamed the lands,
all out of concern for the people's disasters and a desire to secure them from peril.
Thus they bore tripods and sacrificial vessels on their backs, endured imprisonment and bondage, crawled on their bellies to save the people.
Therefore, those who pursue the lost hasten on,
those who save the drowning get themselves wet.
Now that the people have fallen into ditches and ravines,
even if one wishes to avoid getting wet,
how could it be helped?
The Censor remained silent and did not respond.
2.6 "On Worrying about the Frontier, Chapter Twelve"
The Dàfū said:
The Scholar said:
" 'When all under Heaven is unsettled,
and vassal states are unstable,
this is the worry of an enlightened king.'
Therefore, the king in regard to the world
is like the head of a household,
if there is one person in the household unsettled,
it is said none are joyful.
Thus, if the people are drifting or drowning and are not saved,
he is no beneficent ruler.
If the state faces difficulty and is not worried,
he is no loyal minister.
To keep one's integrity and die in adversity
is the duty of a subject;
to provide food and clothing against hunger and cold
is the way of a loving father.
Now, when sons and younger brothers labor far away,
the ruler worries for them day and night,
all officials exhaust their strength and counsel,
records increase the expenditure of the state.
Therefore, the Assistant to the Minor Treasury requests the establishment of a wine monopoly
to supply the border,
to provide for soldiers,
to rescue the people from hardship.
Those who are fathers and elder brothers,
how could they cease in such actions?
Examining within, to provide food and clothing and care for those abroad,
is still not sufficient;
now, if one even wishes to abolish all expenditures,
and reduce the funds for the frontier,
such a one cannot be called a kind father or worthy elder brother."
The Scholar said:
"At the end of the Zhou,
the Son of Heaven was weak,
the feudal lords ruled by force,
thus the state rulers were insecure,
and their counselors rushed about.
Why was this?
Because enemy states were many and the altars of state in peril.
Now the Nine Provinces share the same territory,
all under Heaven is unified,
Your Majesty enjoys leisure in the palace halls,
listens to his officials' thorough arguments and highest counsel,
recites the Odes and Hymns within,
and the harmonious bells sound without,
pure virtue shines forth,
akin to Táng and Yú,
and feats and achievements flow down to your descendants.
As for the peoples of Mán and Mò,
and unproductive lands,
how could they be worth the trouble of worry,
and give rise to the anxiety of the Warring States period?
If Your Majesty does not abandon them,
but applies virtue,
and extends beneficence,
the Northern Barbarians will surely turn toward the interior,
and come to open the borders of their own accord.
Then, using their chieftains as external subjects,
the Xiōngnú would even till death never use what we use."
The Dàfū said:
"The sagely sovereign contemplates the insecurity of Zhōngguó,
and the instability of the northern frontier,
and thus asks the Retired Chief Judge and others to inquire about the sufferings among the people.
To rescue and care for the poor and humble,
to provide for those in want.
What all the officials proclaim of the enlightened king's virtue
in securing the realm,
has not yet reached its proper order,
therefore they consult the scholars.
If the scholars' counsel does not reach the heavens, it falls into the abyss;
now, they wish to apply the order of villages and alleys,
how much less for the great affairs of the state—
such are hardly sufficient!
Words spoken from the ditches and fields,
views arising from secluded lanes,
ignorant of the coldness of ice and water,
like one drunken and newly asleep,
truly not worth discussing with."
The Scholar said:
"The method to secure the people and enrich the state
lies in returning to the root;
when the root is established, the Way arises.
By following Heaven's order,
and utilizing the advantages of the land,
then, without labor, achievements are attained.
If one does not cultivate the source but attends solely to the current,
lacking fundamentals to unify all,
even if spirit is exhausted
and thought is fully spent,
it brings no benefit to governance.
The desire to secure them is just enough to endanger them;
efforts to save them just enough to bring ruin.
The origins of order and disorder
lie solely in root and branch;
the Way can be attained without exhausting the mind.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'He who does not understand debate finds it hard to discuss governance;
with those whose Ways differ,
do not consult together.'
Now, the intentions of the high ministers lean upon their supports;
therefore the words of the scholars
cannot be employed."
The Dàfū said:
"I have heard: a subject must fulfill loyalty to be properly employed,
a son must exert filial piety to inherit.
If the ruler is at fault,
his minister must cover it;
if the father errs,
his son must hide and avoid it.
Therefore, when the ruler dies,
the minister does not change his government;
when the father dies,
the son does not alter his father's Way.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticize the destruction of ancestral tombs
as it destroys what the ancestors established
and spreads the faults of ruler and father.
As for the monopoly on salt and iron and regulated transport,
these have existed for long;
to attempt to abolish them,
would this not harm the deeds of the former emperor
and hinder the virtue of the sagely sovereign?
The administrators rely upon the path of loyalty and filiality,
this Way is different and unlike the counsel of the scholars."
The Scholar said:
"The enlightened change with the times,
the wise adapt their measures to the age.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'A hempen hat
is the ritual,
but now, a silk one is more frugal;
I follow the majority.'
Therefore, the sage esteems the worthy above without departing from antiquity,
and accommodates custom below without leaning to one side.
Dìng Gōng of Lǔ ordered the ancestral sequence,
following ancestral succession;
Duke Zhāo abolished the ministers
to simplify affairs and economize expenditures;
one cannot say thereby that the knowledge of ancestors was altered or the father's Way was changed.
The Second Emperor built the great Epang Palace to continue the line,
Zhào Gāo added to and multiplied Qín's laws for greater power,
yet neither can be called a loyal subject or filial son."
3.1 "On Parks and Pools, Chapter Thirteen"
The Dàfū said:
"The feudal lords regarded their states as homes,
and their worries were internal.
The Son of Heaven took the Eight Extremities as boundaries,
and his concerns lay outside.
So those with small domains use little,
those with great achievements use much.
Thus, officialdom opens parks and pools,
controls mountains and seas,
draws benefits to assist in tribute and taxes,
repairs channels and ditches,
establishes state farms,
expands fields and pastures,
fills the gardens and hunting reserves.
The Grand Coachman, Director of Weights and Measures, Minor Treasury, and Grand Minister of Agriculture
all annually assess profits from fields and flocks,
rent of pools and enclosures,
and appoint officials to manage border fields in the north,
to supply all needs,
and yet still it is not enough.
Now it is proposed to abolish these,
sever the sources,
cut off the flow,
so that both the high and low are exhausted,
and poverty and want must result.
Though it is well to simplify affairs and economize expenditures,
how could this be acceptable?"
The Scholar said:
"In ancient times,
land was apportioned so as to support the people,
and the people were sufficient to sustain their superiors.
A state with a thousand chariots,
lands of a hundred li,
the ranks of gōng, hóu, bó, zǐ, nán,
each adequately supplied to meet their needs and wants.
Qín united the lands of ten thousand states,
possessed the wealth of all within the seas,
yet its desires were not satisfied;
not because its lands were small and its expenditures little,
but because its appetites were many, and the lower people could not bear its demands.
It is said:
“There is rotting meat in the kitchen,
there are starving people in the state,
there are fat horses in the stables,
and hungry men on the roads.”
Now, the care given to dogs and horses
and the food for insects and beasts—
how could it be merely the expenses for rotting meat and fat horses!
Useless offices,
unimportant projects,
the excesses of extravagant attire,
and the many who eat and are clothed by government without merit—
this is why the upper classes find their resources insufficient and the lower classes are left destitute.
Now, without reducing these root problems but wishing to supply the branches,
setting up mechanisms for profit,
developing fields and livestock,
competing with the people for hay and fodder,
contending with merchants for market profits—
this is not how an enlightened ruler shows virtue or assists the state.
Men plow, women weave—
this is the great enterprise of the world.
Thus, the ancients divided the land for people to settle
and assigned fields and plots for them to work.
Therefore, in their enterprises, there was no land where one could not eat,
no citizen lacking work.
Now, the government has spread out many parks, official fields, ponds, and marshes;
the state holds nominal control,
but the profits go to the powerful families.
In the Three Fǔ, pressed against the mountains and rivers,
the land is narrow and the people many,
all the regions come together,
grain, firewood, and vegetables
cannot support each other.
Official fields are transferred and leased;
mulberry, elm, vegetables, and fruit are not cultivated;
the productivity of the land is not fully realized.
In my humble opinion, this is wrong.
As for the late emperor opening up parks,
ponds, and enclosures,
these could be apportioned to the people,
with the officials only levying rent and taxes.
Whether called rent or tax, the reality is the same.
If this is done,
the labor of each man
will be exhausted in the southern fields,
the strength of each woman
will be spent on hemp and ramie.
The fields are opened,
fibers processed,
then both upper and lower prosper,
so how could there be any poverty or want?”
The dàfū fell silent,
looking to his chancellor and censors.
3.2 “On Light and Heavy, Chapter Fourteen”
The censor advanced and said:
“In ancient times, Tài Gōng was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
cleared the unbroken grasslands and dwelt there.
The land was poor and the people few,
so he opened the way for profit through commerce,
and greatly advanced the skills of women’s crafts.
Thus, neighboring states interacted with Qí,
wealth accumulated and goods thrived,
generation after generation becoming a strong state.
Guǎn Zhòng assisted Duke Huán,
inherited the achievements of past rulers,
implemented the system of regulating value,
brought strong Chǔ under submission in the south and became hegemon among the lords.
Now, you, Dàfū, follow the methods of Tài Gōng, Huán, and Guǎn,
unifying salt and iron,
opening up the profits of mountains and rivers so that all things are made abundant.
Therefore, the government has ample resources,
the people are not impoverished,
both root and branch prosper,
both high and low are well provided,
these are the results of careful planning,
not merely the outcomes of farming and raising silkworms.”
The scholar said:
“Rites and righteousness
are the foundation of a state,
and manipulation of power and profit
are the ruin of government.
Confucius said:
‘Can one rule a state by ritual propriety and yielding?
What difficulty is there!’
Yī Yǐn and Tài Gōng raised their lords with but a hundred li;
Guǎn Zhòng devoted himself to Duke Huán,
ruled a thousand-chariot Qí,
yet could not attain kingship;
what they pursued was wrong.
So their achievements were destroyed and the Way failed to prevail.
At that time,
none of the feudal lords could govern by virtue,
but all competed for public profit,
therefore using expediency to undermine one another.
Now the world is unified as one family;
how could the evils of profit-seeking continue?
How could the excesses of crafty skills be applied?
You, Dàfū, plan government affairs with your mind,
form alliances among the lords,
impose wine monopolies,
Xiányáng and Kǒng Jǐn add further salt and iron,
Jiāng Chōng, Yáng Kězhī and others,
each take a sharp edge,
discussing matters of profit and dissecting a hair’s-tip—
one may say there is no crack left unexplored.
This is not only Guǎn Zhòng establishing the nine offices
and exploiting mountains and seas.
Yet, the state is weakened,
the cities and walls lie empty.
Thus, without exalting benevolence and righteousness, one cannot transform the people;
without emphasizing agriculture, one cannot enrich the state.”
The censor said:
“Where there are wild otters in the water, the pond fish suffer;
where there are powerful oppressors in a state, the common people wither.
Thus, beneath dense forest, there is no lush grass;
among great masses, no good sprouts.
The way to govern a state
is to eliminate the impure and weed out the powerful;
only then are the people made equal
and each at peace in his home.
Zhāng Tíngwèi judged and established laws and statutes,
clarified regulations to regulate the realm,
punishing the corrupt and crafty,
cutting off those who annex and combine,
so the strong do not oppress the weak,
and the many do not bully the few.
You, Dàfū, plan and strategize,
establish national policies,
gather in the profits of salt and iron and such,
to restrain the wealthy merchants,
sell offices and redeem crimes,
reduce the surplus,
make up the lack,
thus equalizing the people.
So though troops march east and west to campaign,
taxes are not increased and expenses are met.
Such matters of reduction and increase
are discerned by the worthy,
not known by the common people.”
The scholar said:
“When Biǎn Què examines the pulse, he knows the source of illness;
when the yang energy is excessive,
he reduces it to balance the yin;
when the cold is excessive,
he reduces it to balance the yang;
thus, when the energies and pulses are harmonized,
evil influences have nowhere to lodge.
But an unskilled physician who does not grasp the veins’ interworkings
or the divisions of blood and energy,
pierces at random to no benefit,
and only injures the flesh.
Now, intending to reduce the surplus
and make up the lack,
the rich become richer,
the poor become poorer.
Applying harsh laws and trusting in punishment
is meant to prohibit violence and end crime,
yet crime does not end;
perhaps it is not the skill of Biǎn Què with needle and stone,
thus the common people have not each found their proper roles.”
The censor said:
“When the Zhōu established their realm,
there were about eighteen hundred feudal lords.
Furthermore,
the strong swallowed the weak,
the great swallowed the small,
uniting as the Six States.
The Six States fought wars and made alliances for centuries,
resisting internal enemies,
repelling the outer barbarians.
Observing this:
armor and weapons never rested,
warfare was never lacking,
armies were campaigned abroad,
yet granaries were full within.
Now, with the wealth of the entire realm,
the resources within the seas,
the tribute of a hundred commanderies,
not just the stores of Qí and Chǔ,
nor the treasuries of Zhào and Wèi,
if one were to calculate and measure inputs and outputs,
even in times of urgency,
there truly should be no resort to want.
If officials such as the Minister of Agriculture personally farmed the land by craft,
then the legacies of Hòu Jì would continue;
yet when armies campaign on all sides and supplies do not suffice,
is it that Heaven has given too little?
Is it the skill with needle and stone,
the harmonization of yin and yang,
the equalizing of plenty and want,
and making up the lack—
are these not to blame too?
Now, you, Dàfū, together with the Superintendent of Grain, oversee the Ministry of Agriculture,
moxibustion and acupuncture remove stagnation,
all channels are opened,
so myriad things circulate freely,
and the government coffers are full and sufficient.
At this time,
the four quarters were plagued by campaigns against violence and disorder,
the expenses of chariots and armor,
the rewards for those who captured and subdued enemies,
were counted by the hundreds of millions,
all supplied by the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
All this was due to the power of Biǎn Què,
and the blessings of salt and iron.”
The Learned Man said:
“The border regions are mountain dwellings and valley settlements,
where yin and yang are out of harmony;
the cold causes the ground to crack,
bitter winds scatter salt,
sand and rocks accumulate thickly,
and the terrain is fit for nothing.
The Central Realm,
the center of Heaven and Earth,
the meeting place of yin and yang,
the sun and moon pass to its south,
the Dǒu star rises to its north,
it gathers the vital energies of harmony,
and produces and nurtures all creatures.
Now to depart and invade the borders,
to take up much barren and bitterly cold land,
is like abandoning the fertile banks of the Jiāng and Huánghé Rivers,
and farming instead among mountain slopes or briny marshes.
Moving the stores of the granaries,
scattering the treasures of the government vaults,
in order to provide for the border people.
The Central Realm is distressed by labor and taxes,
the border people suffer from garrison duties.
Vigorous tilling yields no easy harvests,
there is no profit from silkworm or hemp,
they must look to the Central Realm for silk before they can clothe themselves,
their furs and hides still leave them exposed,
insufficient even to cover the body,
in summer they cannot shed their layers,
in winter they never leave their caves,
fathers and sons, husbands and wives, are shut up together in round earthen huts.
Within and without, all is empty and exhausted;
what power does Biǎn Què have?
And what blessing is there in salt and iron?”
3.3 “The Unreconciled, Chapter Fifteen”
The Censor said:
“Within the inner provinces,
the people are numerous,
but springs of water and pastures are scarce,
they cannot provide for each other;
the terrain is warm and damp,
unsuitable for oxen and horses;
the people tread the land with hoes and farm,
carry burdens as they go,
laboring with little result.
Thus the common people are poor and distressed,
and lack sufficient food and clothing;
the old and weak heave loads along the roads,
and even ministry nobles
sometimes ride in ox carts.
Emperor Xiàowǔ pacified the Bǎiyuè and made their lands into parks,
drove back the Qiāng and Hú to make preserves,
thus rare and strange things
filled the inner palace,
fine steeds of every breed
stocked the imperial stables,
every man rode strong and fine horses,
yet among the people oranges and pomelos became so common as to tire of them.
From this, we see:
the border commanderies are also rich indeed!
So why say ‘what blessings are there’?
You are not well versed in calculation.”
The Learned Man said:
“When Yǔ settled the waters and lands,
he fixed the Nine Provinces,
each region offered up its produce as tribute,
enough to fill the palaces
and meet the desires of the ruler;
fertile land stretched for ten thousand lǐ,
the advantages of rivers and mountains
enough to enrich the people,
without relying on the lands of the Mán and Mò,
or the products of distant places.
It is said that before campaigns against the Hú and Yuè,
labor and taxes were light, and the people were prosperous;
clothed warmly and fed abundantly,
storing new and old grain,
with ample cloth and silk,
and cattle and horses in herds.
Farmers plowed and carried loads with horses,
and no one was without a mount;
at that time, even surplus horses were turned out as dung stock.
Afterwards,
the army was raised repeatedly,
war-horses became scarce,
even cows and mares were driven to battle,
so calves and colts were born on the battlefield.
Livestock no longer bred at home,
grains could not be grown in the fields,
and people did not have enough even of coarse food;
so who is weary of oranges and pomelos?
The Zhuàn says:
‘When the grand army has marched,
generations do not recover.’
Now in our commanderies and kingdoms,
fields lie unplowed on the ridges,
houses in cities stand empty,
so of what richness are the border commanderies?”
The Censor said:
“In ancient times,
land was measured as one hundred paces per mǔ,
the people farmed by the well-field system,
and one-tenth was paid as tax.
Righteousness put the public before the self—
such was the people’s duty.
The former emperor, pitying the sorrow and suffering of the people,
that they lacked sufficient food and clothing,
made the mǔ two hundred and forty paces,
and set the tax at one in thirty.
Now, when the lazy do not work the fields,
and hunger and cold reach them,
it is only natural.
If one does not till but wants to sow,
does not plant but wants to harvest,
what further fault is there in salt and iron?”
The Learned Man said:
“A tenth as tax
reflects the strength of the people.
Years of plenty or famine, good and bad harvests,
are shared with the people.
If the people exert themselves,
the rulers do not enjoy the surplus alone;
if the people thrive,
the rulers do not labor alone.
Thus it is said:
‘A tenth as tax
is the right balance for the world.’
Now though the rate is one in thirty,
taxes are still assessed by fields and acres,
in years of abundance, grain is taken only sparingly,
but in years of famine, all is exacted to meet needs.
Adding conscription and corvée on top,
each person must work,
and labor is split evenly.
The farmer gives all he has,
sometimes going into debt to add more.
Thus the people toil to exhaustion,
and yet hunger and cold still strike them.
When building a city, one first reinforces the foundation before seeking height;
when nurturing the people, one first enriches their lot before seeking abundance.
The Lúnyǔ says:
‘If the people are sufficient,
how could the ruler lack?’”
The Censor said:
“In ancient times,
the feudal lords contended for power,
the warring states rose,
arms and armor were never at rest,
and the people deserted the fields.
Even so, taxes were at one-tenth,
no one neglected their duty.
Now, thanks to Your Majesty’s divine power,
arms have not been raised for long,
yet the people do not all come forth to the southern fields;
so that, by head count, the reclaimed land is insufficient,
the granaries are emptied to relieve the poor,
day by day demands grow,
and so they grow more idle, looking to the government for gain.
Those who reign thus are plagued as well,
wearing themselves out in concern for the people;
yet the people turn their backs on grace and abandon righteousness, fleeing afar,
concealing themselves from government service.
The people imitate one another and the fields grow more barren each day,
taxes and levies go unpaid,
and they resist and oppose the government.
Though the ruler would grant sufficiency,
who is there to make it sufficient?”
The Learned Man said:
“Trees cannot thrive if transplanted too many times,
beasts are ruined when forced to new lairs.
Thus the proverb: ‘the northern wind is the horse’s guide,
the flying bird circles its old nest’—
all mourn for their lives.
From this we see:
it is not for profit that people avoid government service and seek exile.
In former times,
armies were raised often,
expenses could not be met,
so property taxes and levies were collected,
always taken directly from the people,
and farming families suffered double toil.
Thus, not all came forth to the southern fields.
Overall, those in arrears and those who fled
are from the wealthy houses;
officials fear and hesitate to prosecute
and do not dare to press them harshly,
but are severe with the humble and poor,
and when the poor can no longer bear it,
they flee far away;
the middle class break away for this reason,
and the later fugitives must toil in place of those already gone;
The registering of the people’s numbers began because of corrupt officials;
thus others imitated them.
Many abandon the worse and accept the slightly better.
The Zhuàn says:
“When government is lax, the people die for it;
when government is harsh, fathers and sons are separated.”
Thus fields and lands become increasingly desolate,
and the walled cities are left empty.
The way to shepherd the people
is to remove what distresses them,
and to provide what brings them comfort;
comfort them without disturbing them,
employ them without exhausting them.
By this, the people are encouraged in their work and take joy in public taxes.
If things are this way,
then the ruler has no need for relief measures for the people,
nor do the people seek profit from the upper ranks;
upper and lower discuss matters together and songs of praise arise.
Thus, when taking from the people, they do not resent it;
when laboring, the people do not feel hardship.
As for the poem Língtái,
it was not done by someone’s command;
the people made it themselves.
If things are like this,
what could the ruler possibly lack?”
The Yùshǐ said:
“In antiquity,
at fifteen, one entered the Tàixué,
and was given minor service;
at twenty, one put on the cap and became an adult,
and was assigned to military duties;
those fifty and above,
whose blood and strength overflowed in sturdiness,
were called àizhuàng.
The Shī says:
‘Fāngshū is the old of the originals,
able to display the strength in youthfulness.’
Therefore, the military of the Shāng was like crows,
while the army of the Zhōu was like grass.
Now, Your Majesty takes pity on the common people,
and has enacted lenient policies on labor service;
assignment to taxes begins at twenty-three,
and exemption is given at fifty-six,
so as to support the robust and allow the elderly to rest.
Adult males manage their fields and neighborhoods,
the elderly repair their embankments and gardens;
economize labor and follow the seasons,
so there is no fear of hunger or cold.
If one does not manage his own household but litigates with the authorities,
this also is a contradiction.”
The Lǐxué said:
“Those under nineteen are considered shāng,
not yet adults;
at twenty, one puts on the cap;
at thirty, one marries,
and can take up military affairs;
at fifty and above, one is called àilǎo,
uses a staff at home,
and does not undertake labor service,
so as to support the weak and give rest to the elderly;
in the village drinking ceremony,
the elders have different dishes,
thus honoring the elders and illustrating the nurturing of the old.
Thus, the elderly are not satiated without meat,
are not warm without silk,
and cannot walk without a staff.
Now those fifty and above up to sixty,
along with their children and grandchildren, wear mourning garments and bear burdens,
all fulfilling corvée labor,
this is not the intention of nourishing the old.
In antiquity, when there was a great mourning,
the ruler did not call at their door for three years,
observing the way of filial piety
and allowing the heart to express grief.
What the gentleman values and exhausts himself for,
is surely the mourning of a parent!
Now sometimes corpses lie stiff,
mourning garments are cast aside for military service,
this is not acting as a parent to the people
nor following the feelings of filial piety and fraternal duty.
Zhōu Gōng cradled Chéng Wáng and listened to all beneath Heaven,
his benevolence filled all within the seas,
his grace extended to the four borders,
how much the more to those bearing the human face!
He embraced benevolence and upheld virtue,
none failed to find their place.
The Shī says:
‘Day and night laying the foundation of commands, pardoning what is hidden.’
Your Majesty flourishes in youth,
entrusts authority to ministers,
the gōng and qīng assist in governance,
but policy and teaching have not yet been made uniform,
which is why the common people discuss these things.”
The Yùshǐ was silent and did not answer.
4.1 “On Vast Territories, Chapter Sixteen”
The Dàfū said:
“A king embraces, contains, and covers all,
giving universal love without partiality,
not bestowing greater rewards for those near,
nor withholding favor from those far away.
Now all are people,
all are subjects;
but security, danger, toil, and ease are not distributed equally—
should this not be adjusted?
If one considers only this and not the other,
is this not a liking for argument?
The people along the border
dwell in lands of cold and hardship,
and withstand the peril of the fierce Hú;
when the beacons are fired even once,
they face the threat of death.
Thus the people of the border fight a hundred battles,
while those in Zhōngguó lie at ease;
they rely on the border regions as a shield and defense.
The Shī says:
‘All is king’s business,
yet I alone bear the toil.’
This is to criticize inequality.
Thus, the sage kings took upon themselves the unique hardship of all directions,
raised armies to repel the Hú and Yuè,
pacified distant enemies and settled disasters,
distributed the surplus of prosperity from Zhōngguó,
to harmonize the borderlands;
if the frontiers are strong,
then Zhōngguó is safe,
and if Zhōngguó is safe, then all is at peace.
What cause is there for silent dissatisfaction?”
The Lǐxué said:
“In antiquity,
the Son of Heaven established himself at the center of the world,
the interior commanderies measuring no more than a thousand lǐ in square length,
the feudal lords and states
did not settle lands where crops could not be grown;
Yǔgòng extended as far as five thousand lǐ;
the people each supported their own ruler,
the feudal lords each protected their own state,
thus the people were equally apportioned,
and corvée labor was not burdensome.
Now, to repel the Hú and Yuè over a thousand lǐ,
traversing circuitous and twisting roads,
the soldiers become fatigued and exhausted.
Thus, the border people face fatal disasters,
while those in Zhōngguó suffer deaths,
this is why the people are noisy and not silent.
As for the method of governing a state,
it moves from the center to the periphery,
beginning from what is near.
When those near are attached and loyal,
only then will the distant come;
when the people’s needs are met at home,
only then will they care for others abroad.
Thus, when the officials discussed whether to cultivate Lúntái,
the enlightened ruler did not permit it,
believing one should first address nearby crises and the fundamental tasks.
Thus the edict said:
‘The current matter
lies in prohibiting cruelty and oppression,
stopping arbitrary taxes,
and devoting strength to agriculture.’
The gōng and qīng should follow this intention,
proposing a reduction or removal of the unfit,
so as to help the urgent needs of the people.
Now, with the deterioration of Zhōngguó being ignored,
all effort is placed on the frontiers.
Perhaps because the land is vast but uncultivated,
there is much planting but no weeding,
labor is spent but without result;
the Shī says:
‘No land for the ploughman to till,
only weeds luxuriantly thrive.’
This is precisely what is meant.”
The Dàfū said:
“The campaigns of Tāng and Wǔ
were not motivated by a love for war;
Zhōu Xuān Wáng expanded his territory a thousand lǐ,
but not out of greed for conquest;
it was to remove bandits and settle the people.
Thus, an army without just aim
the gentleman does not employ;
land of no use
the sage king does not covet.
The Imperial Ancestor raised the army of Tāng and Wǔ
and settled the crises of the Three Borders,
confronting the enemy on one front,
making the Xiōngnú flee.
Relying on the rivers and mountains for defense,
thus abandoning sandy, rocky, salty, and barren lands where crops do not grow,
ceding the Dòubì commandery,
and giving up the land of Zàoyáng to the Hú,
consolidating defenses at Qǔsāi,
relying on the river’s natural obstacles,
guarding the vital passes,
in order to alleviate corvée labor,
and protect the soldiers and people.
Observing this,
it is evident the sage ruler’s intention
is not merely to expand territory and burden the populace.”
The Wénxué said:
"Qín's employment of troops
can be said to have reached its utmost;
Mèng Tián pushing the borders
can be said to have gone far indeed.
Now, having crossed the fortress of Mèng Tián,
and established commanderies and counties in the lands of the bandits and raiders,
the farther the land, the more the people are wearied.
West of Shuòfāng,
north of Cháng'ān,
the accomplishments of the new commanderies,
the expenses of outer fortresses,
cannot all be reckoned.
And not only this,
Sīmǎ and Táng Méng cut roads through the southwestern tribes;
Bā and Shǔ were depleted at Qióng and Zuó;
an army crossed the sea to attack the southern tribes;
tower ships guarded Dōngyuè;
Jīng and Chǔ were exhausted at Ōu and Luò;
the Left General campaigned against Cháoxiān;
opened Líntún;
Yān and Qí were troubled by Huì and Mò;
Zhāng Qiān reached remote and distant places,
but brought back nothing useful;
the contents of the treasury
flowed out to foreign countries;
it was not only the expense of battling bandits,
nor only the labors of Zàoyáng.
Considering it thus,
it is not the lord's use of mind
nor officials fond of exploits who calculate for the county offices, but miscalculation."
The Dàfū said:
"One who possesses the wisdom of Guǎn Zhòng
is not meant for menial service;
one who carries the deliberation of Táozhū
will not dwell in poverty and hardship.
The Wénxué is able to speak but unable to act;
dwelling below, he slanders those above;
living in poverty, he criticizes the rich;
he speaks grand words which are not heeded;
he aims high but acts low;
he censures and criticizes,
seeking name and reputation in the world.
Those whose salaries do not exceed what can be held in the hand
are unfit to discuss governance;
those whose households' eaves are not filled with stones
are unfit to deliberate on affairs.
All scholars are poor and weak,
their clothing and hats incomplete;
how can they know the affairs of the state,
the matters of the county offices?
What are matters of battling bandits and the labors at Zàoyáng to him!"
The Wénxué said:
"Lowly status does not harm wisdom,
nor does poverty impede conduct.
Yán Yuān was often destitute,
yet not lacking in virtue.
Kǒngzǐ was at times not accepted,
yet was not unholy.
If you must judge men by appearance,
and select scholars by talent,
then Tài Gōng would have spent his whole life chopping meat,
and Níng Qì would not have left the feeding of cattle.
The gentlemen of old
kept to the Way to establish their names;
cultivated themselves while waiting for the appropriate time;
did not change their resolve because of poverty,
nor alter their will because of humiliation;
they abided only in benevolence,
and acted only by righteousness.
To seek gain when facing wealth,
and to turn against righteousness at the sight of profit—
to be rich without righteousness,
to be honored without name—
the benevolent do not do so.
Therefore, Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Zǐ
did not exchange their benevolence for the wealth of Jìn or Chǔ;
Bó Yí did not trade his conduct for the position of the feudal lords.
Thus, even though Duke Jǐng of Qí had a thousand teams of horses,
he could not compete for renown with them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Worthy is Huí!
With one basket of food,
and one ladle of drink,
living in a narrow alley,
others could not bear such distress,
yet Huí did not change his joy.'
Thus, only the truly benevolent can dwell in straitened circumstances and find joy
in poverty; petty men, when rich, become violent,
and when poor, become dissolute.
Yángzǐ said:
'To be benevolent is not to be rich,
to be rich is not to be benevolent.'
If one always seeks profit before righteousness,
there is no end to seizing and taking.
The gōng and qīng accumulate millions,
the Dàfū accumulate thousands in gold,
the scholar hundreds,
gathering wealth for self-interest;
yet the common people are cold and bitter,
and drift destitute along the roads,
so how can scholars keep their robes and hats whole?"
4.2 "On Poverty and Wealth, Seventeenth"
The Dàfū said:
"From binding my hair and beginning my studies at age thirteen,
I was fortunate to gain a post as an attendant,
serving at the imperial court,
and rose to the status of qīng and Dàfū,
receiving salary and rewards,
for more than sixty years.
The use of carriages, horses and clothes,
the expenses for wives, children, and servants—
I measured income and limited expenditure,
lived frugally and with restraint,
managed salary and rewards,
planned and calculated carefully,
and thus gradually became rich and successful.
Thus, when the share of land is the same,
the worthy can safeguard it;
when the share of wealth is equal,
the wise can manage it.
The surplus and recession of Bái Guī,
the three accumulations of a thousand gold of Zǐ Gòng,
how can these necessarily rely on the common people?
Move it by six inches,
shift it with the rise and fall of interest,
and obtain it between high and low prices!"
The Wénxué said:
"In former times,
occupations were not doubled,
incomes and salaries were not combined;
and so trades were not greatly separated,
and rich and poor were not far apart.
Those who bore titles and salary with humility
were countless in name;
those who sought profit through power and influence
were countless in income.
Those who ate from lakes and ponds,
controlled mountains and seas:
how could woodcutters and grass gatherers compete with them for marshes?
How could merchants and traders compete with them for profit?
Zǐ Gòng attained this as a plain scholar,
and Kǒngzǐ reproached him;
how much more so those who obtain it through status and influence!
Therefore, the Dàfū of old considered their benevolence and righteousness as the means to fulfill their office,
and did not use their power and profit to fill their private pockets."
The Dàfū said:
"Because the mountains and peaks are abundant,
then the people are supplied;
because the rivers and seas are generous,
then the people have enough.
Ordinary ditches and puddles
cannot irrigate pools and marshes;
wood from hills and mounds
cannot build palaces and mansions.
The small cannot include the great,
the few cannot provide for the many.
Never has there been one unable to supply himself who could supply others;
never has there been one unable to govern himself who could govern others.
Therefore, those who are good at managing people
are those who can manage themselves;
those who are good at governing others
are those who can govern themselves.
The Wénxué cannot govern his own household;
how could he manage external affairs?"
The Wénxué said:
"He who travels a great distance makes use of a carriage,
he who crosses rivers and seas relies on a boat.
Thus, the achievement of merit and renown by worthy men
depends on resources and the use of things.
Gōngshū Zǐ could make use of timber provided by the ruler
to build palaces and terraces;
he could not himself construct even a single cottage or small hut,
for want of materials.
Ōuyě could make use of the copper and iron of the rulers
to craft tripods and great bells,
but could not himself cast pot, jar, tray or basin,
for lack of means.
The gentleman can use the just rule of the sovereign
to harmonize the people,
nourishing the multitude;
but cannot enrich his own house,
for circumstances do not permit.
Thus, when Shùn farmed at Lìshān,
his kindness did not reach the community;
when Tài Gōng slaughtered cattle at Cháogē,
his profit did not reach his wife and children;
but when they were employed,
their kindness extended across the world,
their virtue overflowed the four seas.
Thus, Shùn borrowed from Yáo,
Tài Gōng relied upon Zhōu;
a gentleman is able to cultivate himself and borrow the Way,
but cannot bend the Way to borrow wealth."
The dàfū said:
"The Way is suspended in Heaven,
things are spread upon the earth,
the wise make it flourish,
the foolish are made troubled by it.
Zǐ Gòng became renowned among the feudal lords through evident accomplishment;
Táo Zhūgōng attained esteem in his era through wealth and enterprise.
The rich associated with them,
the poor were supported by them.
Thus, from the ruler above
down to the common scholar below,
none failed to speak of their virtue,
and praise their benevolence.
Yuán Xiàn and Kǒng Jí
suffered from hunger and cold in their day;
Yán Huí was often destitute in a humble alley.
At such times,
pressed to dwell in caves,
confined to coarse robes,
even if they wished to obtain wealth by relying on cunning and flattery,
still they could not."
The scholar in letters said:
"Kǒngzǐ said:
'If wealth may be sought,
even if it required holding the whip,
I too would do it;
if it cannot be sought,
then I follow what I love.'
The gentleman seeks righteousness,
not merely wealth.
Thus Zǐ Gòng is criticized for engaging in trade rather than accepting office.
When the gentleman meets his era, he is wealthy and honored;
when he is not favored,
he withdraws and delights in the Way.
He does not let profit burden himself.
Thus, he does not violate righteousness for reckless gain.
Living in seclusion and cultivating his conduct,
he does not desire to impede his actions;
thus, he does not ruin his reputation by pursuing the trends.
Even if given the households of Hán and Wèi,
if it is not his aspiration,
he will not dwell in them.
Wealth and honor cannot bring him glory;
slander and defamation cannot harm him.
Thus, Yuán Xiàn's coarse robe
is more admirable than Jì Sūn's furs of fox and badger;
Zhào Xuān Mèng's fish meal
is sweeter than Zhì Bó's fodder and meat.
Zǐ Sī's silver pendants
are finer than Duke Yú's drooping thorn ornaments.
Wèi Wén Hóu stopped at the gate of Duàn Gàn Mù,
not for his power;
Jìn Wén Gōng, upon meeting Hán Qìng,
got down from his carriage and hastened forward,
not for his wealth.
It was for their richness in benevolence
and fullness in virtue.
Thus, why must honor come only from wealth?
It is also only benevolence and righteousness!"
4.3 "Condemning Learning, Section Eighteen"
The dàfū said:
"Harboring distortion while speaking straight,
feigning desirelessness while not truly abstaining—
is this not the character of a scholar?
Formerly, Lǐ Sī and Bāo Qiūzǐ both studied under Xún Qīng;
afterwards, Lǐ Sī entered Qín,
attained the position of the Three Excellencies,
and wielded power over the realm with ten thousand chariots,
his merit rivaled Yī and Wàng,
his fame matched Mount Tài;
yet Bāo Qiūzǐ did not escape a leaking window and a high hut,
like a frog in the year’s stagnant water.
His words were not few,
yet he finally died in the ditches and gullies.
Now, having nothing within to sustain oneself,
nothing outward for esteem,
being poor and lowly but fond of righteousness,
though one speaks of benevolence and righteousness,
such a person is hardly worthy of esteem!"
The scholar in letters said:
"When Lǐ Sī was Chancellor of Qín,
the First Emperor entrusted him,
and among ministers, there was none to match him.
Yet Xún Qīng would not eat for it,
seeing how he suffered unforeseen calamity.
Bāo Qiūzǐ ate hemp and bramble,
practiced the Way beneath a humble roof,
delighted in his purpose,
and felt at ease amid simple thatched dwellings with fodder and meat.
He had no dazzling authority,
yet knew no anxious sorrow.
The drooping thorn of Jìn Xiàn
was not unlovely;
Gōng Zhīqí saw it and sighed,
knowing that Xún Xī plotted for it.
Zhì Bó’s wealth covered the three Jìn states,
not unimpressive;
yet he did not know that Xiāngzǐ was scheming for it.
Jì Sūn’s fox and badger fur,
not unstylish;
yet he did not know that the Lord of Lǔ resented it.
Thus Jìn Xiàn used a precious horse to fish for Yú and Guó,
and Xiāngzǐ used a ruined city to entice Zhì Bó.
So Zhì Bó himself was captured by Zhào,
and Yú and Guó were both annexed by Jìn,
because they sought gain heedless of the aftermath,
greedy for land and profit from precious horses.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'If a person lacks foresight,
he will surely have near-at-hand worries.'
Now those in office
see benefits and do not anticipate harm,
are greedy and heedless of shame,
exchange profit for their own persons,
exchange wealth for their very lives.
They lack the virtue of benevolence and righteousness,
yet have rank and emolument;
such is like treading on pitfalls,
dining beneath a swinging doorway.
This is how Lǐ Sī succumbed to the Five Punishments.
In the south, there is a bird called yuānchú;
it does not eat unless it is bamboo fruit,
nor drink unless it is sweet spring.
When it flies past Mount Tài,
the owl of Mount Tài
looks down and pecks at rotten mice,
looks up and is startled by the yuānchú.
Now the exalted lords, seeing their wealth and rank, laugh at scholars and make it their constant practice;
is this not like the owl of Mount Tài startling at the yuānchú?"
The dàfū said:
"Scholars defend themselves with words;
rites adorn coarse behavior.
So learning assists virtue;
rites refine plainness.
Words should be pondered for their expressibility,
actions pondered for their delightfulness.
Evil speech does not pass the lips;
wicked deeds do not touch the self.
Every action accords with rites,
every motion is measured by the mean.
Thus abide by rites in action,
remain modest and yielding in one’s outward manner.
In this way, speaking all day,
there is no fault of the tongue;
acting a lifetime,
there are no grievances or resentments.
Now the ruler proclaims offices and establishes the court to govern the people,
distributes ranks and shares emoluments to honor the worthy,
yet you call it 'mouse beneath the swinging door'—
how base and contrary such rhetoric is to what we have heard!"
The scholar in letters said:
"A sage ruler establishes offices to assign responsibilities,
and the capable fill them;
emoluments are distributed to employ the worthy,
and the capable receive them.
Righteousness is valued for not seeking high position,
and the righteous take without greed.
Thus Shùn accepted the realm from Yáo,
Tàigōng did not avoid the office of Three Excellencies under Zhōu;
if not truly worthy,
even coarse food and thin gruel are still taken at the people’s expense.
Thus when virtue is slight and position high,
when ability is little and responsibility heavy,
how few reach completion!
The owl of Mount Tài pecks rotten mice in the marshes and hidden valleys;
it does not harm people thereby.
Yet today's officials
steal their lord’s wealth and feed on it beside the law,
not knowing that disaster is thus aroused;
and in addition they startle others.
How could their troubles be like those of the owl of Mount Tài?"
The dàfū said:
"Sīmǎzǐ said:
'The world is bustling,
all go forth for profit.'
The lady of Zhào chooses not for beauty or ugliness,
the old woman of Zhèng chooses not by distance or proximity,
merchants feel no shame in disgrace,
soldiers do not spare their strength though facing death,
scholars do not remain with their kin,
nor do they avoid hardship in serving their lord;
all act for profit and reward.
Ruists and Mohists are greedy within and proud without,
go about persuading back and forth,
restless—yet have not attained the Way.
Therefore, honoring and exalting is the scholar’s wish,
wealth and rank are the scholar’s hope.
When Lǐ Sī was at the gate of Xún Qīng,
undistinguished men joined him on equal footing;
but when he spread his wings and soared aloft,
like dragon rising and flying steed racing,
surpassing all but two out of nine,
flying high ten thousand fathoms,
together in company with wild geese and splendid steeds,
not to mention the crippled goats and sparrows!"
To sit at the seat of all-under-Heaven’s power,
to command the multitudes within the universe,
to have a hundred chariots following behind one’s carriage,
to receive salaries worth ten thousand measures;
yet those Confucians, constrained, wear coarse and incomplete garments,
eat chaff and husks and are never full,
not because they cherish beans and wild greens and despise grand mansions,
but because they cannot help it.
Even if they seek to intimidate others,
how could they bring an end to it!
The Scholar replied:
“The gentleman cherishes virtue,
the petty man cherishes his homeland.
The worthy man pursues fame,
the greedy man dies for profit.
Lǐ Sī coveted what he desired,
and brought about what he dreaded.
Sūn Shū’ào perceived disaster before it emerged,
thrice relinquishing the post of Chancellor without regret,
not because he delighted in lowly rank and hated heavy emolument,
but because he anticipated distant troubles and prudently avoided harm.
That sacrificial ox for the suburban rite,
is raised and fed for a whole year,
clad in brocade and embroidery,
to enter the ancestral halls;
the Grand Steward wields the ornamented knife
to part its hair;
at that very time,
it would wish to shoulder a heavy burden to climb steep hills,
but to no avail.
Shāng Yāng was troubled at Péngchí,
Wú Qǐ lay beneath the king’s corpse;
both wished to wear coarse cloth and dwell in a thatched hovel in some remote place,
but could not obtain it.
Lǐ Sī served as Chancellor of Qín,
occupying the power of all-under-Heaven,
his ambition small before the ruler of ten thousand chariots;
when imprisoned in the jail,
and torn asunder in the market at Yúnyáng,
he too wished to carry firewood through the East Gate,
to walk the winding lanes of Shàngcài,
but could not have it.
Sū Qín and Wú Qǐ brought destruction on themselves through power and influence,
Shāng Yāng and Lǐ Sī through respect and rank,
all because they craved emoluments and longed for glory, to their own ruin,
with a hundred chariots following,
yet even these were not enough to bear their misfortune!”
4.4 “In Praise of the Worthy, Nineteenth Chapter”
The Grandee said:
“Bó Yí perished by hunger for the sake of integrity,
Wěi Shēng died for the sake of trustworthiness.
Because of minor matters, they damaged the greater body;
the trustworthiness of ordinary men and women,
may be lost in the trenches and no one would know of it.
What fame or merit is therein?
Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
their wisdom sufficient to strengthen kingdoms,
their courage enough to awe their foes,
with a single fury, the feudal lords trembled,
abiding in peace, all-under-Heaven rested.
Every king of ten thousand chariots,
bowed their bodies and humbled their words,
sending heavy gifts and pledging alliances,
such are those called the eminent men of all-under-Heaven.
Those whose wisdom cannot counsel,
whose authority cannot bear the age,
the people, these are counted as low.
Now what is lost they call having,
what is empty they call full,
garbed in coarse cloth with worn-out shoes,
brooding and walking slowly,
as if they had lost something,
not men of accomplishment and fame,
nor are they free of worldly custom.”
The Scholar replied:
“Sū Qín became renowned for alliances in Zhào,
Zhāng Yí exercised power by horizontal strategy in Qín,
at that very moment,
they were not without honor and prestige,
yet men of insight worried for them,
understanding that what is gained not by the Way will not be lost by the Way;
what is not obtained by righteousness will not be lost by righteousness.
The power of the Jì and Mèng,
the wealth of the Three Huán,
cannot be surpassed,
yet Kǒngzǐ deemed them ‘insignificant.’
For a minister,
if power rivals the ruler’s
and wealth matches the state’s,
ruin results.
Thus the higher the position the heavier the guilt,
the thicker the emolument the greater the blame.
Those who conduct themselves must first preserve themselves before seeking recognition,
officials must first avoid harm before pursuing reward.
Thus sweet bait is not unpleasing,
but turtles and dragons, hearing of it, hide away deeply,
luan birds and phoenixes, seeing it, soar high and depart,
for they know it brings harm.
As for crows, magpies, fish, and turtles,
they seize the sweet bait, then rush madly and scurry about,
drooping heads and dragging tails,
gaining nothing but death.
Now government officials who steal while upholding the law,
push forward not weighing their crimes,
should an emergency suddenly occur,
then carriages dash and men rush,
but it does nothing for the dead.
What is stolen is not enough to redeem even a slave,
the wife and children flee with nowhere to go,
the body lies deep in prison,
no one knows to care for or look after.
At such a time,
who would have leisure for laughter?”
The Grandee said:
“Scholar, your conduct is lofty,
aloof as if never to be bent;
your noble bearing and pure words,
pristine as if never to be stained.
Yet enlisted soldier Chén Shèng unyoked his carriage,
and was first to rebel,
established the state of Zhāngchǔ,
and from the first did not possess the conduct of recluse Huí or Yóu,
nor the station of chancellor or ranked minister.
Moved in the marsh of Dàzé,
within no more than ten days,
scholars and Mohists of Qí and Lǔ, officials in ceremonial dress,
donned long robes at will,
the long robe, the ceremonial garb,
bearing the ritual vessels and texts of the Kǒng family: the Shī and the Shū,
bent their persons as vassals.
Kǒng Jiǎ was made an academician,
but all perished at Chén,
and became the great laugh of the world.
Are those who hide away and withdraw at height truly like this?”
The Scholar replied:
“When the Zhōu house declined,
rites and righteousness decayed,
the central authority was unable to govern,
the feudal lords contended together,
destroying one another,
until they merged as the Six States,
and war was unceasing,
so the people never found rest.
Qín, with the heart of tiger and wolf,
gnawed away at the feudal lords,
and swallowed the Warring States, making them into commanderies and counties,
boasted of its military power and self-congratulated,
claiming to surpass Yáo and Shùn and feeling shame to be counted their equals.
Abandoning benevolence and righteousness, valuing only punishments,
holding that in these times authority should rest not on culture but on arms.
Zhào Gāo managed the prisons within,
Méng Tián waged war abroad,
the common people were in suffering,
and all hated Qín with one heart.
King Chén Shèng, rising suddenly, bared his talons and fangs to undertake the first great cause,
though the way he followed was harsh, some Confucians and Mohists attached themselves to him,
believing there had long been no rightful lord,
the Way being blocked and unable to proceed,
from Confucius to this day,
and Qín further imposed strict prohibitions,
thus they gave vent to their anger under King Chén Shèng.
Confucius said:
‘If there were one to employ me,
might I make the East Zhōu flourish!’
Then perhaps, accomplishing the deeds of Chéngtáng, Wén, and Wǔ,
he could rid the people of the cruel and the villainous,
how could it be for the sake of profit or pleasure in position?”
The Grandee said:
“Scholar, your words and deeds may have the integrity of Bó Yí,
but lack the constancy of Liǔxià Huì;
you see high and look down,
your words are pure but your conduct corrupt,
drinking wine and eating meat,
delaying and yielding to one another,
small refusals but great acquisition,
hen’s modesty but wolf’s greed.
Zhào Wǎn and Wáng Zāng,
were raised to chief ministers for their Confucian arts,
yet had cunning and cruel hearts.
Zhǔfù Yǎn by glib tongue won high office,
usurped weighty power,
deceived the house of the sovereign,
and took bribes from lords,
all finally punished with death.
Dōngfāng Shuò called himself sharp and cunning,
breaking hardness and dissolving stone,
peerless in his age;
yet when one examines his private conduct,
even a madman would not stoop to it,
how much less is there to admire for those lacking his eloquence?”
The Scholar replied:
“Those who set their mind on goodness forget evil,
those cautious in small matters accrue the great.
Between the sacrificial vessels, one can observe rituals;
within the inner chambers, one can judge conduct.
Those who wear ancient dress,
recite the ways of antiquity,
and turn from this to do wrong,
are few indeed.
Therefore, the junzǐ speaks only at the proper time,
accepts only when it is righteous,
and does not retain what is not gained in accordance with the Dào.
He is full without overflowing,
magnanimous without arrogance.
Thus, Yuán Àng, though intimate with Jǐng Dì,
did not acquire more than one span of horses;
Gōngsūn Hóng, though elevated to the position of the Three Excellencies,
had no more than ten chariots at home;
Dōngfāng Shēng, who advised Wǔ Dì in words and actions,
was not arrogant or excessive;
Zhǔfù had long experienced days of hardship,
grieved that those in power disliked the Dào yet were wealthy and honored,
and that none knew how to care for scholars.
Therefore, he took the surplus of Ráo Yǎn to relieve the urgent needs of impoverished scholars,
not for private family gain.
In the present age there is much clamor,
not because the ru are chicken-scrupulous,
but because those in office are tiger-gorged and owl-greedy,
and in their pursuit leave nothing unscathed.”
5.1 “Xiāng Cì, Chapter Twenty”
The dàfū said:
“In ancient times,
the well-field system was followed,
wards and neighborhoods were regulated,
men tended their fields,
women handled hemp and silk,
there was no wasteland,
no idle folk.
Thus, none but merchants and artisans ate the profits of trade,
none but good farmers ate of the harvest,
none but officeholders ate of rank.
Now, the ru abandon their plows and study unverifiable words,
idly letting time pass,
without benefit to governance,
drifting to and fro,
eating without farming,
clothed without sericulture,
deceiving honest people with cunning,
to usurp agriculture and hinder governance,
this too is a trouble of our age.”
The literati said:
“Yǔ endured the great flood,
personally toiling,
sleeping on roads in marshes,
passing his door without entering.
At such a time,
if his hairpin fell he did not pick it up,
if his cap slipped he did not look back,
did he have leisure to farm?
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘The poets are troubled and cannot remain silent;
I, Qiū, am troubled and cannot endure it in silence.’
Thus, having expounded seventy times in east, west, south, and north yet not being employed,
he retired and cultivated the royal Way,
composed the Chūnqiū,
and let it linger for ten thousand ages thereafter,
so that under Heaven all measured themselves by it.
How can this be the same as commoners tilling and weaving!
The Zhuàn says:
‘The junzǐ, at the right time, does not act,
and the people have no spectacle.’
Therefore, none but the junzǐ can govern the small people,
and without the small people there is no way to support the junzǐ.
Tilling and weaving are not the role of the junzǐ.
If the junzǐ tills but does not study,
this leads to disorder.”
The dàfū said:
“You, literati, speak of governance surpassing that of Táng
and Yú, speak of righteousness loftier than the skies,
your words are flowery,
but I have not seen their reality.
In the time of Lǔ Mù Gōng,
Gōngyí was Chancellor,
Zǐ Sī
and Zǐ Liǔ were ministers,
yet in the north they were cut back by Qí,
making the Sì River their border,
in the south, they feared the people of Chǔ,
in the west, they served Qín,
and when Mèng Kē resided in Liáng,
his forces were defeated by Qí,
his chief general killed and the crown prince captured,
in the west, defeated by Qín,
and lost land and territory,
losing both within and beyond the Hé.
Now, among Kǒngzǐ’s disciples,
the seventy followers,
left their parents,
abandoned their homes,
shouldered burdens and followed Kǒngzǐ,
studied but did not farm,
yet disorder only increased.
Thus, though boxes are filled with jade dust,
this is not to possess treasures;
though one recites the Shī and Shū and carries books on one’s back,
this is not to possess the Dào.
The essential thing is to secure the state,
benefit the people,
and not merely indulge in ornate language in abundance.”
The literati said:
“Yú perished for not using the plan of Bǎilǐ Xī,
but Qín Mù used him and so attained hegemony.
Thus, not employing the worthy brings ruin;
how, then, can one not be cut down?
When Mèngzǐ went to Liáng,
King Huì asked about profit,
and he replied with benevolence and righteousness.
As their aims did not accord,
he was not used but left,
and cherished his treasure without speaking.
Thus, though grain existed, if uneaten,
it avails nothing for hunger;
beholding the worthy but not employing them,
it does nothing to prevent being cut down.
In Zhòu’s time,
within there were Wēi
and Jī, two sons,
without there were Jiāo Gé
and Jí Zǐ,
yet none could preserve him.
When words are not heeded,
and remonstrance is not listened to,
then, however worthy,
how can one be of benefit to governance?”
The dàfū said:
“Oranges and pomelos grow south of the Jiāng,
and people all find them sweet to the taste,
the flavor is the same;
melodious sounds arise from Zhèng
and Wèi, and people all take delight in hearing them,
the sound is the same.
From Yuè came Zǐ Zāng,
from Róng came Yóu Yú,
yet only with interpreters could they be understood;
still, they became illustrious in Qí
and Qín; in people’s hearts good and evil are alike.
Thus, when Zēngzǐ chanted by the mountains,
the mountain birds flew down;
when Shī Kuàng played the qín,
all the beasts joined in dancing.
Never has it been that good does not find harmony,
or sincerity meet with no response.
Is the intention perhaps not sincere?
Then why are speech and action not followed?”
The literati said:
“Biǎn Què could not cure those who refused needle or medicine;
the worthy and the sages cannot rectify a lord who will not accept remonstrance.
Thus, Jié had Guān Lóngpéng, yet Xià perished;
Zhòu had three worthies, yet Shāng fell.
The problem is not lack of speakers like Yóu Yú or Zǐ Zāng,
but lack of listeners like Huán
and Mù.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ wandered without finding welcome,
and Qū Yuán was exiled from the state of Chǔ.
Thus it is said:
‘To serve others with uprightness,
where does one go without being thrice dismissed?
To serve others by crookedness,
why leave one’s parents’ land?’
In the end, it is not because speech is unheeded
or action unsupported.”
The dàfū said:
“A singer does not seek profit in his notes,
but values proper rhythm;
a debater does not seek ornate words,
but insists on substance.
If one is skilled in voice yet cannot modulate,
he cannot be called a true singer;
if skilled in speech but knows not adaptation,
he cannot be called a true persuader.
To hold a compass yet reject the square,
to use a plumb but spurn the line,
to know only one aperture,
be enlightened by a single principle,
but be ignorant of balance and weighing,
and to not believe others because one has not seen something oneself,
is like the cicada which knows not of snow.
Stubbornly adhering to ancient writings to respond to the present age,
is like the confusion of Chén and Shēn stars,
or tuning a se by gluing the bridge—
unyielding and hard to accord with indeed.
This is why Kǒngzǐ was not used by his age,
and Mèng Kē was despised by the feudal lords.”
Wénxué said:
"The light of the sun and moon,
yet the blind cannot see it;
the sound of thunder and lightning,
yet the deaf cannot hear it.
To speak to those who do not understand music,
is like speaking to the mute and the deaf;
how is this different from the cicada being ignorant of the weight of snow?
Even with the wisdom of Yī Yǐn,
and the virtue of Tài Gōng,
they could not open their words to Jié
and Zhòu—not the fault of the speaker,
but the error of the listener.
Thus, Jīng Hé embraced his uncut jade and wept blood,
saying:
'How can I get a skilled artisan to cut it open!'
Qū Yuán walked and chanted by the side of the marsh,
saying:
'How can I get Gāo Yáo to examine it!'
Now, every ruler wishes to seek the worthy to assist himself,
and to appoint the capable to govern the state.
Yet, swayed by fashionable talk,
and puzzled by flattery,
thus the virtuous and the sage are concealed and covered,
while slanderers and flatterers hold power.
Because of this, states are destroyed and families ruined,
and worthy gentlemen go hungry in caves and ravines.
In the past, Zhào Gāo had no ambition above others,
yet occupied a post above ten thousand.
Thus he toppled the state of Qín and brought disaster to his clan,
completely lost his zither;
why persist in tuning the glued tuning pegs?"
The Dàfū said:
"The so-called men of high rank in learning
possess wisdom and strategy which can illuminate the methods of the Former Kings,
and their character and qualities are sufficient to practice those ways.
Thus at home they serve as teachers of men,
and in use, as models for the world.
Now, when speaking of government, men of learning cite Yáo
and Shùn; in conduct, they speak of Kǒng
and Mò. But when entrusted with administration, they are inept,
they cherish ancient ways but cannot practice them,
their words are upright but their conduct is crooked,
their Dao is right but their sentiments are wrong,
their dress and hats distinguish them from the local commoners,
yet in truth they are no different from ordinary men.
Those among the students so-called upright and impartial
encounter fortune by meeting the times,
and are included merely by chance,
hardly matching, as you say, a wise selection.
Thus, we cannot yet discuss government matters with them."
Wénxué said:
"Heaven establishes the three luminaries to illuminate and record;
the Son of Heaven appoints dukes and ministers to shine in governance.
Thus it is said:
Dukes and ministers
are the models for the four seas,
the painted embodiment of divine transformation.
Above, they have the duty to assist an enlightened ruler;
below, they are tasked with bringing about sagely transformation.
They harmonize yin and yang,
regulate the four seasons,
give peace to the masses,
nurture all living things,
cause the hundred surnames to dwell together in harmony,
so that there is no look of resentment or regret,
the four tribes submit to virtue,
so there is no fear of rebellion.
This is the office of dukes and ministers,
and the duty of the worthy.
As for the talents of Yī Yǐn,
the Three Dukes Zhōu and Zhào,
the Nine Ministers like Tài Diān
and Hóng Yǎo—
if men of learning are not properly selected by a sagely ruler,
then those in power today
still cannot be called men of great virtue."
The Dàfū was displeased,
and with a changed expression did not reply.
Wénxué said:
"When there are no loyal ministers in the court, government is blind;
when there are no upright officials among the great officers, positions are in peril.
When Rèn Zuò spoke directly to his lord's faults,
Wén Hóu changed his words and actions,
and was thus called a worthy ruler.
Yuán Àng admonished Lord Jiàng Hóu to his face for his arrogance,
and finally secured his happiness.
Thus, those who risk death to remonstrate with their ruler about his faults
are loyal ministers;
those who brave stern faces to correct the failings of dukes and ministers
are upright officials.
Common people cannot speak in the alleys and oppose in person.
Nowadays, the teaching and directives on entering the valley
are displayed but not exercised,
many who receive salaries are not the right people,
thereby hindering farmers, merchants, and artisans,
and the profits of the marketplace,
do not return to the people.
The people's expectations are not satisfied.
Moreover, the way of emperors and kings
has mostly fallen into ruin and disrepair.
The *Shī* says:
'Numerous and able are the officials.'
The intent is truly to employ their stratagems,
not merely to speak empty words."
5.2 "Different Paths, Chapter Twenty-One"
The Dàfū said:
"The seventy disciples personally received the Sage's teachings,
were named among the followers of Kǒngzǐ,
all were talents fit for minister or premier among the feudal lords,
and those able to sit in the seat of authority were but a few.
Rǎn Yǒu and Jì Lù were in charge of governance;
in speech, it was Zǎi Wǒ
and Zǐ Gòng.
Zǎi Wǒ was in office,
favored in Qí,
but when Tián Cháng caused trouble,
the Way was not practiced,
and he died in the court.
Duke Jiǎn killed him at Tán Tái.
Zǐ Lù served Wèi,
but Kǒng Kuǐ created disorder,
and he could not save his lord or escape,
and his body was pickled in Wèi.
Zǐ Gòng
and Zǐ Gāo fled in exile,
unable to die for their difficulties.
They ate heavy salaries but could not reform them,
held honorable offices but could not preserve them.
How is it that they were so generous to themselves yet so ungenerous to their rulers?
They were fellow disciples and shared the same teaching,
considering themselves versed in the principles of past and present,
and clear in the rites of lord and minister.
Yet some perished, some were exiled;
you fellows took different paths;
how contradictory were the ways you followed!"
Wénxué said:
"Duke Shāng of Sòng knew of the worthiness of Kǒng Fù, yet did not employ him promptly,
and thus met his own death.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ knew of Jì Yǒu's talents,
but employed him late and disorder came to the state.
The lord of Wèi favored flatterers and distanced the worthy;
Zǐ Lù lived in Pú,
while Kǒng Kuǐ held office.
Duke Jiǎn did not listen to Zǎi Wǒ and leaked his plot.
Therefore, both rulers suffered exile and death,
and disaster befell upright ministers.
These two had official matters but were not consulted in plans;
thus whether they died
or survived,
left or stayed,
their conduct remained consistent in principle.
Yàn Yīng did not die in the troubles of Cuī
and Qìng,
but this does not mean he was not righteous;
did Wēi Zǐ's departure from the chaos in Yīn
make him unrighteous?"
The Dàfū said:
"Utmost beauty is in the plain jade,
which nothing can embellish.
The utmost virtue preserves genuineness,
which no ornate words can add to.
Therefore, gold and jade are not carved,
fine pearls are not painted.
Now Zhòng Yóu
and Rǎn Qiú lacked the qualities of sandalwood and Chinese catalpa,
their jade was like that of Suí and Hé,
yet they forced ornament upon themselves;
it is like carving rotted wood or sharpening a leaden knife,
or adorning ugly Mó Mǔ or painting clay figures.
Clothed in five colors,
appearing splendid in form,
but when they encounter a flood or surging waves,
they are ruined.
Those who heavily cherish ancient ways,
rest their heads on the *Shī*
and *Shū*
yet cannot bring safety in danger,
nor order in chaos,
even if they chase chickens through the villages,
the chickens will have no allies."
Wénxué said:
"Without learning, one cannot cultivate oneself;
without lǐ, one cannot assist virtue.
The uncut jade of Hé,
is the finest treasure under Heaven;
it awaits the craftsman Jiānzhū before its brilliance is revealed.
Máo Qiāng,
the most beautiful woman under Heaven,
relies on perfumes and cosmetics before her beauty is apparent.
Zhōu Gōng,
the utmost sagely man under Heaven,
depended on worthy teachers and learning before achieving understanding.
Now, people who are ordinary men of the state of Qí in this generation,
do not love learning,
but still rely on their own ignorance to shoulder great responsibility;
this is like having no oar or helm,
crossing Jiāng or Hǎi and meeting a great wind,
being swept away and drowned in an abyss a hundred rèn deep,
carried eastward by the boundless river,
how could there be any way to halt or stop it?"
The Dàfū said:
"In nature, there is firmness and gentleness;
in form, preferences and aversions;
even the sages can follow these but cannot change them.
Kǒngzǐ could alter the clothes of his disciples,
but could not change their hearts.
Thus Zǐlù removed his long sword,
set aside his lofty cap,
and bent his pride at the gate of the Master,
yet as he learned together with his peers,
and walked among them,
his base mind still remained.
Zǎi Yǔ slept during the day,
and wished to shorten the three-year mourning period.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'A wall made of dung and earth
cannot be plastered,'
'He will likely meet with an untimely death.'
Thus, without the principle within but learning the forms without,
even with worthy teachers and good friends,
it is like painting on fat or carving ice—
time is wasted and effort destroyed.
Thus a good teacher cannot make Qī Shī beautiful,
nor can fragrances transform Mómǔ."
Wénxué said:
"If Xīzǐ were covered with filth,
base men would still cover their noses;
if an evil man wore splendid attire,
he could still perform sacrifices to Shàngdì.
If these two never crossed the gate of the sage,
they would not escape being poor men;
how could they gain the title of minister or great officer?
Thus the whetstone brings sharpness to the blade,
learning enables one to exhaust his talent.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'A goblet that is not a goblet—
is it a goblet?
Is it a goblet!'
Thus when human effort is added, it becomes a vessel for the ancestral temple;
otherwise, it is but firewood for cooking.
If the steel from Gàn or Yuè is not sharpened,
even a commoner would despise it;
but when the craftsman applies his skill,
the ruler will wear it at court.
The ugly think themselves beautiful,
so do not adorn themselves;
the foolish think themselves wise,
so do not study.
They see their own laughter but do not realize it,
do not know how to employ others,
and thus fall into self-righteous error."
5.3 "Disputing Worthies, Chapter Twenty-Two"
The Dàfū said:
"The firm is broken,
the gentle is rolled up.
Thus Jì Yóu died from his violence,
and Zǎi Wǒ was destroyed by his weakness.
If the two men had not learned,
it is not certain they would not have died as they did.
Why?
Being self-conceited and boasting of ability,
possessing little knowledge yet herding many,
desiring others to follow them,
but unable themselves to follow others,
being unseen but thinking themselves seen,
unrewarded but thinking themselves valuable,
thus they perish by their own hands and end up as salt meat and pickles.
I have never seen them become vessels for the ancestral temple,
but have only seen them disgraced in the world.
At such a time,
could the east-flowing current find any solace?"
Wénxué said:
"A fine horse pulling a salt cart,
hangs its head on the slopes of Tàiháng,
and the butcher watches it with his knife in hand.
Tài Gōng once destitute,
peddled goods at Cháogē,
with disheveled hair, people gathered and mocked him.
At such a time,
it was not for lack of distant vision or superb talent,
only Wén Wáng
or Bólè could truly appreciate their worth.
Zǐlù
and Zǎi Wǒ were born not at the rising of Bólè,
but met reckless butchers;
therefore, the gentleman laments them.
It is as if
'they met an untimely death,'
'Heaven curses me indeed.'
As for Kǒng Fù suffering hardship at Huádū,
one cannot call him unrighteous;
and Qiú Mù, encountering the disaster of Sòng Wàn,
one cannot call him unworthy."
The Dàfū said:
"Scholars of today,
possess not the ability of Tài Gōng,
nor the talent of a fine steed,
but, using the venom of bees and scorpions, end up harming themselves.
Chéng Yǒng of Dōnghǎi
and Hú Jiàn of Hédōng are such.
These two were raised by their techniques,
rose from the common soldiery,
and became district magistrates.
But being conceited and out of harmony with others,
they had no one to join with.
Called they would not come,
pushed they would not go,
wild and impetuous, lacking in humility,
malicious and disrespectful,
oppressing the princess,
affronting the great ministers.
Knowing the impossible and forcing it,
they sought to make a name.
Thus their way went astray,
and finally they perished themselves.
Before any achievement was seen, calamity befell them in the Eastern Archives,
and they were heavily punished,
failing to live out their years.
Crafty yet thinking themselves wise,
outspoken and thinking themselves upright,
insolent and claiming courage,
their meeting with disaster
was as it should be."
Wénxué said:
"The two gentlemen cherished pure and honest hearts,
walked the path of loyalty and rectitude,
kept themselves upright in serving their superiors,
gave their utmost in serving the public,
upheld the law and promoted principle,
shrank not from the strong and violent,
did not flatter those close to them,
valued not the support of wife and children,
nor considered the interests of their own families.
Yet in the end, they could not escape those jealous of their worth,
and were pushed aside by the many for wrongful reasons.
Thus they suffered unforeseen punishments and their merit went unfulfilled.
If the royal clans are not upright, law and decree will not be enforced;
if the limbs and sinews of government are not upright, treachery and evil will arise.
Zhào Shē led the way in Píngyuán,
Fàn Jū served in the court of Ráng Hóu;
both states were well governed and both houses were preserved.
Thus, when the lord errs and the minister is upright,
the superior is impeached and the subordinate comments,
when the great ministers are upright,
what difficulty for the district magistrates?
Failing to examine oneself and blaming others,
is the great error of those in power.
Qū Yuán's drowning in the abyss
was due to the slander of Zǐ Jiāo;
Guǎnzi was able to practice his way
because of Bào Shū's effort.
