Now we see not the support of a Bào Shū,
but only the tragedy at Mìluó;
though one would wish to live out his years,
how could he hope to attain it?"
5.4 "Following the Way, Chapter Twenty-Three"
The Dàfū said:
"Yùshǐ!"
The Censor did not respond.
He said to the Shǐ of the Chancellor’s staff:
“The literati have studied language since tying their hair,
embracing it without letting go,
their words circling endlessly,
turning as if molded by a potter’s wheel.
Their writings are as abundant as spring blossoms,
but as useless as clutching at the wind.
Adorning empty words to confuse reality,
speaking of antiquity to harm the present.
If you follow them,
then the functions of the county offices are abandoned,
as empty words cannot be put into practice;
if you do not follow them,
the literati deem you wrong,
and the clamor of many mouths
cannot all be heard.
You, esteemed officials, have served in the great bureau for a long time,
understanding the ancient,
and being enlightening to the present age.
Now, what should we follow to make things right?”
The Shǐ of the Chancellor’s staff, Jìn, said:
“Jìn Wén Gōng was cunning but not upright,
Qí Huán Gōng was upright but not cunning,
though their methods differed,
both attained hegemony.
But if one must always follow the ancients without change,
imitate the old without reform,
then culture and substance never change,
and yet the oxcart would still exist.
Thus, some originate things,
others transmit them,
only then are laws and orders harmonized among the people,
and tools adapted to their use.
Kǒngzǐ responded differently to three lords,
Yànzǐ assisted three lords each by different ways,
not out of mere opposition,
but because their concerns fit the times.
Once the court and nobility have set the path for grand enterprise,
and established inexhaustible foundations,
let there be no talk of trivial matters,
entangling us in the debates of Rú
and Mò.”
The literati said:
“Master Kuǎng in tuning the five notes
never lost Gōng or Shāng.
The sages’ governance of the world
never departs from benevolence and righteousness.
Thus we may have reforms in name,
but not in the actual Way.
From Huángdì above,
down through the Three Kings,
all enlightened virtue and teaching,
attended carefully to schools,
exalted benevolence and righteousness,
and established moral education.
This is the unchanging Way of a hundred generations.
Yīn and Zhōu prospered by following it,
Qín perished by changing the laws.
The Shījīng says:
‘Though there are no elders or sages,
still there remain the models and laws.’
This speaks of rule by law and teaching;
thus, though extinct, it abides,
take it and thread it through,
thread it and put it into practice,
what more is needed?”
The Shǐ of the Chancellor’s staff said:
“To talk of the beauty of Xī Shī brings no benefit to one’s appearance,
to speak of the virtue of Yáo
or Shùn brings no benefit to governance.
Now, the literati do not speak of what is done to govern,
but talk of governance without achievement,
like praising the granaries of the rich,
without saying how to farm the fields.
He who wants grain must attend to the proper season,
he who wants good governance must suit the age.
Thus, Lord Shāng alone clearly saw the distinction of survival and ruin and did not align with the common customs,
because common talk hinders achievement by being too close at hand.
The mediocre man is content with old ways,
the foolish are convinced by what they have heard.
Thus, the building of ships and carts
only made the people comfortable after three years.
The laws of Lord Shāng were established,
only afterwards did the people trust them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘One may study together,
but may not yet weigh decisions together.’
The literati can be made to draw lines or follow the marks,
but are not those with whom to discuss the great strategies of governance.”
The literati said:
“The gentleman hears much and omits what is doubtful,
transmits but does not create,
the sage comprehends and plans for the greatest,
wise and insightful, he undertakes little.
Thus, when achievements succeed, they do not collapse,
and when reputation is established, it does not vanish.
The petty man is shallow in wisdom yet plans for greatness,
weak yet takes on heavy burdens,
thus fails midway—
Sū Qín
and Shāng Yǎng are examples.
Lacking the laws of former kings,
not following the way of sages,
relying only upon themselves,
and so are ruined.
The Yìjīng says:
‘When the petty man occupies high rank,
though exalted he must collapse.
Lacking fullness in the Way,
unstable in virtue,
and able to accomplish good to the end of life—
such has never been.
Thus, first ascends to Heaven,
then ends in the Earth.’
When Yǔ controlled the floods,
the people knew its benefit,
and all were encouraged to strive.
When Shāng Yǎng enforced his laws,
the people knew their harm,
and all dreaded his punishments.
Thus, the achievements of Xiàhòu established kingship,
the laws of Shāng Yǎng brought ruin.
Shāng Yǎng alone had the resolve to plan,
the world lacked proof of his unique insight.
The literati are not fit to weigh the present age,
nor need they be encumbered with disaster.”
5.5 "Discourse on Slander, Twenty-Fourth"
The Shǐ of the Chancellor’s staff said:
“Yànzǐ once said:
‘The Rú adorn words but lack substance,
dwell in music, but slacken the people,
keep mourning too long and harm life,
bury thick and damage livelihoods,
rites are cumbersome and hard to carry out,
the Way is circuitous and hard to follow,
they praise the ancient and criticize the present,
belittle what they see and value what they hear.’
Such a person is inherently bent,
takes himself as the model.
This is why Yán Yì was executed,
and Díshān died among the Xiōngnú.
Occupying their office yet not fitting the court,
alive in their times but slandering their superiors,
in the end are destroyed and lose their bodies;
who, then, would carry such a burden and endure disaster for them?”
The literati said:
“Rites are to prevent excess,
music to transform habits,
when rites are established and music correct, punishments are moderate.
Thus, with dikes established, the people have no flood calamity,
with rites and righteousness established, the people have no disorder.
But when rites and righteousness collapse,
the dikes burst,
and those who seek to govern,
never succeed.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘In rites—
better frugality than extravagance;
in mourning—
better grief than formality.’
Thus, the creation of rites
was never to harm life or damage livelihood,
nor were ceremonial regulations made to disturb transformation or injure custom.
Governing the state depends on attentiveness to rites,
a perilous state on strictness in law.
Formerly, Qín conquered the world by force of arms,
but it was Sī
and Gāo who—for their monstrous deeds—brought misfortune upon it,
abolishing ancient arts,
destroying old rites,
relying only on laws and punishments,
so that the teachings of Rú
and Mò were already lost.
The paths of knights were blocked,
people’s voices were stifled,
while flatteries multiplied and those above heard no criticism,
thus Qín lost the world and destroyed its altars of state.
Therefore, when sages ruled,
slander was the first thing punished,
for skillful words assist wrong and overturn the state.
Now, why do you cite the words of fallen states?
When court officials hold office,
but do not correct the way,
and adapt themselves according to the winds of favor,
hating only the petty men who flatter with superficial compliance,
thus facilitating others’ faults.
Therefore, those who understand words are doomed,
unable to follow those who consort for convenience,
and thus do not escape imprisonment.
Alas!”
The Chancellor’s scribe said:
“The sandalwood and the zhe tree have their own groves,
the reed and the rush have their own thickets;
thus it is said that things of the same kind gather together.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘Virtue is not alone;
it surely has neighbors.’
Thus when Tāng rose to power, Yī Yǐn came to assist him,
and the unrighteous fled far away.
Never has there been an enlightened lord above and rebellious ministers below.
Now the previous sovereign personally practiced the way of benevolence and sageliness,
governing all beneath heaven,
recruiting and recommending talented and virtuous men,
employing only the benevolent,
putting to death or expelling treacherous ministers,
not sparing even his relatives,
striving to seek out the worthy and to dismiss the unworthy,
just as Yáo raised up Shùn,
and Yǔ chose among his kin,
punishing Guǐ and banishing Huān Dōu.
Yet to call them
‘a band of opportunists’—
is this not accusing the lord unjustly and flattering the minister?
Is it so?”
The Scholar said:
“Gāo Yáo replied to Shùn:
‘It is in knowing men;
only the Emperor finds it most difficult.’
When the flood was ravaging,
Yáo alone was sorrowful and could not bring order;
upon finding Shùn
and Yǔ, the Nine Regions were at peace.
Therefore, though there may be an enlightened lord such as Yáo,
if there is no assistant like Shùn
and Yǔ,
then pure virtue will not spread.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* rebukes those with a lord but no minister.
In the time of the previous sovereign,
worthy ministers were not yet gathered,
so wicked ministers found opportunity.
Yáo found Shùn
and Yǔ, and thus punished and exiled Guǐ and executed Huān Dōu;
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ obtained Shū Xiàng and thereby suppressed Qīng Jiān and Qū.
As the saying goes:
‘Before meeting the noble man,
one cannot recognize the false minister.’
The *Book of Songs* says:
‘Before seeing the noble man,
my heart is anxious and heavy.
When at last I see the noble man,
my heart is then at peace.’
This is what is meant.”
The Chancellor’s scribe said:
“Yáo entrusted affairs to Guǐ
and Huān Dōu,
and upon obtaining Shùn
and Yǔ, expelled and executed them for their crimes,
and all under heaven submitted,
for he punished the unrighteous.
Rulers employ men to manage the people,
whereas Yán Yì differed;
he had been prefect of Jǐnán,
whom the previous sovereign promoted to high office,
and he became chief minister.
Díshān rose from commoner origins
to act as a Han dynastic consultant;
he occupied a post like Shùn
and Yǔ,
and held the center of the realm,
but could not govern with order;
instead he was condemned for slandering his superiors;
therefore the punishment of Huān Dōu befell him and execution was his fate.
The worthy receive rewards while the unworthy are punished;
such is only right.
Why should the Scholar marvel at this?”
The Scholar said:
“Those who debate support each other by righteousness,
explain each other by the Way,
follow goodness without quarrelling for victory,
uphold justice without shame in hardship.
But if one confuses another with falsehood,
entangles with rhetoric,
boasts of eventual success,
aims only for momentary triumph,
he is not one who truly values what is noble.
Sū Qín
and Zhāng Yí,
beguiled the feudal lords,
overturned the mighty,
and caused rulers to lose their bearings;
it was not that they lacked eloquence,
but it was the Way of disorder.
The noble man detests that the lowly cannot serve their lord together,
and worries that, in listening to them, there is nothing they will not go to.
If now you refuse to heed righteousness to assist the chancellors,
but instead follow and conform,
preferring brief arguments
without regard for the outcome,
if you were an official,
you ought to suffer execution from above.
For now, you should remain silent!”
The Chancellor’s scribe said:
“I have heard that, for a scholar living in the world,
his clothing should be enough to clothe himself,
his food and drink enough to provide for his relatives,
within he is able to support his family,
without, he does not rely on others.
So only when one’s self is cultivated can one regulate the household,
and only when the household is regulated can one govern offices.
Thus, one who can eat only coarse vegetables and grain cannot speak of filial piety,
one whose wife and children suffer from hunger and cold cannot speak of kindness,
one whose family business is not managed cannot speak of order.
Dwelling in this world,
acting with oneself,
and yet burdened by these three shortcomings,
ought indeed to keep silent.”
5.6 "On Supporting One’s Parents, Chapter Twenty-Five"
The Scholar said:
“The truly skillful provider need not always use meat and grain fodder;
the truly skillful supplier of clothing need not always use brocade and embroidery.
If with what one has, one does one’s utmost to serve one's parents,
that is the utmost of filial piety.
Therefore, even an ordinary man laboring diligently,
is still able to fulfill ritual compliance;
sipping beans and drinking water,
is enough to show his reverence.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘In today’s filial sons,
those who are called able to provide
do not show respect;
how do they differ from others?’
Therefore, the highest filial piety is attending to the parents’ intent;
next is attending to their countenance;
next is attending to the body’s well-being.
Value is placed on ritual,
not on the mere provision of nourishment;
with ritual in accord, the heart is in harmony,
even if the provision is insufficient,
it is acceptable.
The *Book of Changes* says:
‘Though the eastern neighbor slaughters cattle,
it is not so good as the western neighbor’s simple sacrifice.’
Therefore, wealth and status without ritual
amount to less than poverty and humble rank with filial and fraternal devotion.
Within the family’s inner quarters, fulfill filial piety;
outside the gates, fulfill fraternal reverence;
in the relations with friends, fulfill utmost trust.
These three
are the utmost of filial piety.
To manage the household
is not to accumulate wealth;
to serve parents filially
is not only to offer fine meats;
but rather, to maintain a harmonious demeanor,
attend to their intent, and fulfill all rites and righteousness.”
The Chancellor’s scribe said:
“At eighty one is called diē,
at seventy one is called mào.
The elderly, unless they eat meat they do not feel full,
unless they wear silk, they do not feel warm.
Therefore, the filial son gives them delicacies and tender food to nurture their mouths,
and light, warm garments to nurture their bodies.
Zēngzǐ served Zēng Xī,
and there was always wine and meat.
Lacking proper mourning garb,
even Gōng Xī Chì could not present a respectable appearance.
Without dishes and meats,
even Mǐn and
Zēng could not complete their service.
For ritual should never be performed without substance;
thus, only when the reality is present should the decorum be observed.
Rather than having superfluous rites and insufficient provisions,
it is better to have sufficient provisions and lack in rites.
To cleanse goblets only to hold water,
and to offer only coarse grain in proper order,
though ritual is complete,
it is not of highest value.”
Wénxué said:
“The mother of Zhōu Xiāngwáng lacked neither wine nor meat;
her clothing and food were not inferior to that of Zēng Xī;
yet she bore the name of being unfilial,
because she was unable to serve her parents.
The jūnzǐ values the ritual;
the petty man seeks only sustenance.
If one calls a beggar to come and summons him,
throws food to give it,
even the beggar will not accept it.
If the jūnzǐ is without the proper ritual,
even if the food is fine, he will not eat it.
Thus, if the host does not personally offer the food,
the guest will not perform the sacrifice.
Here the giving is light but the ritual weighty.”
The Chancellor’s Scribe said:
“The greatest filial piety is to nourish one’s parents as if nourishing the whole world or a state;
next is nourishing them with official emolument;
lower is by personal effort.
Thus the king or lord
are the highest;
ministers and great officers
are next.
Speaking in terms of a household:
if a worthy son holds a prominent post in the world,
there are grand halls and deep chambers,
comfortable carriages with great horses,
light and warm clothing,
fine and tender food.
Without these,
coarse robe and leather cap,
dwelling in poverty and mean alleyways,
having breakfast but lacking supper,
eating vegetables, coarse grain, and pungent herbs,
with preserved meat seen only after the sacrifices.
An old parent’s belly is not the orchards of Tángyuán;
only vegetables fill the dishes.
Coarse fare and vegetables
are food even beggars would not take,
yet sons use them to nourish their parents;
though they wish to do so with ritual,
it is not truly precious.”
Wénxué said:
“To lack the ability but usurp the position,
to lack merit but enjoy the emolument,
even the wealth and honor one has
come from the feeding of Zhé
and Jiǎo.
Lofty towers giving far views,
tables full of delicacies,
and yet this cannot be said to be filial.
An old parent’s belly is not a thief’s sack:
why should it be always filled with ill-gotten things?
If what is taken is not rightfully held or deserved,
then as wealth comes in, trouble follows;
the body verges on death and disaster,
so how can one eat preserved meat?
Zēng Cān
and Mǐn Zǐ had not the nourishment of ministers or chancellors,
but had the name of filial sons;
Zhōu Xiāngwáng was wealthy and owned all under heaven,
yet was burdened with being unable to serve his parents.
Thus, impoverished ritual but lavish nourishment
is not filial piety;
raiding the granary to nourish parents
is not filial piety.”
The Chancellor’s Scribe said:
“The highest filial piety is to care for both appearance and feeling;
next is to bring comfort to parents;
next is to keep oneself whole.
In the past,
Chén Yú turned his back on Hàn,
and was beheaded at Zhīshuǐ;
Wǔ endangered by villainy,
and had three clans exterminated.
In recent times,
Zhǔfù Yǎn acted unlawfully and was destroyed;
Lǚ Bùshū played with words and was executed;
by conducting oneself carelessly,
punishment reached even innocent kin.
From this it may be seen:
empty ritual is of no benefit to oneself.
When words and deeds match,
ritual and nourishment are both fulfilled,
then one may speak of filial piety.
Filial piety lies in sincerity,
not in ornament;
preserving oneself lies in caution,
not in running mouths.”
Wénxué said:
“To speak without sincerity,
to make agreements but be untrustworthy,
to face difficulty without courage,
to serve one’s lord without loyalty—
these are the greatest forms of unfilial conduct.
Mèngzǐ said:
‘The gentlemen of today,
the great officers of today,
are all men of guilt.
All simply conform to others’ wishes to please their evil.’
Now you are not loyal or trustworthy,
with clever words to confuse government,
using flattery to seek acceptance.
Such people
cannot be tolerated in the world.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
‘A scholar holds to the one and does not waver,
follows principle and seeks no outside help,
performs his office and that is all.’
Thus, to hold a low position and speak loftily
is a crime;
to speak beyond your station
is arrogance.
Now, having been summoned by edict to deliberate with the nobles,
why do you merely battle with words in vain?”
5.7 “On Criticism, Chapter Twenty-Six”
The Chancellor’s Scribe said:
“Mountains and mounds do not reject peppercorns and blades of grass,
and so become high;
the jūnzǐ does not refuse words from those who carry firewood,
and so his reputation spreads.
Hence, he who sees much is broad,
he who hears much is wise;
those who block remonstrance are cut off,
those who act alone are isolated.
Thus, he who consults inferiors in planning does not miss the strategy;
he who seeks many opinions in action does not stumble in his achievements.
The Book of Odes says:
‘Consult even the grass-cutters and wood-gatherers.’
Thus, even commoners may speak their opinions;
how much more so the court historians and ministers!
Spring and Autumn Annals does not record literary adornment for officials,
but writes down ‘shouting’
to indicate they were administrators.
Confucius said:
‘Even if I am not used,
may I not at least hear of it?’
Though I am not clever,
yet I have always inclined my ear to the wind below,
trimmed my nails and pointed,
and received teaching along the path to the way of the worthy.
If Wénxué is correct in his argument,
what harm is there in what I say?
If Wénxué is mistaken,
then even without the Chancellor’s Scribe,
who would not also object?”
Wénxué said:
“To use righteousness to assist others is called loyalty;
to use evil to lead others is called flattery.
Those who take offense at faults but accept good
are a lord’s loyal ministers,
a great officer’s upright men.
Confucius said:
‘If a great officer has three who debate with him,
though he be immoral,
he will not lose his estate.’
Now you hold a place among administrators,
but lack a loyal and upright heart;
you cannot correct what is crooked,
cannot right what is wrong,
go with the flow to preserve yourself,
follow the wind to please those above.
What the ruler says, you blindly listen;
what he does, you crookedly follow;
like a shadow to a shape,
an echo to a sound,
never judging right or wrong.
Wearing the scholar’s robe,
donning the scholar’s cap,
yet unable to fulfill the scholar’s way,
you are not a true scholar.
Like an earthen dragon—
though complete in form, not a dragon;
tīnglì is like a vegetable but tastes different;
jade and stone are alike but not of the same kind.
You are not a follower of the Kǒng clan, holding to the classic and the Way,
but a minister who flatters the influential;
you are not one of us.
Rǎn Yǒu served as steward for the Jì clan and helped them;
Confucius said:
‘Let the disciples beat the drum and attack such as him—
so be it!’
Thus, to assist a tyrant is not wise,
to help a tyrant amass wealth is not benevolent.”
The Chancellor’s Scribe was silent and made no reply.
5.8 “On Profit, Chapter Twenty-Seven”
The Dàfū said:
“He who rules as an enlightened lord for an age,
takes on the toil and care for the myriad people,
pondering the unrest in the northern frontier;
therefore, he sends envoys to recommend worthy and good men,
and outstanding disciples of letters,
carefully extending invitations to men of the Way,
wishing to observe diverse arguments and alternative strategies,
keeping an open mind and attentive ear to listen,
hoping thereby to achieve success.
Yet none among the learned produce extraordinary plans or far-reaching schemes,
nor strategies to strike the Xiōngnú and secure the borders;
they clutch dead bamboo,
holding fast to empty words,
knowing not the proper course between advance and retreat,
nor the changes of the times;
their arguments lack foundation,
like scratching one’s back when the itch is on the knee,
contending endlessly in the courts,
with such clamorous noise as to be intolerable,
as if they believe that simply tasting items by mouth brings a task to completion;
is this what an enlightened lord wishes to hear?”
The scholar of literature said:
“All the learned, when answering the registers,
travel divergent roads but return to one end,
pointing invariably to upholding propriety and righteousness,
withdrawing from profit-seeking,
restoring the ways of antiquity,
correcting the errors of the present time,
none failing to propose the attainment of peace;
though not all proposals are fully reliable,
there should be some that are workable.
Those in office are blind to illustrious virtue,
but well aware of trivial profits;
thus they thwart affairs and undermine plans,
weighing and calculating,
thereby leading to indecision until now.
Without Ru, nothing is accomplished;
what the gōng and qīng wish to accomplish is gain.”
The Dàfū said:
“A severe appearance masking a weak heart,
such is one who confuses true and false.
Fine words outside but hemp within,
such is one who confuses reality.
Scholars of letters wear ample garments and broad sashes,
stealthily adopting the attire of Zhōu Gōng,
bend low and behave timidly,
secretly mimicking the manner of Zhòng Ní;
in their discussions and recitations,
they covertly use the language of Shāng
and Cì;
with critical words on government,
they appropriate the talent of Guǎn
and Yàn.
Their hearts are inferior to ministers,
their ambitions are beneath the ruler of ten thousand chariots.
When entrusted with administration,
they fall into confusion and misrule.
Thus, to select a man by his words
is like judging a horse by its hair.
This is why, so often, nominations prove unsuitable.
The imperial rescript states:
‘We commend the worthy within our realm,
thus we carefully invite heroic and learned men from all quarters, and grant them swift promotion.’
Yet those who speak are not necessarily virtuous;
why is this?
Because it is easy to speak, but difficult to act.
There are those who forsake their cart but recognize their ox;
such value the unspeaking, who nevertheless accomplish much.
Wú Duó destroyed himself with his tongue,
Zhǔfù Yǎn killed himself with his tongue.
The hédàn cries at night,
but brings no more brightness;
Zhǔfù’s hoot as an owl
brings no benefit in death.
It is not that officials wish only to secure gain,
but that scholars are shackled by obsolete methods,
and are led by idle talk.”
The scholar of literature said:
“He who can both speak and act
is Táng or Wǔ.
He who can speak but not act
is an official.
Scholars of letters may steal the garb of Zhōu Gōng,
but it is the officials who seize the office of Zhōu Gōng.
Scholars are bound by the strictures of old teaching,
while officials are bound by profit.
Zhǔfù Yǎn met his end by his tongue,
officials ruin themselves for profit.
A fine horse has talent to run a thousand leagues,
yet none but Zàofù can drive it;
Yǔ possessed wisdom over ten thousand men,
but unless Shùn served as minister, it could not be used.
Thus when Jì Huánzǐ presided in government,
Liǔxià Huì suddenly vanished;
when Kǒngzǐ became Minister of Justice,
only then did the rebels rise up.
To raise a noble horse is Bólè’s task,
but its true use is Zàofù’s.
When Zàofù holds the reins,
the horse cares not if it is swift or slow,
either way it covers the road.
In the time of Zhōu Gōng,
no matter if a man was worthy or not,
all could discuss perfect order.
Thus, a good charioteer can guide any horse;
a wise minister can use any man.
But today, if extraordinary talent is appointed, only to have Zāng Zōu drive the coach,
it is like yoking a noble horse to a salt wagon and blaming it for being slow.
This is why so many worthy and able candidates fail when recommended.”
The Dàfū said:
“Alas!
The learned are commonplace and lacking in merit,
they speak much but nothing is accomplished,
their words and actions do not match.
Like thieves who burrow through walls,
they have caused trouble since ancient times.
Thus Kǒng Qiū was denounced and cast out by the Lord of Lǔ,
never to be employed in any age.
Why was this?
For their words are entangled with many loose ends,
roundabout and impractical.
Therefore the King of Qín burned their books and would not follow their methods,
cast them into the Wei and would not use them.
How, then, can they drum their tongues,
raise their eyebrows,
and press forward with arguments?
Such matters are not for the state!”
5.9 “The Illness of the State, Chapter 28”
The scholar said:
“If a state has worthy men but does not employ them,
it is not the fault of the men,
but the shame of the ruler.
Kǒngzǐ,
the Great Sage,
was not employed by any feudal lord;
though he held a minor post in Lǔ,
in three months
order was achieved without issuing commands,
prohibitions needed no enforcement,
and virtue flowed like timely rain nourishing all things,
causing all to rise up.
How much more, then, if he held office at the imperial court and spread the virtue and teachings of a sage king?
Today, the gōng and qīng hold high office,
grasp the levers of the realm,
and for over ten years
have failed to confer benefit or virtue on the people,
though they claim toil on behalf of the people,
yet the common people grow poor and destitute,
while private households accumulate wealth in the millions.
This is a shame to the gentleman,
and what ‘Fá Tán’ censures.
In former days,
Shāng Yǎng was minister of Qín,
succeeding in rites of humility,
but putting greed for profit before integrity,
valuing merit over virtue,
pursuing advancement at all costs,
without deepened virtue for the people,
but strict with punishments for the state,
and so customs declined and resentment grew.
Thus King Huì cooked him in brine
to apologize to the world.
Even at that time,
one could not argue policy.
Now, those in power scorn scholars for being poor and verbose,
while scholars in turn lament that those in power are rich, noble, and beset with troubles.”
The Dàfū gazed at the scholar,
sorrowful and silent.
Chancellor Shǐ said:
“When disputing the affairs of state,
and discussing the rights and wrongs of those who hold office,
why not reason with each other calmly and persuasively?
Why must it be so vehement and urgent as this!
The reason why the dàfū find it difficult to abolish the state monopolies on salt
and iron
is not out of private interest,
but out of concern for the state's expenses
and the costs on the frontiers.
The scholars earnestly dispute over salt
and iron, and this also is not for themselves,
but because they wish to return to ancient ways and uphold rényì.
Both sides hold to their principles;
but responsibilities change with the times.
How can one stubbornly cling to ancient methods and reject present policies?
Even the Xiǎoyǎ is not above people,
and must at times be revised.
If any among the scholars were able to bring peace and order to the realm,
attract people from distant regions,
and ensure the borders suffered no calamity from raiders,
then all taxes might be remitted for the scholars—
how much more so the management of
salt, iron, and balanced delivery!
The esteem for the methods of the rú
is in their humility and willingness to yield,
and their ability to move people by the Way.
Now your disputes are bewildered and abrupt,
without the fair and measured words of Chì or
Cì,
but display only looks of disdain and rejection—
this is not what I have heard should be.
The dàfū may overstate their case,
but so too do the scholars;
the scholars simply do not admit error to the dàfū.”
The Worthies [xiánliáng]
and the Literary Scholars [wénxué] all rose from their seats, saying:
“We are indeed ignorant and narrow-minded,
daring to step into the great court,
and have spoken rashly,
even to the point of contradicting those in authority.
Just as medicine and wine are bitter to the mouth but cure the illness,
so loyal words may be disagreeable to the ear but are beneficial in practice.
Thus, those who startle and confront are a blessing,
whereas those who flatter and fawn are a curse.
Where the forests are thick, fierce winds abound;
and where wealth and honor gather, so too do sycophantic words.
Though for ten thousand leagues we hear only ‘yes, yes’ day after day,
it is only later that we hear the scholars’ bold words—
these indeed are the needed medicine and needle-stone for the lords and ministers.”
The dàfū relaxed somewhat,
turned to the Literary Scholars and said to the Worthies:
“In remote alleys there is much quibbling debate,
yet those who are inexperienced are hard to persuade.
The Literary Scholars stubbornly cleave to remote and obscure words,
and refuse ever to change.
As for ancient affairs,
and sayings from the past,
these are well known and may be observed.
But to judge the present age,
we must use our own eyes to see
and our ears to hear;
for times differ and so too do events.
In the age of Wén and Jǐng,
at the beginning of Jiànyuán,
the people were simple and returned to their roots,
officials were honest and valued themselves,
all was diligent and harmonious,
people were abundant and households were prosperous.
Yet today, though neither policies nor teachings have changed,
why then has custom grown ever more corrupt and society more and more decadent?
Officials have little honesty,
the people little sense of shame,
punishments do not root out evil,
and yet crime does not cease.
People these days say:
‘The rustic scholars are no match for the urban officials.’
The Literary Scholars all come from Shāndōng,
hoping to join in great debates.
Since you, dàfū, have long deliberated in the capital,
I would like for you to make clear the rights and wrongs of policies,
and the reasoning behind them.”
Xiánliáng said:
“As for Shāndōng,
it is the heart of the world,
and the battlefield of worthy men.
Gāo Huángdì ascended like a dragon and soared like a phoenix between Sòng and
Chǔ;
the youths of Shāndōng—Xiāo,
Cáo, Fán,
Lì, Téng,
Guàn, and their kind—served as his aids.
Even though in different ages,
there were only the likes of Hóng Yǎo
and Tài Diān.
Yǔ sprang from Xīqiāng,
King Wén was born among the Běiyí,
yet their sagely virtue surpassed their times,
they possessed the talent of ten thousand people,
shouldered the responsibilities of the multitude,
entered and left the cities,
and one day knew not to return,
often ending up as mere attendants or laborers.
Though I was not born and raised in the capital,
my talent is sluggish and my wisdom low,
unfit to join in grand discussions,
yet I dare to draw from the words of the elders in my village.
In former times,
ordinary people wore warm clothing that was not extravagant,
their tools were simple and sturdy, yet effective;
clothes sufficed to cover the body,
utensils sufficed for daily use,
horses sufficed to ease walking,
carts sufficed for self-transport,
wine sufficed to bring cheer but did not lead to excess,
music sufficed to harmonize the mind but was not licentious,
inside, there was not the sound of feasting,
outside, there was not the sight of idle wandering,
on the move they carried baskets,
at rest they hoed and weeded,
living frugally yet with abundant resources,
improving the fundamentals and so enriching the people,
sending off the dead with mourning but not with ostentation,
nourishing the living in contentment but not with extravagance,
the great ministers were upright and free of desires,
the officials were lenient but not harsh;
thus the common people found their nature at peace,
and the hundred officials secured their positions.
At the beginning of Jiànyuán,
literature was honored and virtue cultivated,
and the world was governed in peace.
Afterwards,
treacherous ministers, each using their skills and tricks,
undermined the era of perfect order;
on the outside, they erected barriers at the mountains and seas,
on the inside, they sought profit in all things.
Yáng Kěkào set the string currency,
Jiāng Chōng forbade certain apparel,
Grand Master Zhāng changed the laws,
Dù Zhōu oversaw the courts,
penalties and redemptions were apportioned,
minute details were enforced,
their number could not be exhausted.
Xià Lán and his ilk arrested at random,
Wáng Wēnshū and his followers murdered recklessly,
cruel officials arose,
disturbing the honest people.
At that time,
the people could not preserve their own heads,
and the wealthy and powerful could not ensure the safety of their clans.
The sagely lord became aware,
and so punished and executed Chōng and others,
exterminated the cruel traitors,
to end the resentment of capital crimes,
and answer the demands of the people.
Thus the people became calm and at peace again.
Yet the woe accumulated over generations did not end,
the wounds and pains remain unhealed to this day.
Thus officialdom still clings to policies of cruelty and violence,
and strongmen still harbor thoughts of forceful seizure.
Great ministers monopolize power and make summary judgments,
powerful and cunning men form factions and encroach upon others;
the rich and noble are extravagant,
the poor and base plot murders;
women’s work is difficult to complete and easily ruined,
carriages and tools are hard to make and easily broken,
carriages do not last a year,
utensils do not last a full year,
a cart costs a thousand stones,
a garment ten zhōng.
Ordinary folk have carved cups and painted tables,
stands and mats embroidered with patterns,
maids and concubines wear fine silk and silk shoes,
even commoners eat refined rice and meat;
every neighborhood has its customs,
every clan has its gatherings,
broad avenues where they race and chase,
narrow lanes where they tread the ball;
few now grasp hoes and carry spades,
few plow and weave with their own hands,
many gather for show and strike poses,
many paint their faces white and use blue and black for eyebrows.
They have nothing, yet pretend to have;
are poor, yet boast of riches;
splendid outside, empty within;
silk and hemp costumes,
not nurturing life in the living,
but lavish in funeral send-offs for the dead,
impoverishing whole households when burying the deceased,
sending off daughters by the cartful,
the rich wish to surpass others,
the poor strive to catch up,
the rich hoard their treasures in vain,
the poor take on debt.
Thus, the people’s years are hurried and their lives shortened,
the poor have little shame,
the destitute little integrity;
this is why punishments do not eliminate evil, and villainy still does not cease.
Therefore, when a state has severe and urgent exactions,
it inevitably suffers the disease of want and scattering.”
6.1 “On Scattering and Want, Chapter 29”
The Grandee said:
“In my view, Xiánliáng is not much improved,
but only turns darkness and light,
like two chariots following and clattering together.
Have the scholars never seen the cicala of late summer?
Its sound enters the ear,
but when the autumn wind arrives, its voice ceases.
These men do not change their ways through advice,
do not heed their troubles,
and only fall silent when disaster comes,
but then it is too late.”
Xiánliáng said:
“Kǒngzǐ, reading the Shǐjì,
heaved a deep sigh,
sorrowing at the collapse of right virtue,
at the peril of lord and subject.
Noble and worthy men
are those who take the world as their responsibility.
Those with great responsibility think far ahead,
and those who think far forget what is near.
Their sincerity is sorrowful and compassionate,
with empathy for others,
thus their loyalty stands alone, unencumbered.
This is why poets grieve and compose,
why Bǐgàn
and Zǐxū gave their lives, forgetting their own peril.
How anxious are the labors for the people—
how could one keep silent?
The Book of Poetry says:
‘My heart is heavy as burning,
I dare not jest or idly talk.’
Kǒngzǐ was unsettled,
grieving for the age’s hardship.
Mòzǐ was harried,
lamenting the world.”
The Grandee was silent.
The Chancellor said:
“I wish to hear about ‘scattering and want.’”
Xiánliáng said:
“Palaces, carriages and horses,
clothing and implements,
funerals, sacrifices, food and drink,
music and beauty, lovely playthings—
these are desires that people cannot put aside.
Therefore the sage-kings created systems and standards to restrain them.
Yet recently,
men of rank strive for profit and advantage,
neglecting propriety and righteousness;
so the people follow and imitate,
often exceeding the regulations.
Therefore, I present this:
it is said:
“In ancient times,
grain, vegetables, and fruits
were not eaten out of season,
birds, beasts, fish, and turtles
were not eaten if not properly taken.
Thus hunting nets did not enter the marshes,
mixed coats were not taken.
Now, the rich chase and drive, laying waste with nets and snares,
seizing fawns and nestlings,
soaking themselves in drink along the length of the rivers.
They eat rare lamb and veal,
nearly unborn thighs and shoulders,
yellow hides and unweaned mouths.
Spring goslings and autumn chicks,
winter greens and hot leeks,
wild ginger, smartweed, perilla,
mushrooms, tree fungus, bracken,
furry fruit, insects, badger.
In ancient times,
rafters were gathered and roofs thatched with reeds,
boats of clay returned to humble caves,
sufficient to ward off cold and heat,
to shelter from wind and rain, that was all.
In later generations,
the rafters gathered were not hewn,
the thatch not trimmed,
there was no work of chopping and shaving,
nor any labor of grinding and polishing.
Dàfū used well-joined beams,
shì capped their pillars,
commoners used axes to shape wood for constructing their dwellings, that was all.
Now, the wealthy reinforce wells with crossbeams and add layers,
engrave patterned balustrades and railings,
and adorn the walls with jade and fine ornamentation.
In ancient times,
clothing did not fit precisely,
utensils were not perfectly suited for use,
and these things were not traded in the market.
Now, among the people, things are intricately carved though unfit for use,
objects inscribed and decorated though useless.
Black and yellow mixed with blue,
garments embroidered with five colors,
toys and trinkets among commoners and women,
shows with wild beasts, horse plays wrestling tigers,
Tángtí chasing people,
strange insects and foreign entertainers.
In ancient times,
the zhūhóu did not feed their horses,
unless the Tiānzǐ gave orders
to use carriages to go to pasture.
For commoners who rode horses,
it sufficed to ease their labors, that was all.
Thus, on the road one wore coarse hemp,
when stopped, returned to the plow.
Now the wealthy arrange processions of carriages and lines of riders,
with matched teams and adorned carriages.
Those of middling means have light sedans and short-axled carts,
decorated with plaited ropes and ornaments on hoofs.
Yet a single horse kept stabled,
consumes the food of six members of an average family,
and equals the work of one able-bodied man.
In ancient times,
commoners only wore silk when old and weak,
otherwise, clothing was of hemp and ramie, that was all,
thus they were called “common-clothed.”
In later days,
silk lined with ramie,
straight collars without lapels,
robes joined without seams.
Brocade and embroidered silks
were the attire of rulers and their consorts.
Fine cocoon-spun silks
were proper adornment for weddings.
Therefore, patterned silks and fine weaves
were not traded in the market.
Now, the wealthy wear elaborate embroidery, gauze, and silk,
those of middling means plain calico and fine brocade.
Commoners now wear the garb of royal consorts,
base people dwell among wedding ornaments.
Thus, the price of fine silk doubles that of regular silk,
yet the use of regular silk doubles that of fine silk.
In ancient times,
wooden carts were solid and unadorned,
shoulder carriages lacked fitted frames.
In later times,
the wooden rims were left unwrapped,
long axles had several spokes,
reed mats covered the canopy,
the canopy bore no decoration of lacquer and thread.
Dàfū and shì had only simple or double-layered wood wares,
baskets lined with soft leather.
Commoners used lacquered carriages, large wooden rims, chariot wheels.
Now, wealthy commoners use silver and gilded ornaments,
adorned toggles and covered shafts.
Those of middling means have inlaid bits and painted trappings,
jewel-studded bridle ornaments and flying wheel covers.
In ancient times,
deerskin robes and fur coverings
were worn with hoofs and feet unremoved.
Later on,
dàfū and shì wore stitched fox and raccoon pelts,
lamb and leopard-sleeved garments.
Commoners had woolen trousers with red borders,
sheep-fleece hats and fur-lined coats.
Now, the wealthy wear sables and otter furs,
white fox and duck down.
Those of middling means wear tapestry garments stitched with gold thread,
swallow-tail caps and “Dài” yellow.
In ancient times,
for riding, commoners used plain rope reins,
with leather saddle and animal-hide mat, that was all.
Later on,
leather saddles were made with yak hair,
iron bits remained undecorated.
Now, the wealthy have jeweled ear-plates, silver hairpin decorations,
golden pendants and jade-studded bridles,
tapestry-embroidered saddle blankets,
splendid bright saddle gear.
Those of middling means use lacquered leather straps,
painted and left to dry in the sun.
In ancient times,
drinking was by scooping wine with a common vessel,
without ritual cups and sacrificial sets.
Later on,
commoners used only bamboo, willow, clay, and gourd for their vessels.
Only jade and lacquered ritual vessels received carved decoration.
Now, the wealthy use silver-rimmed, gold-handled cups,
golden pitchers and jade goblets.
Those of middling means use “Yěwáng”-type linen vessels,
decorated gilt and painted cups.
A single fine cup can buy ten copper cups,
yet their use is the same despite cost.
The reproach of Jīzǐ
was once for the Tiānzǐ,
now it is found among commoners.
In ancient times,
millet was roasted and wild grains eaten,
with pork used sparingly for entertaining each other.
Later on,
when villagers drank,
the elders would have second helpings,
the young would eat standing,
one sauce, one meat dish,
and a simple meal together, that was all.
In later times,
at marriage feasts and mutual invitations,
there were vegetable soup and white rice,
pickled shredded meat and cooked meat.
Now, among the people, at feasts,
dishes are stacked upon each other,
roast and grilled foods fill the table,
braised turtle, carp sashimi,
venison, quail eggs, mandarin, dogwood,
salted fish, sweet wine, sauces, and cured vegetables,
myriad foods and mixed flavors.
In ancient times,
commoners in spring and summer tilled and weeded,
in autumn and winter stored their harvests,
toiled from dawn to dusk,
working through the night to continue the day.
As the Shī Jīng says:
“By day you toil at thatching,
by night you twist rope,
quickly climb the house,
and sow all the grains from the start.”
Unless during the sacrifices of preserved meats, they did not rest,
and except for ritual feasts, there was no wine or meat.
Now, at weddings and banquets,
the food and drink follow one upon another,
hangovers last for days,
chores are neglected in succession,
and fear of want is gone.
In ancient times,
commoners ate coarse grain and wild herbs,
and apart from village drink, sacrifices at the winter solstice, and ritual feasts, there was no wine or meat.
Thus, zhūhóu did not slaughter cattle and sheep without cause,
dàfū and shì did not slaughter dogs and pigs without reason.
Now, in lanes and hamlets,
at the intersections and markets,
they kill and cook without cause,
gathering in the wild.
Carrying grain there,
they return home with meat.
The flesh of a single pig,
equals the yield of a year’s harvest,
fifteen dǒu of grain
serving half a month’s food for an able-bodied man.
In ancient times,
commoners used fish and beans for ancestors’ sacrifices,
offering at their ancestral shrines each spring and autumn.
Shì had one ancestral temple,
dàfū had three,
conducting the five seasonal rites at the proper times,
but did not sacrifice outside the gate.
Now, the wealthy pray at famous mountains,
expecting blessings from streams and rivers,
slaughter oxen and beat drums,
with theater, singing, and dance.
Those of middling means occupy buildings on the road to the south,
cloud towers over water,
killing sheep and dogs,
playing lutes and blowing flutes.
The poor offer chicken and pork with five-flavored spices,
guard effigies and scattered offerings,
and gather at community altars with tents.
In ancient times,
virtue and conduct were sought for the sake of fortune,
therefore they performed sacrifices with generosity.
Benevolence and righteousness were sought for the sake of auspiciousness,
thus divination was rare.
But now, the common people are lax in conduct yet seek from spirits,
slack in ritual yet devoted to sacrifice,
neglectful of kin yet valuing power,
given to absurdity yet trusting in the calendar,
listening to vain words in hopes of gain,
offering real goods in exchange for empty blessings.
In ancient times,
the jūnzǐ, from early to late, diligently pursued virtue;
the xiǎorén, morning and evening, tirelessly sought labor.
Thus, the jūnzǐ did not eat without cultivation,
and the xiǎorén did not eat without toil.
But now, the common people embellish deception and practice fraud,
acting as shamans and priests,
to obtain offerings and thanks,
firm of brow and sharp of tongue,
some thereby achieve enterprise and attain wealth;
thus, people who are wary of real work
abandon their true calling to learn these arts.
Thus, in the streets and alleys there are shamans,
in every neighborhood there are priests.
In ancient times,
there were no beds of hardwood poles,
no tables of curved wood.
In later ages,
the common folk took to using hardwood beams,
birch for mattress supports.
The shì did not cut boards for completion,
the dàfū used only rush mats.
But the wealthy now have embroidered curtains and canopies,
painted screens and ornamented beds.
Those of moderate means hang brocade high,
with colored painting in cinnabar lacquer.
In ancient times,
bedding was of skins, furs, and grass mats,
without the addition of cushions or layered seats,
or the beauty of felt and fine mats.
Later on,
the dàfū and shì again used grass edges on mats,
flat mats of rush and single-layered reeds.
The common people had only grass mats with rope borders,
single mats of rush or cattail.
Now the wealthy have embroidered cushions and soft feathered beds,
and beds covered with rush mats.
Those of moderate means use dog or sheep skins instead of felt,
and simply sit on flat mats.
In ancient times,
there was no porridge or cooked soups,
nor buying of food in the marketplace.
Later on,
there were butchers and brewers,
wine and dried meats, fish, and salt could be had at the market.
Now cooked foods are laid out everywhere,
delicacies fill the markets,
industry and labor fall into sloth,
meals are always punctual,
with pork, chives, and eggs,
dog intestine and horse penis,
fried fish and sliced liver,
pickled mutton and chilled chicken,
milk curd, fermented horse milk wine,
dog’s stomach and dried meat,
boiled lamb and bean dishes,
young animal flesh and goose stew,
strong-scented abalone and sweet melon,
roasted millet and grilled venison.
In ancient times,
they used earthen drums and clapped percussion sticks,
struck wood and slapped stones
to fully express their joy.
Later,
among qīng and dàfū appeared pipes and chimes,
the shì had zithers and lutes.
Formerly,
at village wine-feasts among the people,
each followed local custom,
playing zithers and drumming on jars, nothing more.
There were no refined sounds,
no changing modes.
Now the wealthy have bells, drums, and orchestras of the five musics,
with many singing boys.
Those of moderate means play the reed pipe and string zither,
and perform dances of Zhèng and songs of Zhào.
In ancient times,
a clay coffin sufficed to contain the corpse,
wooden boards formed a simple enclosure,
enough to collect the flesh and bones,
to store hair and teeth, nothing more.
Later,
they used paulownia coffins with no wrappings,
painted caskets left uncarved.
Now, the wealthy have embroidered chambers with written inscriptions joined together.
Those of moderate means use catalpa coffins and elm caskets,
the poor paint rough garments and robes,
with silk bags and coarse satchels.
In ancient times,
mingqì burial objects had form but no substance,
to show people these things could not be used.
Later,
they kept jars of pickles and sauces,
paulownia horses and figurines served as sacrifices,
but the objects were incomplete.
Now, much wealth and many treasures are amassed,
and burial items are used as if for the living.
In prefectures and commanderies, officials
prepare mulberry-wood chariots with paired figures and turning wheels;
the common man, if he lacks images with faces and necks,
dresses wooden figurines in fine silks and satins.
In ancient times,
there was no mounding or planting of trees,
and the posthumous rites were conducted at the sleeping hall;
there were no altars or halls as dwellings,
no ancestral temples or audience chambers.
Later,
they made burial mounds;
the common people’s graves were scarcely half a man’s height,
high enough for concealment only.
Now the wealthy pile earth into mountains,
and arrange trees into groves,
with terraces and pavilions joined in succession,
multi-storey halls and added towers.
Those of moderate means have shrine halls with screens and doors,
walls with watchtowers and palisades.
In ancient times,
if a neighbor was in mourning,
the mills would not pound in rhythm,
the street would not sing or chant.
When Kǒngzǐ ate beside one in mourning,
he never ate his fill;
if Zǐ wept that day,
then he would not sing.
Now, people use another’s funeral as a pretext to demand wine and meat,
rejoicing if given a seat and insisting on distinction,
singing, dancing, comic actors,
and continuous laughter with jesters and juggling.
In ancient times,
relations between men and women were held in high respect,
clothes for marriage were
not yet prescribed.
After the time of Yú
and Xià,
outerwear was linen, lined with silk,
bone hairpins and ivory earrings,
wives of feudal lords were granted brocade and fine sashes, no more.
Now the wealthy wear fur coats of red fox,
with elaborate ornaments and tinkling pendants.
Those of moderate means have long trailing skirts and cross-layered robes,
jade hairpins and auspicious jewelry.
In ancient times,
all love was bestowed upon the living,
all grief upon the dead.
Thus the sages set up measured rites,
not added in vain.
Now the living receive no real love or respect,
but in death, people compete in extravagance;
even without true feelings of grief or mourning,
those who lavishly bury with rich goods
are said to be filial,
and establish a famous reputation in the world,
earning public glory and renown.
Thus the people imitate and emulate one another,
even to the point of dismantling their houses and selling their livelihoods.
In ancient times,
the harmony of husband and wife
was one man and one woman,
thus realizing the way of family and household.
Later,
the shì had one concubine,
the dàfū had two,
the zhūhóu had cousins and sisters for consorts, nine women in all.
Now, the zhūhóu have them by the hundreds,
the qīng and dàfū by the tens,
those of moderate means have attendants,
the wealthy fill their chambers.
Thus, women may languish in resentment and miss their time,
men may be cast off and die alone, without a match.
In ancient times,
when there was famine and scarcity,
abundant years compensated for losses,
and old customs continued without alteration.
Now, artisans innovate and officials harbor different intentions,
ruining accomplishments,
so as to conceal their motives.
Their minds are fixated on achievements,
concerned only with appearances.
Merits are accumulated to trade for reputation,
without regard for the people’s urgent needs.
Fields and countryside remain untilled,
yet pavilions and lodges are adorned,
cities and villages lie in ruins,
but their walls are raised ever higher.
“In ancient times,
human strength was not exhausted in rivalry with beasts,
nor was the people’s wealth taken to feed dogs and horses;
thus resources abounded and labor was ample.
Now, fierce beasts and rare creatures cannot till or weed,
yet those who ought to farm and labor are made to feed them.
The common people sometimes lack even rough clothing,
while dogs and horses dress in embroidered silk.
The masses may not have coarse husks and bran to eat,
but birds and beasts consume grain and meat.
“In ancient times,
rulers respected their duties and cherished their subjects,
mobilizing the people according to season.
The Tiānzǐ regarded All-Under-Heaven as his family,
and ministers and concubines each contributed to public service in due time—
this was the universal principle of past and present.
Now, county officials keep many slaves and servants,
who sit and receive food and clothing,
work privately to amass wealth,
engage in illicit profit,
and fail to exert themselves in their labors,
so the county offices are deprived of productivity.
Some commoners have no small store of grain,
while official slaves possess wealth numbering in hundreds of gold pieces;
the common people toil from dawn until dusk without reprieve,
while slaves and servants lounge, hands-folded, in leisure.
“In ancient times,
one drew near those of kin and kept distant from the far-removed,
valuing those of the same kind, slighting those of different sorts.
No reward for the unworthy,
no sustenance for the useless.
Now the Mán,
and Mò are without merit,
yet hold posts in county offices,
enjoying large houses and great mansions,
sitting to receive food and clothing.
Some among the people struggle from morning to night and still lack,
yet the Mán and Yí sometimes feast on wine and meat to excess.
The common people sweat and strain at their toil,
while now the Mán
and Yí stretch out and lounge with legs entwined.
“In ancient times,
the multitude wore coarse and plain clothing of grass and rush;
their silk was crude, and shoes were only of leather.
In later times,
their soles were unreinforced,
their shoes merely simple leather;
now the rich commission famed craftsmen for leatherwork,
favoring light and extravagant styles for appearance,
with fine silk linings and elaborate bands,
decorated and ornamented all around.
Middle-class folk in Dènglǐ still make straw sandals.
Lowly servants and maids
wear various leather and silk shoes.
Runners and porters are left with rough grass or twisted hemp.
“The sages of old labored with their own bodies to nurture their spirits,
tempered desires to preserve their feelings,
revered Heaven and respected Earth,
walked in virtue and practiced benevolence;
therefore Heaven delighted in them,
their dynasties long-enduring and their years prosperous.
Thus Yáo’s brows were elegant and complexion radiant,
and he enjoyed his realm for a hundred years.
But when Qín Shǐ Huáng beheld strange and eccentric things,
believed in omens and auspices,
and sent Lú Shēng to seek the gate of immortality,
and Xú Shì and others to the sea in search of the elixir of life,
at that time,
the men of Yàn and Qí
cast aside their hoes and plows,
and vied in speaking of spirits and immortals.
Fangshi flocked to Xiányáng in their thousands,
claiming immortals eat gold and drink pearls,
and thus their lives would endure with Heaven and Earth.
Thus he made repeated tours of inspection to the Five Sacred Peaks,
and to coastal pavilions,
seeking spirits and immortals of Pénglái and similar realms.
He often visited the districts and counties,
where the wealthy gave funds in support,
while the poor built roadsides.
Afterward,
the lesser vanished and fled,
the greater hid themselves;
officials pursued and seized them with rough violence,
without any sense of justice.
Beside the royal palace,
huts and hamlets fell to ruin,
not a living seedling or standing tree;
the people became alienated,
with more than half expressing grievances and resentment.
The Shū says:
‘To offer many ceremonies,
and for ceremony to fall short of reality, is not to offer at all.’
Thus the sages would never embody in themselves anything but benevolence and righteousness,
or guide themselves by anything but the correct path.
Therefore the previous Emperors punished Wénchéng
and Wǔlì,
and Emperor Xuān established schools,
drawing close to the loyal and virtuous,
seeking thereby to cut off the origins of strange and evil practices,
and to make manifest the road of ultimate virtue.
“Lavish palaces and mansions
are the bane of the forests and trees;
elaborate tools and ornamental wares
are the bane of treasury resources;
luxurious and extravagant clothing
are the bane of cloth and silk;
feeding dogs and horses with human food
is the bane of the five grains;
giving free rein to appetite
is the bane of fish and meat;
unrestrained expenditure
is the bane of the storehouses and treasuries;
leaks unchecked and unrestrained
are the bane of the fields and countryside;
funerals and sacrifices without measure
are the bane of human life;
ruin and change bring harm to accomplishment,
and commerce and industry, when above, injure agriculture below.
Thus a single goblet may require the labor of a hundred men,
a single screen the toil of ten thousand;
the damage is indeed great!
The eye is exhausted by five colors,
the ear is wearied by the five tones,
the body pursues ultimate lightness and extravagance,
the mouth craves the utmost sweetness and crispness.
Effort is spent on useless things,
wealth consumed by the non-essential;
appetite for food and drink cannot be without limit.
Therefore, if a country’s troubles and shortages are amassed, then government becomes lazy;
if a man’s troubles and shortages are amassed, then his person is endangered.”
The Chancellor said:
“What should be done to treat accumulated shortages?”
6.2 《Rescuing from Want, Section Thirty》
The worthy replied:
“Crookedness in excess turns to the opposite of uprightness;
superficial embellishment must be restrained by substance.
In former times,
when Yànzǐ was Minister of Qí,
he wore a single fox-fur robe for thirty years.
Thus, when the people were extravagant,
he set an example of frugality;
when the people were frugal,
he showed them propriety.
Now, if the sons and grandsons of the Gong, Qīng, Dàfū,
truly would restrain their carriages,
moderate their clothing,
personally practice thrift,
and lead in honest simplicity,
abolishing ornamental gardens and ponds,
reducing lands and estates,
refraining from unnecessary trade in the markets,
eschewing idle pursuits in mountains and lakes,
so that farmers have scope to devote their strength,
and women tasks to occupy their labor—
thus,
the pulse of energies will be balanced and harmonious,
and there will be no illness of accumulated want.”
The dàfū said:
"The orphan speaks of filial piety,
the cripple speaks of walking staffs,
the poor speak of benevolence,
the lowly speak of good governance.
It is easy to comment on matters that do not concern oneself,
and for those standing aside it is easy to affirm;
but those in the midst of affairs are prone to confusion.
Thus Gōngsūn Hóng wore coarse hemp,
Ní Kuān wore unbleached robes,
their clothing was like that of servants,
their food like that of commoners.
Huáinán rebelled within,
while the Mán and Yí were violent without,
thieves and bandits were not restrained by prohibitions,
extravagance was not limited by moderation;
like shamans in times of plague,
they were only able to drum their mouths,
how could such dispersing insufficiency be capable of governing?"
The worthy and good said:
"In the time of Gāo Huángdì,
Xiāo and Cáo served as gōng,
Téng and Guàn and their associates served as qīng,
in such abundance, indeed, they were worthy.
In the era of Wén and Jǐng,
at the beginning of Jiànyuán,
there still remained ministers competing to uphold uprightness.
After that time,
many carried out the sovereign’s desires and followed their own wishes,
few dared to speak straightforwardly or argue face-to-face and offer correct criticism,
using public office to pursue private interests.
Therefore at the time when Wǔ’ān Chancellor disputed the gardens and fields,
he debated right and wrong before the ruler;
yet if the nine-tiered terrace tilts but once,
even Gōngshū Zǐ could not set it straight;
when the current court strays once,
even Yī and Wàng could not restore it.
Thus Chancellor Gōngsūn,
Dàfū Ní walked humbly along the Way,
shared their stipends to nurture the worthy,
humbled themselves and honored those below,
their merits and deeds shone forth,
but their days were insufficient,
and there were no successors to Zǐchǎn among officials.
Yet Gé Yì,
Péng Hóu and others,
ruined their legacy,
tangled and confused the proper order,
destroyed the guest halls and council chambers,
turning them into stables and women’s quarters,
with no rites for supporting the worthy,
and yet proudly maintained arrogant airs,
integrity and shame decayed while they contended for profit.
Thus, though there were fertile fields and spacious estates,
the people had nowhere to go;
those unashamed to seek profit filled the court and market,
great landholders and herders spread over all regions of the country,
they were violent and oppressive,
beside their great mansions and large houses,
even the roads became impassable,
truly, this is hard to cure and beyond the skills of artisans."
The dàfū’s face changed in anger,
he fell silent and did not reply.
6.3 "Admonishing the Stone, Section Thirty-One"
The Chancellor said:
"I heard the elder of Zhèng say:
'When a gentleman composes his expression,
he puts violence and insolence at a distance;
when his words are measured,
he keeps away vulgarity and treachery.'
Thus, his speech can be recorded,
and his conduct can be emulated.
This is what the officers have long wished to see.
As for duels of swordsmen,
or debates over games of chance,
intense looks stirring one another,
power established with no mutual concession,
such that the officers cannot adopt the worthy’s counsel,
and worthies and
scholars acquire a reputation for disrespect,
I am deeply ashamed for the students not to accept such conduct.
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
‘When reasoning with the Way, clarity is necessary,
thus one must attend with care,
and be mutually tolerant,
for mutual tolerance prevents contention,
but contention without yielding
becomes vulgarity.’
Now the officers act without benevolence,
and are clouded by longstanding habits,
so there is no way to hold them further accountable or erase shame.
Although officials are charged with selecting worthies
and men of letters,
and fine officials close to the people,
yet I have not seen them able to use ‘Admonishing the Stone’ to cure the sufferings of the people."
The worthy and good said:
"Jiǎ Shēng said:
‘If one speaks sincerely, the words are plain and not persuasive;
if one speaks profoundly, the words grate on the ear and miss their mark.’
Thus it is said:
‘How easy it is to talk!’
If even talk is not easy,
how much more so is it to put into practice?
This was why Hú Jiàn could not avoid his ill fate,
and why Wú Déjǐ barely escaped misfortune.
As the saying goes:
‘Five thieves seize one honest man,
a warped log abhors a straight line.’
Now if one would lower ‘Admonishing the Stone’,
and make all climes communicate,
I fear it might bring about the troubles of Shèng and
Hú,
and that those who harbor admonition and ‘tuo’ai’
will be labeled unskilled.
‘The wolf treads on his muzzle,
his tail tucked under his body.’
The path of the gentleman,
whether walking or standing still, is truly narrow.
This is why Zǐshí sighs."
6.4 "Eliminating Narrowness, Section Thirty-Two"
The dàfū said:
"A worthy dwells in the great forest,
meets wind and thunder without losing his way.
A fool, though on a broad open road,
is still confused and deluded.
Now, the shǒu and
the xiāng hold authority and perform ceremonies,
presiding over a whole commandery of people,
inheriting the ancient office of regional commander.
Entrusted with delegated power,
they divide and govern a thousand li,
without being checked within;
good or evil depends on themselves,
and if they fail it is only from their own incapacity,
so how can the Way be said to be narrow?"
The xiánliáng said:
“In ancient times, when promoting shì candidates,
selection was made in the villages and chosen from the neighborhoods,
their talents were discussed,
and only then were they appointed to office.
When they excelled in their duties, then they were ennobled and rewarded with stipends.
Thus, scholars cultivated themselves in their native regions,
ascended to the court,
practiced virtue even in seclusion,
and made their reputation clear and well-known.
Distant and remote places did not lose virtuous men,
and achievements great and small were not neglected.
Therefore the worthy were promoted and employed,
while the unworthy were selected out and dismissed.
But now, the way of officials is mixed up and not selective;
the wealthy purchase offices with their riches,
the brave seek achievements through risking their lives.
Those who gamble at chariot races or leap around cauldrons
all end up being appointed as officials;
by accumulating achievements over days,
some may attain the rank of qīng or xiàng.
Wearing blue cord-singlets,
girded with silver turtle decorations,
they monopolize the power of life and death,
and hold sole authority over the lives of ten thousand people.
As for the weak,
this is like making a sheep lead the wolves,
chaos is inevitable.
As for the strong,
this is like giving a sharp sword to a madman,
reckless slaughter is inevitable.
Therefore, in the past,
the people of the commanderies and states oppressed each other and could not be managed,
some went so far as to saw through necks and kill the innocent, yet justice could not be rectified.
To hold to rules and principles in a wrong manner
only made disorder worse.
In ancient times,
when worthy men were enfeoffed and able men rewarded,
their holdings were no more than a hundred lǐ;
within a hundred lǐ would be the capital,
the farthest borders not exceeding fifty,
this was still considered manageable for one man;
yet his wisdom could not reach everywhere,
nor his hearing be everywhere effective.
Therefore, ministers called qīng,
dàfū,
and shì were established to assist him,
thus the government became complete.
Now, governors
and chancellors may not possess the virtue of even the ancient zhūhóu,
yet govern territories a thousand lǐ across,
rule over the population of an entire commandery,
apply the virtues of a sage-lord,
and wield the authority of life and death;
this is a grave responsibility.
Only a humane person can bear this charge,
only the right person can fulfill these duties.
In a single individual,
order or chaos depends on him,
and a thousand lǐ are transformed at his hand;
selection must be made with utmost care.
Thus, the ruler bestows gifts of wealth on his private associates,
but not official positions;
he sets rewards to await meritorious deeds,
arranges ranks to wait for the worthy;
praises the good as if it were not enough,
removes the bad as though against bitter enemies,
because wrongdoing brings harm to the people.
To assist the ruler’s virtue,
to open a path for ministers,
it lies in selecting the worthy and employing them appropriately,
choosing practiced governors
and chancellors before entrusting responsibility to them.”
6.5 "Jí Tān, Section Thirty-Three"
The dàfū said:
“That is so.
To heal with lack of skill is one thing,
but then to ask for much in return.
Among officials, many are poor in conduct,
moreover, they exploit and prey upon the common people.
Senior officials are harsh to the lesser ones,
and minor officials are harsh toward the people.
Thus, the worry is not that selection is not careful,
but that those who seek and those who attain are not the same;
one does not worry there are too few,
but that greed knows no bounds.”
The xiánliáng said:
“In antiquity, the allocation of rank and stipends
ensured that qīng and dàfū sufficiently enriched the worthy and honored the scholars;
scholars had enough to support themselves and their groups;
among the common people, those who became officials,
received enough to stop farming yet feed themselves from their stipend.
But now, petty officials’ stipends are meager,
while conscription and service extend throughout the commanderies and states,
reaching as far as the Sānfǔ region;
grain and rice are expensive,
not enough to sustain each other.
If they stay put they lack food and clothing,
when trouble arises, they sell their livestock and pawn their livelihoods.
Not only so,
but conscripted officials are sent by one another,
compelled by officials’ summons at court,
subject to the calculations of crafty petty officials,
acting on advice and borrowing as they go;
senior officials exploit and oppress,
upper offices make demands of counties below,
counties make demands of the villages—
where can the villages obtain what is required?
As the saying goes:
‘Bribes and gifts flow downward,
just as water flows to the lowlands,
ceasing only when exhausted.’
Now the great rivers like the Jiāng and Hè pour into the vast sea,
and the great sea receives them,
yet demands can never be sated for the streams and valleys;
the integrity of the officials,
cannot be attained.
If you want a shadow to be straight, put the marker upright;
if you want those below to be honest, first be honest yourself.
Thus, greed and baseness are determined by those above, not below;
teaching and instruction reside in the government, not the people.”
The dàfū said:
“Worthy and unworthy have innate nature,
and greed and baseness are matters of disposition;
the gentleman may purify himself inwardly but cannot fully instruct others.
Thus it was not that Zhōugōng failed to correct the deviousness of Guǎn and
Cài,
nor was it that Zǐchǎn failed to correct the falseness of Dèng Xī.
When at home one does not follow the teachings of father and elder brother,
and outside does not fear the punishment of laws and regulations,
not even Zhōugōng or
Zǐchǎn can reform such a person,
it must be so.
Now if in every case responsibility is demanded of the officials,
how could the officials bind their hands and feet and ensure no wrongdoing?”
The xiánliáng said:
“If a team of horses is unmanageable,
the fault lies with the driver.
If the people go unordered,
the blame is on the officials.
The *Chūnqiū* annals criticize not the common people,
but hold responsible those who set an example.
Thus, of old when a dàfū was about to be executed,
his demeanor was composed;
death was just,
yet always after the third bringing out he would sigh in regret.
He was shamed for not effecting reform, and saddened by his failure.
When the administration and education are obscure and not evident,
the people stumble and fall and are not uplifted,
like infants on the verge of a well,
who are left to fall in.
If things are thus,
what does it mean to be a parent of the people?
Therefore the gentleman is urgent in teaching,
and lenient in punishments.
Punish one to correct a hundred,
execute one to warn ten thousand.
Thus Zhōugōng executed Guǎn and
Cài, and Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī.
When punishment is applied to one,
the people follow ritual and righteousness.
The transformation from above to below
is like the wind bending the grass,
none do not follow its guidance.
Why bind each one individually?”
6.6 "Hòu Xíng, Section Thirty-Four"
The dàfū said:
“Of old, the gentleman
praised the good and detested the bad.
The ruler did not harbor evil citizens,
just as the farmer does not keep useless shoots.
Useless shoots
harm the crops;
useless people
are the bane of others.
Pruning a single harmful weed enables a thousand shoots to thrive;
punishing one villain causes ten thousand people to rejoice.
Not even Zhōugōng or
Kǒngzǐ could do away with punishments and make use of evildoers.
In a household there are wailing children,
and utensils never stay in place,
how much worse with malicious people!
The people, coddled by love, are nonetheless attentive to punishments.
Thus punishment
is what corrects the people,
as pruning weeds distinguishes the crops.”
Xiánliáng said:
“In ancient times,
firm instruction was used to guide the people,
and clear law was used to regulate punishments.
Punishment in governance
is like the whip in driving a chariot.
A good charioteer cannot drive without a whip,
nor have a whip and not use it.
The Sage borrowed the law to complete instruction;
when instruction is complete, punishments are not applied.
Thus, authority is stern but does not kill,
punishments are set but not transgressed.
Now the regular standards are abandoned and cannot be upheld,
rites and righteousness are broken and cannot be prevented.
The people fall into snares,
and yet one follows up and hunts them with punishments;
this is like opening the cage,
and shooting forth with poisoned arrows.
It will not cease until none are left.
Zēngzǐ said:
‘When the ruler loses the Way,
the people have long been scattered.
If one understands their circumstances,
then pity them and do not exult.’
To feel no pain for the people’s disorder,
and to boast in one’s ability to catch the wicked
is like a hunter who, seeing birds and beasts hanging in his net, rejoices.
Now those punished with death in the world
are not necessarily like those of Guǎn
and Cài in their wickedness,
or Dèng Xī in their falsity,
but for fear that all the sprouts are cut and none distinguished,
and the people deceived and lacking order.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘If a person is not humane,
and one’s hatred grows too great,
there will be disorder.’
Thus, when the people are disorderly, return to government;
when government is in disorder, return to the person;
when the person is upright, the world will be at peace.
Therefore the gentleman praises the good and pities those who cannot,
and his kindness extends even to penalized men;
virtue nourishes the impoverished,
benefits are bestowed gladly,
and punishment is carried out without joy.”
6.7 "On Granting the Seasons, Section Thirty-Five"
The Dàfū said:
“They share the land,
and dwell in this world;
it is not disaster, plague, or pestilence,
but simply poverty and distress;
if not through sloth, then through extravagance;
without some unusual trade,
yet still provided with wealth;
if not through frugality, then through labor.
Now, it is said to bestow benefits gladly
and to execute punishments with no joy;
this is to grieve over those without conduct,
and to nourish a populace who are lazy and extravagant.
Thus, blind giving does not count as benefit,
and to benefit the wicked is not benevolence.”
Xiánliáng said:
“Of the flourishing of the Three Dynasties, there was no budding of disorder—
this was due to instruction;
in the late ages of Xià and Shāng there was no obedient people—
this was due to custom.
Thus, the king established schools and seminaries,
made teaching and transformation clear,
to protect and guide his people;
when government and instruction were in accord,
their natures turned benevolent and they understood goodness.
Thus, when rites and righteousness stood,
the farmers yielded fields to others;
when rites and righteousness failed,
then gentlemen contended at court.
When people contend, there is disorder;
when there is disorder, the world is unequal;
thus some are poor and some are rich.
When rich, then benevolence arises;
when well provided, contention ceases.
At dusk, one may knock on another’s door
to ask for water or fire:
the greedy man does not withhold it.
Why so?
Because he has abundance.
If the government makes grain and beans as common as water and fire,
how could there be those who are not benevolent?”
The Dàfū said:
“Those given to gaming and horse-racing
are all sons of the wealthy;
they are not lacking.
Therefore when the people abound, they become extravagant and arrogant;
when rich, they become proud and excessive.
Seated, they indulge in idleness;
rising, they commit transgressions;
I have not seen their benevolence.
If one dwells in affairs but does not work hard,
spends wealth without moderation,
even if he possesses wealth like water and fire,
poverty and want can be expected at any moment.
With people not stored up,
even if officials assist in plowing and weaving,
can they suffice?”
Xiánliáng said:
“When Zhōu Gōng assisted King Chéng,
the people were abundant and content,
and there were no poor in the state;
it was not due to officials plowing and weaving on their behalf.
The fields and plots were exchanged,
taxes and levies were made light,
then the people became wealthy.
Above, they served ruler and parents;
below, they had no worries of hunger or cold;
then instruction could be fulfilled.
The ‘Sayings’ says:
‘Once wealthy,
what further can be added?
It is instruction.’
Instruct them with virtue,
equalize them with rites,
then the people turn toward righteousness and goodness;
all become filial at home and respectful abroad,
what extravagance, violence, or arrogance can there be?
Guǎnzǐ said:
‘When the granaries are full, they know rites and moderation;
when the people have enough, they know honor and shame.’
Thus, it is easy to guide the wealthy toward propriety,
but difficult to guide them toward the Way.”
The Dàfū said:
“For the county officials to the people,
it is as a loving father to his son:
