with loyalty, how could he not instruct him?
With love, how could he not labor for him?
Thus in spring, he personally plows to encourage farming;
gives relief and loans to support the lacking;
regulates stagnant waters;
issues light taxes;
makes the people labor with the seasons.
Having received favor and grace,
yet to this day still they are poor and distressed;
how difficult it is to guide them toward the Way!”
Xiánliáng said:
“In ancient times,
in spring one inspected the plowing to supplement insufficiency;
in autumn one examined the levies to assist the needy.
If the people labor for wealth, then contributions and taxes were lessened;
if the people labor physically, then works and construction were rare.
To serve the people by cherishing their strength,
not depriving them for even a moment,
thus Shàobó gave judgments under the sweet pear tree,
lest farming duties be disturbed.
Now, although timely rain brings moisture,
yet the seeds hang, unable to be sown;
in autumn, the crops wither in the fields, unable to be gathered.
The fields are bare and scorched,
while goods are left unsold in the market;
only after the start of spring,
are the green flags hung and the clay oxen driven about;
surely, this is not the meaning of an enlightened ruler encouraging farming,
nor the intention of the Spring Ordinance.”
6.8 "On Flood and Drought, Section Thirty-Six"
The Dàfū said:
“Yǔ
and Tāng were sagely rulers,
Hòujì
and Yī Yǐn were worthy ministers,
yet there were still calamities of flood and drought.
Flood and drought
are acts of Heaven;
famine and abundance
are the workings of yin and yang;
they are not from human effort.
Thus, the number of ‘Grand Years’:
in yang years comes drought,
in yin years comes flood.
Every six years comes famine,
every twelve years comes disaster.
This is the way of Heaven,
and surely not the fault of the officials alone.”
The Worthy and Good said:
"In ancient times,
when government possessed virtue,
then yīn and yáng were in harmony,
the stars and constellations in order,
the wind and rain came in season.
Thus, when conduct was cultivated within,
reputation was heard without;
doing good among the people below,
blessings responded from Heaven.
When Zhōu Gōng recorded the chronicles, the world was at great peace,
no disasters befell the state,
and there were no years of famine.
At that time,
rain never broke the clods,
the wind did not howl through the branches,
ten days brought one rainfall,
and rain always fell at night.
Whether land was high or low, all ripened alike.
The Shī says:
'There are thick clouds, lush upon lush;
raising plentiful rains, copious and steady.'
Now, failing to examine why this was so,
people say
'It is simply the movement of yīn and yáng,'
but this is not what has been learned.
Mèngzǐ says:
'If there are starved corpses in the wilds,
knowing nothing of taking up the harvest;
if dogs and pigs consume what men would eat,
lacking any restraint;
to be the people's father and mother—
yet the people starve and die,
and then to say,
"It is not I,
it is the year,"
—how is this different from killing them with a blade,
and then saying,
"It was not I,
it was the weapon"?'
What must be done now
is to eliminate the woes of hunger and cold,
abolish state salt
and iron, withdraw priviledged profit,
distribute the land,
hasten people back to their proper occupations,
cultivate mulberry and hemp,
and exhaust the land's productivity.
With few undertakings and thrift in spending,
the people naturally become wealthy.
If it is so,
then floods and drought cannot cause worry,
and years of disaster cannot oppress them."
The Officer said:
"When discussing matters, one values conciseness of words and clarity of intent,
so they may suit the ear of the multitude,
not reaching the point of elaborate phrasing and dense words.
Too much speech harms the officials' plans to transform customs,
and becomes household chatter.
Táo Zhū managed his livelihood,
with root and branch pursuing different paths;
one household had many activities,
yet all the ways of managing a livelihood were complete.
Now the commandery government casts farming tools,
making the people focus on the fundamentals,
not seeking profit in secondary pursuits,
so they suffer no hardship of hunger and cold.
What harm is there in salt and iron to warrant their abolition?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"Agriculture
is the greatest enterprise under Heaven,
and iron implements
are of utmost use to the people.
If tools and utensils are convenient,
then less effort produces more results,
and farmers enjoy their work and are eager to perform well.
If tools are insufficient,
then the fields go to waste,
grain is not produced;
little effort is exerted,
and results are naturally halved.
Whether tools are convenient or not,
the difference in their effectiveness is by tenfold and more.
When the commandery office spurs the casting of iron implements,
in general they produce only large tools,
aiming to meet quotas,
but do not supply what the people need.
What the people use grows dull and damaged,
so cutting grass is not sharp,
hence farmers toil harder,
while what they gain is little,
and the common people suffer greatly thereby."
The Officer said:
"Laborers and artisans
work daily on state tasks for the commandery office,
the finances are ample,
and tools are prepared.
Households gather together,
pressed for time in the day and diligent in use,
the strength of the iron is not refined,
hardness and softness are not blended.
Thus officials have requested to unify salt
and iron, bringing their use under one system,
and standardizing their price
for the convenience of people both public and private.
Even the governance of Yú
and Xià
would not be superior to this.
If officials are clear in instructing,
and craftsmen exert themselves in their work,
then hard and soft are blended,
and tools are convenient in use.
Under such circumstances, why would the common people suffer?
And why would the farmer be troubled?"
The Worthy and Good said:
"Laborers and artisans!
Thus the people once could, by taking shares, profit from casting and forging,
or boiling salt,
and salt was priced as grain is,
and implements were harmonious, sharp, and adequately useful.
Now the commandery office produces iron tools,
most of poor quality,
with no saving in expense,
and the laborers are exhausted, yet the work is never complete.
When households work together,
fathers and sons join forces,
each striving to make fine implements,
and tools not well made do not circulate.
When farming work is urgent,
transport by carts extends among the fields and paths.
The people trade among themselves,
obtaining farm tools by exchanging goods, grain, or newly-minted coins;
sometimes people extend credit to one another,
never ceasing their occupations.
The storage of agricultural implements
enables each to acquire what he desires.
Draft labor is light and simple,
and when the commandery employs laborers for repairs,
mending roads and bridges,
it all serves to benefit the people.
But now the origin is monopolized,
the price is made uniform,
tools are mostly hard and coarse,
with no way to select between good and bad.
Officials rarely remain in one place,
and tools are hard to obtain.
Households cannot store up many,
and if they do, the supply is suppressed.
When the best days for using rich soil are missed,
and farm tools are sought so far away,
this means losing the optimal seasons.
When the prices of salt and iron rise,
the people are inconvenienced.
Poor folk may resort to plowing with wood and weeding by hand,
using wooden seeders and eating bland food.
At the iron office, tools are sometimes unsold, or irregularly assigned to the people.
When the laborers' work is not up to standard,
temporary mandates provide assistance.
The levies are unlimited,
and draft labor is assigned to balance heavy tasks,
and so the common people suffer hardship thereby.
In ancient times,
a town of a thousand households,
or a family of one hundred chariots,
had its own potters, metallurgists, craftsmen, and merchants;
the four occupations each supplying one another's needs,
all sufficient for mutual exchange.
Thus farmers did not leave their beds of cultivation,
yet always had enough farm implements;
artisans did not chop wood, yet always had enough timber,
potters and metallurgists did not farm, yet always had enough grain and rice.
Everyone among the people obtained what was convenient to them,
and those above had nothing to do.
Therefore, the true king pursued the fundamentals and did not take up the secondary crafts,
rejected extravagant ornamentation,
abolished elaborate carvings,
steeped the people in ritual,
showed to them plainness,
so the people pursued the fundamentals and did not seek petty gains."
7.1 "Chóng Lǐ, Section Thirty-Seven"
The dàfū said:
"Adorning the table and staff,
preparing the vessels and trays,
is for the sake of guests,
not for the host.
Displaying dazzling oddities
is to present to the four yí,
not for the people.
When a family has visitors,
they still offer performances with actors and marvelous entertainments;
how much more so for the state authorities?
Therefore, banners with feathers and yak tails are arrayed,
warhorses are displayed,
to show military might;
rare insects and curious beasts
are to exhibit a broad and far-reaching embrace,
to manifest splendid virtue,
so that distant lands are sure to arrive."
The xiánliáng said:
"The king upholds ritual and dispenses virtue,
esteems benevolence and righteousness while disregarding rare marvels and brute force,
hence the sages refrained from speaking of them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Speak with loyalty and trust,
act sincerely and respectfully,
and even in the states of the Mán
and the Mò
such conduct should not be abandoned.'
Now the lords of myriad distant lands who offer tribute
do so because they long for the splendid virtue of the Son of Heaven
and wish to witness the rituals of Zhōngguó.
Therefore, the Míngtáng is erected,
the Bìyōng is opened to display these rites,
the shields and axes are raised,
the odes of the "Yǎ"
and "Sòng" are performed to influence them.
But now, to parade amusements and useless vessels,
rare insects and unkept beasts,
wrestling and various entertainments,
and dazzling objects to show off,
this is surely different from Zhōu Gōng’s way of receiving distant guests.
In olden days, Zhōu Gōng conducted himself with humility to associate with lowly officers,
upheld ritual and virtue to lead all under Heaven;
thus he declined the tribute of Yuèshāng,
demonstrating the etiquette of deference;
and afterwards, when entering King Wén’s ancestral temple,
he manifested the great filial piety.
With their eyes, the guests saw the dignified manner of shields and axes,
with their ears, they heard the pure songs of the "Yǎ"
and "Sòng",
their hearts were filled with utmost virtue,
and they departed joyfully.
For this reason, the four yí admired righteousness and submitted themselves,
not because interpreters led the Dí and Dī to gape at ferocious beasts and bears.
As for the rhinoceros, elephant, wild ox, and tiger,
these abound among the southern yí;
mules, donkeys, and camels
are commonly kept by the northern Dí;
these are rare in Zhōngguó,
and are disdained by foreign lands.
The people of Nányuè hang peacock feathers on their doors;
on the slopes of Kūnshān,
lumps of uncut jade are thrown at the crows and magpies.
What is prized among us may be despised by others;
what others value may be abundant for them;
these are not means by which Zhōngguó is enriched or splendid virtue displayed.
Suí and Hé
are renowned treasures of the world,
yet they cannot secure peace or avert disaster.
Therefore, to exemplify virtue and demonstrate power,
relies upon worthy ministers and good advisors,
not upon dogs, horses, or rare curiosities.
Thus, the sage kings regarded the worthy as treasures,
not pearls and jade.
In ancient times, Yànzǐ cultivated his skills amid vessels and trays,
yet was able to resolve conflicts over a thousand leagues;
those who lacked such ability,
though they had trunks full of Suí
and Hé,
gained nothing in the matter of survival."
The dàfū said:
"Yànzǐ served as minister to three rulers of Qí;
Cuī Qìng acted without principle,
held his lord at knifepoint,
plunged the state into disorder;
under Lord Líng, the country was besieged;
Lord Zhuāng was murdered;
during the reign of Lord Jǐng,
the men of Jìn came to attack,
took Chuí Dū,
seized Línzī,
border towns were reduced,
city walls burned,
palaces destroyed,
precious vessels lost—
what conflicts was he able to settle?
Judging from this,
the words of the xiánliáng,
that the worthy are treasures,
have neither greater nor lesser consequence for gain or loss."
The xiánliáng said:
"Guǎn Zhòng departed from Lǔ to enter Qí;
then Qí flourished, Lǔ declined,
not because he brought multitudes, but by returning to Qí.
Wǔ Zǐxū carried a bow to Hélǜ,
defeated Chǔ and entered Yǐng,
not because he bore an army when he went to Wú.
Thus, where the worthy reside, a state is strong;
where they leave, a state is weak.
Chǔ had Zǐyù
and Déchén,
so Duke Wén sat humbly;
Yú had Gōng Zhī Qí,
so Jìn Xiàn lost sleep.
Wherever worthy ministers serve,
dangers and openings may be averted from afar.
Therefore, the "Chūnqiū" says:
'When mountains have tigers and leopards,
even the local plants are not plucked;
when a state has worthy men,
its borders suffer no harm.'
7.2 "On Preparation against the Hú, Section Thirty-eight"
The dàfū said:
"There is a saying:
'The worthy are above disgrace.'
In common parlance,
if there is a fierce man in a village,
people still avoid him.
Now that the enlightened Son of Heaven sits above,
yet the xiōngnú chiefs raid as bandits,
harassing the borders,
it means benevolence is violated and even wild plants are plucked.
In days past, the Dí invaded the Grand Duke;
the people of Kuāng feared Kǒngzǐ;
thus, the unkind are enemies to the kind.
Therefore, the authorities must arm themselves to punish the unrighteous,
set up devices to prepare against the wicked."
The xiánliáng said:
"The Xiōngnú dwell in the midst of the desert,
live in unproductive lands,
despised and abandoned by Heaven;
they have no proper dwellings,
no distinction between men and women,
take the open plain as their village,
the felt tent as their house,
wear skins and hair,
eat meat and drink blood,
hold markets on the move,
herders as residents—
just like the deer and elk of Zhōngguó.
Overzealous ministers,
seeking their own righteousness,
demand of them etiquette,
causing discord and war in Zhōngguó to this day without cease;
preparations must be made over ten thousand miles,
this is what the "Tùjiā" satirized,
so petty men are not the bulwark or trusted vassals of princes."
The dàfū said:
"The Son of Heaven
is the father and mother of all under Heaven.
The people of the four quarters,
by principle, wish to be his subjects;
yet cities are still fortified,
passes and bridges are maintained,
warriors are kept trained,
guards stationed in the palace,
all to keep dangers afar and prepare for all eventualities.
Now the Xiōngnú are not yet subject,
and though there is no trouble now,
to wish to relax preparations—
how could that be?"
The xiánliáng said:
"The reason the King of Wú was captured by Yuè
was because he neglected the near for the sake of the distant.
The reason Qín perished
was because they guarded against the Hú
and Yuè abroad, yet lost their own government at home.
Waging war externally
while government fails within,
preparations become the source of disaster,
and increase the ruler’s worries.
Thus, when a ruler gains the Way,
the near and far alike come to submit;
King Wén of Zhōu was such a case.
If he does not obtain the Way,
then subjects become rebels;
Qín Wáng is such an example.
When culture declines, the martial prevails;
when virtue is abundant, defense is slight."
The dàfū said:
“In former times,
the Sìyí were all strong,
and together they acted as bandits and oppressors;
Cháoxiǎn crossed the border,
seizing the eastern lands of Yān;
Dōngyuè crossed the Eastern Sea,
raiding south of the Zhèjiāng;
Nányuè invaded the interior,
their submission was nominal;
the Dī, Bó,
Rǎn, Máng,
Xī Táng,
Kūnmíng and their kind,
harassed Lǒngxī,
Bā, and Shǔ.
Now the Three Frontiers have been pacified,
only the northern border remains unsettled.
With one campaign, the Xiōngnú would be shaken with fear,
within and without there would be relief from vigilance,
so why hesitate?”
The worthy and good said:
“In antiquity,
the gentleman established benevolence and cultivated righteousness,
in order to pacify his people,
so those nearby learned to be good,
and those afar submitted to him.
Thus Kūngzǐ served in Lǔ;
after three months of service, Qí was at peace;
after three more months, Zhèng was at peace.
He strove by virtue to secure the near and pacify the far.
At that time,
Lǔ had no troubles from enemy states
nor afflictions from neighboring borders.
Powerful ministers changed their ways and became loyal and obedient,
thus Jì Huán demolished his own capital.
Great states feared righteousness and made alliances,
and the people of Qí returned to Lǚ the lands of Yùn,
Huān, and Guīyīn.
Thus, governing by virtue,
is not only warding off harm and repelling attacks;
what one desires is obtained without seeking it.
Now, the reason why the people are so restless,
and there is no peace within or without,
the blame lies with the Xiōngnú.
Within, there is no defense of homes;
without, there is no accumulation of crops;
they follow the good grass and sweet waters, driving their herds;
Xiōngnú change not their occupations,
yet Zhōngguó is disturbed by them.
When the winds gather, the clouds disperse;
if you pursue them, they vanish;
if you attack them, they scatter;
they cannot be defeated in a single generation.”
The dàfū said:
“In antiquity,
enlightened kings punished the violent and protected the weak,
righted the overthrown and supported the endangered.
Protect the weak and support the endangered,
and the lords of the small states rejoice;
punish the violent and right the overthrown,
and blameless people rally to them.
If we do not campaign,
then violence and harm will not cease;
if we do not prepare,
then the common people are thereby left to the enemy.
The Chūnqiū denounced the descendants of regional lords,
criticizing them for not completing their garrison duties.
To send out expeditions and guard the borders,
this has always existed, since ancient times,
not only now.”
The worthy and good said:
“The lands of the Xiōngnú are vast,
and their cavalry swift and nimble,
so their situation is easily stirred to unrest.
When advantageous, they retreat like tigers;
when ailing, they break like birds;
evading sharp attacks, seeking exhaustion in the enemy.
If the forces dispatched are too few, they cannot change the situation;
if too many, the people cannot endure the burden.
When labor is excessive, their strength is exhausted;
when expenditures are high, resources are depleted.
If both never end,
then resentment is left among the people.
This is why Qín lost the hearts of the people
and its state perished.
In former times,
the Son of Heaven had a thousand-lǐ domain,
with corvée service extending five hundred lǐ;
news of victory could be heard,
and illnesses mutually cared for.
There were no armies overstaying the proper time,
nor labors extending beyond their season.
Within, feelings of the people were considered;
in affairs, efforts matched their strength.
Thus, those in service were diligent in their tasks,
and those who remained at home were at peace in their occupations.
Now, the armored cavalrymen from east of the mountains garrison the frontier commanderies,
cut off at great distances far away,
their bodies among the Hu and
Yuè, but their hearts longing for their aged mothers.
The aged mother weeps with tears streaming,
the household wife sorrows and resents,
thinking on their hunger and thirst,
remembering their cold and suffering.
The Shī* says:
‘Long ago I went away,
the willows swayed gently.
Now I return,
rain and snow fall thickly.
On the road I travel slowly,
parched with thirst and hunger.
My heart is full of sorrow,
and none grieves for me.’
Thus, the sage pitied such as this,
understanding their long separation from parents, wives and children,
exposed in the open fields,
dwelling in cold and bitter lands.
Therefore, in spring he sent envoys to offer comfort and reward,
and sought out those who lost their posts,
in order to grieve for those far from home and soothe their aged mothers.
The kindness is great indeed,
but the officials have not kept their duties and implemented the orders in sympathy,
and some oppress and insult the soldiers,
barter with them,
force them together for labor,
and treat them without principle.
Therefore, soldiers lose their positions,
and their mothers, wives, and children are resentful and grieve.
When Sòng Bǎijī pined in sorrow, the state of Sòng caught fire;
when a concubine in Lǔ was dissatisfied, disaster fell on Lǔ’s palace.
Today, those dissatisfied under heaven
are not only the women of the Western Palace
or the aged mothers of Sòng.
In the Chūnqiū, whenever the masses are mobilized, it is recorded,
to show the importance of the people.
When the Sòng people besieged Chánggě,
they were reproached for the length of the campaign.
The mind of the gentleman must be thus.”
The dàfū fell silent and did not reply.
7.3 “On Duties, Section Thirty-Nine”
The chancellor said:
“The Way of the former kings
has long been neglected and is hard to restore;
the words of the worthy and learned
are profound and far-reaching, but difficult to put into practice.
Speaking of the lofty conduct of the greatest sages,
and the fine words on ultimate virtue,
these cannot be attained by men of this age.
I wish to hear of urgent matters of the present age,
that can truly be implemented in government;
so the common people will all have enough food and clothing,
without worries of lack and want;
the winds and rains come in season,
the five grains will ripen,
pests will not arise;
the realm will be at peace and happy,
and thieves and robbers will not appear;
exiles will return home,
each going back to his fields and village;
officials will all be honest and upright,
reverently keeping their duties,
and every commoner will attain his just place.”
[*Shī refers to the Book of Songs, as instructed: no explanatory notes are required; this bracket is just for clarity.]
The virtuous and talented said:
“Mèngzǐ said:
‘The Way of Yáo
and Shùn
does not belong to distant people;
it is just that people do not think of it.’
The Shījīng says:
‘I seek it but cannot obtain it;
awake or asleep, I long for it.’
There are those who seek as in Guān Jū,
and love virtue as in Hé Guǎng.
Why should there be any failure to achieve or cross over?
Thus, for lofty mountains one looks up in admiration,
for great paths one follows after;
though one cannot reach them,
one is not far from the Way.
Yán Yuān said:
‘What sort of man was Shùn alone,
and what sort of man was Huí?’
If one thinks upon the worthy and admires the able,
pursuing goodness without ceasing,
then the customs of Chéng
and Kāng can be attained,
and the Way of Táng
and Yú can be approached.
The gōngqīng have not yet reflected on this;
how can the Way of the former kings
be considered distant?
Qí Huán Gōng, by having the feudal lords ponder royal governance,
was anxious for the house of Zhōu,
rectified the crises among the realm of Zhūxià,
quelled the disorders of Yí
and Dí,
sustained lives and continued severed ties,
enacted trustworthiness and justice on a great scale,
and made it manifest throughout the world.
At the assembly of Shàolíng,
Yú was the leader.
The Zhuàn says:
‘Yú accumulated.’
Thus earth, accumulated, forms hills and mounds;
water, accumulated, forms rivers and seas;
conduct, accumulated, forms a gentleman.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘From Hé Guǎng,
I know the utmost of virtue.’
To seek this,
each must return to his origin,
revert to the ancient ways, and nothing more.
In ancient days,
those sent on service did not exceed their appointed times,
they went forth in spring and returned in autumn,
or went in autumn and came home in spring;
before cold or heat changed,
clothes did not need to be altered,
and so return was assured.
Husbands and wives did not miss their appointed times;
people were peaceful and harmonious as though at home.
Litigation was impartial,
punishments were appropriate,
the yīn and yáng were thereby regulated,
and wind and rain came in season.
Those above were not severe or oppressive,
those below not wearied by toil;
each cultivated his own occupation,
and was at ease in his nature.
Thus caterpillars and locusts did not appear,
nor did floods or droughts arise.
Taxation was light and farmers did not miss their seasons,
so the people had abundance,
and those who had become wanderers returned to their fields and villages.
When those above were pure, tranquil, and without desires,
those below were honest and not greedy.
But nowadays, deployments are sent to great distances,
to lands of bitter cold,
dangerous and troubled places,
traversing the domains of the Hú
and Yuè,
leaving this year and only returning the following year.
Parents strain their necks westward in longing,
men and women sorrow over their prolonged separation,
the person’s body is in Dōngchǔ,
but his mind is on the Xīhé.
So one traveler causes his village to grieve,
and one death brings sorrow to ten thousand.
The Shījīng says:
‘The king’s affairs are never-ending;
I cannot cultivate millet and grain,
on whom can parents rely?’
‘Thinking of that respectful man,
tears fall like rain.
How could one not wish to return home?
Yet I fear the nets of punishment.’
When officials do not uphold the law to care for and nurture,
but discard public duty for private interests,
each uses his power to gratify his own desires,
so people are filled with grief and resentment.
If those above do not take thought for good governance,
then bad government prevails and evil influences arise;
when evil influences arise,
insects and pests breed, and floods and droughts occur.
In such conditions,
even if sacrifices and prayers are made without ceasing to all the spirits,
they cannot harmonize yīn and yáng or put an end to robbers and thieves, can they?”
7.4 “Ability in Words, Number Forty”
The dàfū said:
“A blind man’s mouth can speak of black and white,
but he has no eyes to distinguish them.
The Ru scholars’ mouths can speak of order and disorder,
but lack the means to realize them.
To sit and talk without acting—
then a shepherd boy would possess the strength of Wū Huò,
a tousled youth would possess the virtue of Yáo
and Shùn.
Therefore, if speech accords with reality,
then what trouble could Ru scholars have with order or disorder,
and what trouble could blind men have with distinguishing black or white?
When words cannot be put to use,
one is ashamed that one’s actions do not measure up.
Thus those who speak lowly but say lofty things,
or those who are able to speak but not able to act,
the gentleman is ashamed of them.”
The virtuous and talented said:
“Those able to speak but not act
are the treasures of the state.
Those able to act but not speak
are the implements of the state.
Those who are both
are gentlemen.
Those who are neither
are shepherd boys
and tousled youths.
When words fill the world
and virtue covers the four seas,
Zhōugōng was such.
To speak with the mouth
and practice with the body
—how does this compare to being silent while fully practicing one's conduct?
Then what trouble or shame could those in office possibly have?
Now, when the Way is not upheld and petty profit is pursued,
and men are drawn to what is unurgent and thus disrupt the minds of the many,
even if a gentleman is poor,
he must not act in such a way.
Medicinal wine
benefits the sick;
forthright words
are medicine for governance.
If the gōngqīng can truly strengthen and restrain themselves,
nourish themselves on the utmost words of scholarship,
remove selfish scheming,
abolish grasping officials,
and return all to the people,
and emulate the Way of Zhōugōng,
then the realm will be orderly and the songs of praise will arise.
How then could Ru scholars be troubled by order and disorder?”
7.5 “Taking the Low, Number Forty-One”
The dàfū said:
“The unruly people
are troubled by constraints on public benefit
and wish to control mountains and lakes for themselves.
According to the intentions of the scholars and the virtuous and talented,
then profit would return to the people,
and the district officials would have nothing left to do.
If what the superiors implement is opposed by them,
if what the superiors say is criticized by them,
they wish only to diminish the higher in order to benefit the lower,
to weaken the ruler and strengthen the ministers,
then how can the right relationship between high and low,
and the propriety between ruler and subject, be maintained?
How then could songs of praise be produced?”
Xiánliáng said:
“In ancient times,
the ruler took according to measure,
and sustained himself with moderation.
In years of abundance, he did not take by force;
when years were lean, he opened the granaries.
The use of the people’s labor
did not go beyond three days in a year;
the collection of taxes
did not exceed one-tenth.
If the ruler was sincerely loving,
the ministers exerted their utmost strength.
When superiors and inferiors yielded to each other,
the world was at peace.
‘Dig out your private wealth,’
means that the superior yields to the inferior.
‘Then and only then involve my own wealth,’
means putting public duty first.
Mèngzǐ said:
‘There has never been one who is humane and neglects his parents,
nor one who is righteous and puts his lord last.’
When rulers rule and subjects serve,
how could there be no propriety and righteousness?
By the end of Zhōu,
virtue and benevolence were blocked while desires became many.
Rulers were extravagant and sought more from above;
the people toiled below,
and grew lax in supporting official tasks.
Thus, there was the taxing of land by the mu,
and the poem ‘Shuǒshǔ’ was composed.
Wèi Líng Gōng, in the dead of winter, mobilized the people to dig a pond;
Hǎi Chūn remonstrated, saying:
‘The weather is cold,
the people suffer from frost and hunger;
I beg that you halt the labor, my Lord.’
The Duke replied:
‘Is it truly cold?
Do I not feel cold myself?’
Hǎi Chūn said:
‘People say,
“Those who are safe cannot pity those in danger;
the well-fed cannot imagine the hunger of the starving.”’
Therefore, those who have grain and meat in excess cannot speak of hardship;
those who dwell in comfort and ease cannot speak of toil and suffering.
Those with lofty halls and deep chambers,
broad mansions and lofty rooms,
do not know the stench of those in cramped shacks,
where the roof leaks above and the floor is wet below.
Those who tether a hundred chariots of horses,
whose wealth fills their households,
whose stores receive the new before the old is consumed,
do not know the urgency of those who have enough for morning but not for evening,
nor the plight of those who must borrow to survive.
Those whose broad estates adjoin vast gardens,
with fertile fields joined in succession,
do not know the struggle of those with no occupation to follow,
nor the toil of those expelled to shabby dwellings.
Those who let their horses graze on mountains,
and fill their valleys with cattle and sheep,
do not know the poverty of those with no piglet or gaunt calf.
Those who sleep the night, pillows high in leisure,
with none to wail around them,
do not know the sorrow of those anxious for kin and pressed by officials.
Those clad in fine silk and treading on soft leather,
feasting on rich cakes and fat meats,
do not know the cold of short coarse coats,
nor the bitterness of bran and chaff.
Those who stroll easily among inner chambers,
resting at table and dining in comfort,
do not know the labor of those who till the fields with their own hands.
Those who ride sturdy steeds and drive fine horses,
whose retinues arrayed in ranks,
do not know the fatigue of those who carry burdens and travel on foot.
Those who recline on fine mats of felt,
attended by servants on every side,
do not know the hardship of those who drag carts and tow boats,
or the peril of scaling heights and fording depths.
Those clothed lightly yet warmly,
wrapped in splendid furs,
dwelling in heated chambers,
riding comfortable carriages,
do not know the cold and danger of those sent to garrison the borders,
buffeted by the winds of Hú,
Dài, and rural wilds.
Those whose wives and children are united in harmony,
whose descendants are safely kept,
do not know the gauntness of aged mothers,
nor the grief and bitterness of lone women.
Those whose ears hear sweet music,
whose eyes behold performers and entertainers,
do not know the mortal danger of those shot by stray arrows,
or defending the border from outside enemies.
Those who kneel eastward and rest on desks,
their brushes flying as they compose essays,
do not know the stress of those bound in ropes,
nor the pain of those beaten with rods.
Those who sit on felt cushions,
discussing laws and plans with seeming ease,
likewise do not know the hardship of those who must walk and wade.
In former times, when Shāng Yāng held office in Qín,
he punished men as if cutting straw or sedge,
and used the army as if tossing pellets.
Those who joined the campaigns left their bones exposed at the Long Wall,
those sent to guard the transports formed a line of carts as far as the eye could see.
They left alive,
and returned dead—
were they not also sons of men?
Therefore, the gentleman practices benevolence with forgiveness,
righteousness with measure,
and shares his likes and dislikes with all under Heaven.
He does not practice what is unkind.
Gōng Liú loved to accumulate wealth:
those who stayed behind had stores;
those who traveled possessed bags.
The Grand King cherished women:
within, there were no resentful maidens;
without, no unwed bachelors.
King Wén established punishments:
within the state, there were no grievances or unjust imprisonments.
King Wǔ led armies:
soldiers gladly died for him;
the people gladly contributed their service.
If it is thus,
what hardship would make the people complain,
or what desire would cause them to find fault?”
The lords and ministers became solemn,
silent as if none were there.
At this, the discussion was ended and the debate ceased.
A memorial was submitted, stating:
“Xiánliáng
and the Learned Scholars do not understand the matters of the local administration
and rashly judge salt and iron to be inconvenient.
We request that the government monopolies on wine and
iron within the passes be temporarily abolished.”
The petition was approved.
7.6 "Jí zhī, Section Forty-two"
Xiánliáng
and the Learned Scholars, having performed their farewells,
all obtained posts as senior officials
and took leave of the Prime Minister
and the Chief Censor.
An official said:
“In previous discussions of government affairs,
Xiánliáng
and the Learned Scholars quoted ancient times,
but sometimes departed from practical affairs of the age.
Those who deliberate need not oppose each other,
but aim for what can be carried out.
In times past,
before the state had affairs with the Hú
and Yuè,
the border cities were attacked on all sides,
and the northern frontiers suffered the most.
The former Emperor resolved the threefold perils,
pacified the neighboring states,
and made them serve as our defenses.
He exhausted the resources of the commanderies
to punish the Xiōngnú.
In those days, the Xiōngnú’s territory was like a beast in a cage,
isolated and with none to aid them—
this was their time of distress and peril.
When our power failed to reach their distant lands,
they regained breath,
rested and reared their horses,
and deceived and betrayed the Western Regions.
The Western Regions, pressed by the Hú invaders,
lost heart within,
and are certain to become a source of trouble for our court.
For this reason, His Majesty wishes to sweep them away
despite the burdens on our granaries and treasury.
To pursue prey all day
and then let it go
is no sound plan.
Now, Yǔ succeeded Shùn,
and achieved success.
If we wish now to suppress such disorder by raising troops,
what say you?”
Wénxué said:
"In former times,
when the county officials reduced light taxes,
public resources were abundant,
and the people were prosperous and well-supplied.
Afterwards,
in guarding the Hú and
Yuè, when relations were opened with the Four Barbarians,
expenditures became insufficient.
Thus, profit and harm were discussed,
the number of carts and boats counted,
and monetary assessments used to support the frontiers,
with redemption of crimes and declarations of offenses by cash,
causing troubles for the people.
Armored soldiers died in the army,
middle-ranked men were exhausted by transport service,
and furthermore by forced labor levies,
the officials’ conscriptions became extreme.
To labor and then grant rest,
to exhaust and then return to the root,
is the Way of the ancients,
and even Shùn and
Yǔ, when they arose,
could not alter it."
The Dàfū said:
"In the past, when the Xià sovereign faced the disaster of the great flood,
the people toiled greatly,
exhausted in dams and dikes,
but afterwards,
all shared in the benefits of those labors.
In the time of the former Emperor,
the commanderies and kingdoms were rather burdened by military affairs,
yet the corvée labor at the three frontiers was also relieved.
As the saying goes:
'He who perceives opportunity but does not pursue it loses merit.'
If for one day the enemy is neglected,
successive generations will be harmed.
Labor and rest serve to supply needs,
relying on breakdowns and seizing chances.
This is the Way of emperors and kings,
what even sages cannot neglect.
When achievements have a thread of continuity,
to dislike toil and not finish the work,
is like the ploughman stopping to rest and falling into hardship.
For in tasks interrupted there is no accomplishment,
and for the idle ploughman, no harvest."
Wénxué said:
"A country with vast territory yet unable to hold it is in danger,
an army strong and oppressing its enemies brings ruin to itself.
When tiger and rhinoceros contend for territory,
it is the ants and termites that gain their will.
When two enemies face off,
a lone commoner exploits the gap.
Therefore, the sage king considers dangers when he sees profit,
and, seeing the distant, preserves the near.
Nowadays, for those who calculate for the county officials,
nothing is better than putting aside arms and letting the soldiers rest,
generously bestowing wealth to establish harmony and alliances,
and cultivating civil virtue—nothing more.
If one does not empathize with the people’s distress,
does not reckon with the difficulties,
spending strength relying on seizing useless lands,
losing ten for every one gained—
such is not the way known to Wénxué."
8.1 "On Making Ties of Harmony, Chapter Forty-Three"
The Dàfū said:
"Since the rise of the Hàn,
friendly relations and ties of alliance have been formed,
and the gifts presented to the Chán​yú have been extremely generous;
yet there is no record of them, on account of heavy pledges and lavish bribes, changing their allegiance,
while violence and harm have only increased.
The former Emperor saw that they could be subdued by arms
but not mollified by virtue,
so he increased the ranks of generals,
summoned men of courage to fight,
to punish their crimes.
The achievements have been brilliant and
renowned throughout the empire,
stored in the palace archives—
how could one speak of
'losing ten and gaining one'?
Those who seek ease will later face danger,
those who look only to the near will worry about the immediate.
The worthy become estranged from the world,
the wise weigh the circumstances in their actions,
what the gentleman is concerned with,
and what the common people doubt.
Thus the people can observe the completion
but cannot plan the beginnings together.
This is something only the appropriate officials can see,
but not what Wénxué can comprehend."
Wénxué said:
"Formerly,
the Xiōngnú formed an alliance of mutual harmony,
all the tribes presented tribute,
so the ruler and subjects, inner and outer, trusted one another,
with no threat from Hú
or Yuè.
At that time,
the emperor sought little and it was easy to supply,
the people were at peace with nothing to do,
tilling fields for food,
cocooning silk and hemp for clothing,
each family had years of stores,
the county officials had surplus wealth and goods,
elders in hamlets and villages
all benefitted from its grace.
Later,
civil government retreated and the martial was employed,
the armies suffered and the people grew weary,
annexing useless lands,
establishing commanderies amid sand and rocks,
where people could not defend themselves,
troops were dispatched to garrison the cities,
and they had to be fed by transport carts.
I, in my ignorance, foresee their ruin,
but do not see their accomplishment."
The Dàfū said:
"The Xiōngnú use an empty reputation to trade with Hàn,
but in reality do not submit;
they are often deceived by the Mán
and Mò,
yet do not grieve for it—
why is that?
Gāo Huángdì relied on the sword to settle the Nine Provinces;
yet now, though owning the Nine Provinces, he cannot act among the Xiōngnú.
The ordinary people in hamlets,
even they desert and scatter,
how much more so the sovereign beyond ten thousand miles and a small state like the Xiōngnú?
With the might of all under Heaven, how can they not be broken?
With all the gentlemen and commoners under Heaven, how can they not submit?
Now, possessing the title of Emperor,
yet power is not respected beyond the Great Wall,
instead, bribes and gifts are sent while they remain proudly aloof—
this is what the Five Emperors could not tolerate
and what made the Three Kings rage utterly."
Wénxué said:
"Tāng served Xià and ultimately subdued it,
Zhōu dealt with Yīn and finally destroyed it.
Therefore, to rule greatly over the small is to be a king;
to use strength to oppress the weak is to court ruin.
The sage does not exhaust his people in annexing states,
nor does a good charioteer exhaust his horses in taking extra roads.
For Càofù's driving skills never lost harmony,
and the governance of sage kings never forsook virtue.
Qín, grasping at benefit, used the bit to drive all under Heaven,
held the lash to whip the eight directions,
until the horses were worn out,
yet the whip and goad were only applied more harshly,
so there arose the disaster of broken bits and cast-off whips.
The people were not few,
nor was their effort insufficient,
but all inwardly rebelled and outwards depended on others and none were of use.
This is why Gāo Huángdì relied on the sword to take all under Heaven.
If two rulers are amicably united,
with the inside and outside interlinked,
under Heaven there is peace and quiet,
and for generations there is no trouble,
then what is there for the gentlemen and commoners to worry about?
What then should the Three Kings be angry at?"
The Dàfū said:
“When Bó Yì first received the fief of Qín,
the territory was seventy lǐ in extent.
Mù Gōng brought hegemony,
and Xiào Gōng expanded the enterprise.
From lowliness to exaltation,
from smallness to greatness.
Thus, the ancestors laid the foundation,
and the descendants perfected it.
Xuān Yuán fought at Zhuōlù,
slew the two Hào
and Chī Yóu, and became Emperor;
Tāng and Wǔ attacked Xià
and Shāng, executed Jié
and Zhòu, and became kings.
The Huáng Dì achieved success by war,
Tāng and Wǔ accomplished filial duty by conquest.
So it is the diligence of hands and feet,
and the nurture of belly and intestines.
The labor of the age
is the benefit for later generations.
Now the Four Barbarians are invading within;
if we do not repel them,
this great affliction will persist for ten thousand generations.
The Former Emperor raised righteous arms to punish the violent and strong,
destroyed Cháoxiān in the east,
pacified Rǎn
and Máng in the west, captured Bǎi Yuè in the south,
and checked the powerful Hú in the north.
He pursued the Xiōngnú to expand the northern provinces;
the undertakings of Tāng and Wǔ,
and the soldiers of Chī Yóu.
Thus a sagely lord expands territory,
not out of selfish profit;
he uses force,
not merely out of anger.
Thus to correct disorders and avert harm,
so as to provide distant considerations for the common people.”
The Scholar said:
“Qín captured the strong Yuè in the south,
and repelled the powerful Hú in the north.
They exhausted Zhōngguó in service against the Four Barbarians,
the people were fatigued to extremes and the ruler did not care,
the country fell apart within and those above did not know.
Thus one man raised his voice and the world responded;
Chén Shè's army was defeated,
land was seized from the feudal lords;
what profit was there for the successors?
The Shī says:
‘The harmonious cries of the crested ibis,
as the morning sun first rises.’
They climbed to seize immediate profit,
not thinking of future disaster.
Thus the King of Wú saw the gain in attacking Qí,
but did not recognize the disaster of Gān Suì.
Qín knew the profit in advancing and seizing,
but did not foresee the difficulty at Hóngmén.
Thus one knows one but not ten.
Zhōu was cautious in small things and attained greatness;
Qín desired greatness and perished for lacking the small.
The saying goes:
‘When the cart in front capsizes,
the one behind takes warning.’
‘The lesson of Yīn is not far,
it is in the era of the House of Xià.’
8.2 "On the Punishment of Qín, Forty-Fourth"
The Dàfū said:
“Qín,
Chǔ, Yān,
Qí were all feudal states of Zhōu;
the rulers of the Three Jìn,
and the Tián clan of Qí
were all retainers of the feudal lords.
Internally, they defended their states;
externally, they attacked the unrighteous.
Their territory expanded and their lands advanced;
thus, they were called ten-thousand-chariot states
and became feudal lords.
The ruling house of Zhōu cultivated ritual and lengthened culture,
yet the country grew weak and diminished,
and could not sustain itself.
To the east, it ceded to the Six States;
to the west, it feared Qín.
The court was exiled and displaced;
the ancestral temple’s rites were severed.
Relying on the great beneficence of the Former Emperor,
he revived its inheritance,
enfeoffed the illustrious Yǐngchuān,
and bore the title Lord Zhōu Zǐnán.
After Qín unified All Under Heaven,
it broke off the waters of Pèi in the east,
annexed and destroyed Cháoxiān,
seized Lùliáng in the south,
repelled the Hú
and Dí in the north, and, to the west, subdued Dī
and Qiāng. It took the imperial title
and received homage from the Four Barbarians.
Wherever boats and carts could reach,
wherever footprints passed,
all, without exception, came.
Not because they admired its virtue,
but because they feared its power.
With superior strength, men would pay it court;
with inferior strength, it would pay court to others.”
The Scholar said:
“Yǔ
and Shùn were counselors to Yáo;
Tāng and Wén
were ministers of the Xià and Shāng,
and the reason they gathered from the Eight Directions and received tribute under Heaven
was not due to the lands of Lùliáng,
nor the power of arms.
Qín, Chǔ,
and the Three Jìn were called ten-thousand-chariot states,
but did not cultivate virtue, only mutual aggression.
They raised armies and contended for power, and in the end, all perished.
Though they expanded their territories and enlarged their lands,
it was as if filling one’s stomach with reeds:
seeking security and existence,
how could that be attained?
Those who establish the nation on ritual and humility are like the great rivers
and the seas, their flow enduring and never exhausted;
their foundation is beautiful.
But if there is no foundation,
it is like fire in mugwort—sudden fury without continuance;
its demise is certain and to be awaited,
as with the Warring States.
When the virtue of Zhōu declined,
then it joined the other feudal lords;
but to this day it is not extinct.
Qín exhausted its strength and extinguished its lineage;
how could it possibly pay court to others?”
The Dàfū said:
“Zhōngguó and the borderlands
are like the limbs and the vital organs.
If the skin chills on the outside,
the inner organs fall ill within;
the labor of inside and outside
is not for the benefit of the other!
If the lips perish, the teeth grow cold;
injury to the limbs brings pain to the heart.
Thus, without hands and feet, the body is crippled;
without the borders, the internal state is harmed.
In ancient times,
the Róng and Dí attacked Tài Wáng at Bīn,
crossed over Qí
and Liáng, and bordered Qín at Jīng
and Wèi; east to Lùhún in Jìn,
they invaded and ravaged Zhōngguó,
and Zhōngguó suffered for it.
Now the Xiōngnú encroach and eat away within;
those at distance do not escape their suffering,
while only the frontiers bear their calamity.
The Shī says:
‘The anxious heart grows drear;
I think of how the state brings harm.’
If we do not campaign in preparation,
then violence and harm will not cease.
Thus, the Former Emperor raised righteous arms to punish their transgressions,
broke through Qílián
and Tiān Shān,
scattered their assembled bands,
pressed north to Lóngchéng,
encircled the Xiōngnú greatly,
until the Chányú lost spirit,
barely escaping with his life.
He rode his rapid horse and fled north,
and more than a hundred thousand heads were taken and captives caught.
The bow-wielding peoples
and the lords in felt and fur
could not but lose heart;
their courage was crushed and they fled far away.
Then the army was displayed in triumph.
Hún Yé led his people to submit,
and five border commands were established to guard against the Hú,
so that within the Great Wall,
and beyond the Yellow River and the mountains,
few suffered invasion.
Then an edict was issued
to reduce garrisoning and grain levies,
and lighten labor duties.
Though there was hardship in the beginning,
in the end, we obtained its blessings.”
The literatus said:
“Zhōu accumulated virtue over generations,
and there was no one under Heaven who did not wish to make him their lord,
thus he became king without toil.
His beneficence extended from near to far,
so that the Mán
and Mò came of their own accord.
Qín relied on victories in war to unite the realm,
narrowed all within the seas yet coveted the lands of the Hú
and Yuè,
sending Mèng Tián to attack the Hú,
taking Hénán as the new Qín,
and so lost the old Qín.
He built the Great Wall to guard against the Hú,
yet lost what he sought to defend.
In the past,
arms were frequently in motion,
troops and expeditions were often raised;
north of the Great Wall,
the wheels of chariots and discarded arrowheads could be seen everywhere.
When Lǐ Guǎnglì and others made light of their calculations,
counting only how far their horses could go,
none but felt chilled to the heart.
Even though the camp at Hún Yé was taken,
they could not recover what had been lost.
This is not the utmost plan for the Altars of State.”
8.3 “On Conquest, Chapter Forty-Five”
The dignitary said:
“Qí Huán Gōng crossed over Yān to attack the Shānróng,
defeated Gūzhú,
and destroyed Lìngzhī.
Zhào Wǔ Líng Wáng crossed Jùzhù,
passed through Dàigǔ,
and nearly exterminated Línhú
and Lóufán.
Yān attacked and drove off the Dōnghú,
opening up a thousand lǐ of territory,
crossed Liáodōng to attack Cháoxiān.
Lord Mèng for Qín struck at and routed the Xiōngnú,
like a raptor chasing sparrows.
The Xiōngnú were cowed,
and for over ten years did not dare face south and look towards us.
Afterwards,
when Lord Mèng died and the feudal lords rebelled against Qín,
the realm fell into disorder,
and the Xiōngnú, in turmoil,
then dared resume raiding the frontiers.
That even small states such as Yān
and Zhào could still repel marauders and expand their lands,
yet now, with the great state of Hàn,
the might of soldiers and people,
not only the entire hosts of Qí Huán,
and the armies of Yān and Zhào;
yet the Xiōngnú have submitted for so long, but
the ministers have not united their efforts,
and the upper and lower ranks have not been in harmony.
The literatus said:
“In ancient times, those who raised troops
did not covet the gain of territory,
but to rescue the people from distress.
The people who longed for this
were like the parched awaiting rain,
greeting the royal army with basket meals and jugs of wine.
Therefore, those who grieved for the people’s suffering
gained their wholehearted allegiance—
such were Tāng and Wǔ.
Those who cared nothing for the people’s deaths,
who exhausted their strength and caused them to collapse and rebel—
such was the Qín king.
Mèngzǐ said:
‘If the ruler does not cleave to the Way,
does not follow humaneness and justice,
and compels the people to fight with force,
though he may gain victory, he will surely perish.’
This is why the realm is in disorder,
not because Mèng Tián died and the lords rebelled against Qín.
Of old, when the Zhōu house flourished,
the Yuè Cháng clan came to offer tribute,
and all the Mán brought gifts.
Afterwards, as Zhōu declined,
the feudal lords fought by force,
the Mán and Mò scattered,
each forming their own faction,
none able to unite;
thus Yān
and Zhào were able to take advantage.
Later,
the Xiōngnú gradually grew strong,
devouring the feudal lords like silkworms,
thereby driving off the Yuèzhī,
and relying on military power,
they shifted small kingdoms,
drew in archery peoples,
and united them as one family,
with one mind and one accord;
therefore, they are hard to subdue.
The former lord, for the late emperor, devised the stratagem against the Xiōngnú:
‘Station troops in the Western Regions,
seize all the advantageous positions,
to monitor changes.
With the might of Hàn,
attack the hosts of the Xiōngnú,
as strong crossbows pierce carbuncles;
the capture of Wú by the fowlers of Yuè—
how can that compare!’
The Emperor accepted this.
Acting on your sense of justice,
following your plan,
even the ability of Rèn Zhòng and Lí would not surpass it.
Appointing the Sōu Sù Commandant as Yùshǐ Dàfū,
entrusting him with government for more than ten years,
yet no achievements of Rèn and Lí have been seen,
but rather exhaustion and ruin,
the Xiōngnú no more abased,
while the masses and common people have become impoverished.
So your strategy cannot weaken the Xiōngnú,
but instead has enfeebled the Middle Kingdom.
Is this how a good strategist acts?
8.4 “The Western Regions, Chapter Forty-Six”
The dignitary said:
“In the past,
the Xiōngnú occupied the advantageous passes
of the rivers and mountains,
enjoyed the profit of farming and herding,
the people flourished and the armies were strong.
Whenever they entered as raiders,
all within Jùzhù was thrown into alarm,
and all the cities south of Shàngjùn fortified themselves.
In the time of Emperor Wén,
the barbarians entered Xiāoguān,
beacon fires connected through Gānquán,
and the officials, all afraid, did not know where to send forces.
Therefore they requested to garrison the capital to guard against the Hú.
To the west, the Hú imposed tasks on Dayuān,
and places like Kāngjū,
while to the south they allied with all the Qióng peoples.
The former emperor made advances and seized the broad and fertile lands,
established outposts from Zhāngyì westward,
cutting off the Qióng
and the Hú, dividing up their aid.
Therefore the states of the Western Regions
all opposed the Xiōngnú internally,
severed their right arm,
and fled with swords drawn.
Thus, men were recruited to farm and herd so as to enlarge supplies;
south of the Great Wall,
in all the border commanderies,
horses and cattle ran free,
stores accumulated across the plains—
yet I have not seen where this plan goes wrong.
If weak Yuè thereby succeeded in conquering mighty Wú,
though they differed in land and numbers,
the ruler used the ministers’ counsel,
so their accomplishment was assured.”
The wénxué said:
"Wú
and Yuè are confined by the Jiāng
and the Hǎi, with the three rivers encircling them;
they dwell amid the Five Lakes,
their lands pressing against each other,
their territories following in succession,
such that it is easy for them to subdue each other.
Before the sound of drums and bells is heard,
before banners and flags are unfurled,
before ranks and files are set,
troops have already engaged.
The army incurs no cost for transport and supplies,
and the soldiers do not labor under exhaustion or deprivation.
This is what is called ‘eating from granaries and fighting at the gates and suburbs.’
Now the Xiōngnú herd their flocks in boundless marshes,
spanning east, west, south, and north,
with no end in sight.
Even with light chariots and swift horses,
they are not easily caught,
let alone if one pursues them with burdensome baggage and encumbered soldiers.
The situation is such that pursuit cannot keep up.
Vast and indistinct, like walking in the nine marshlands, ignorant of where to stop;
bright and empty, like fishing in the Jiāng
and the Hǎi without a net or trap—though you may reach them,
the three armies will be weary and exhausted,
merely to be left as bait for them.
Thus an enlightened king knows there is no profit in it,
and deems that such campaigns cannot be frequently undertaken,
nor power indefinitely sustained.
Therefore he commands the gōngqīng, dàfū,
xiánliáng,
and wénxué,
so as to revive the path from decline to prosperity.
The gōngqīng ought to consider the urgent needs of the people,
the harm from the Xiōngnú,
accord with the heart of the sagely sovereign,
and establish a peaceful and secure enterprise.
Now, however, attention is given to petty strategies,
undermining fundamental plans,
going against the ruler’s wishes,
which is not to fully exhaust loyalty.”
The dàfū said:
“At first,
when Èrshī failed to conquer Yuān and returned,
the deliberators wished the ruler not to pursue his anger,
so that the Western Regions all disintegrated and submitted to the Hú.
The Hú gained multitudes of states and became ever stronger.
The previous Emperor listened to unexpected counsels,
displayed martial power,
returned and attacked Yuān,
Yuān surrendered with its entire country,
rendering up their implements,
presenting their precious horses.
The likes of Wūsūn were struck with terror,
requesting to become vassals and servants.
The Xiōngnú lost their wits,
fled and escaped,
though not fully subdued,
they dwelt afar in the cold and bitter wastelands,
the strong died at Qílián
and Tiānshān,
and the orphans have yet to return.
Therefore, all the ministers judged that the Xiōngnú were distressed by Hàn arms,
had their wings broken and their feathers bruised,
and could then be struck and subdued.
When the former Emperor passed from the ministers,
it was thus the Xiōngnú did not change their ways.
It is like building a mountain,
and stopping before a basketful remains,
so one’s achievements have no means of completion,
thereby abandoning and strengthening the enemy.
To stop short and spoil what was about to be accomplished,
and to make calculations for the ruler thus,
can scarcely be called loyal.”
The wénxué said:
“The officials speak of foreign affairs,
the deliberators all grasp at temporary expedients,
never considering the consequences.
Zhāng Qiān spoke of the blood-sweating heavenly horses of Dàyuān,
the true jade and great birds of Ānxī;
when the officials heard of this, it was as if they delighted in it,
and so marshaled great armies to attack Yuān,
after many campaigns only then was it conquered.
To travel ten thousand leagues to attack another’s state,
with more than half lost without a battle fought,
though Yuān was broken and precious horses obtained,
it was not a worthy plan.
At that time,
the officers and soldiers turned red-faced dealing with the four barbarians,
armies and expeditions appeared everywhere,
all the commanderies and principalities were called forth,
the common people suffered,
deceit and falsehood arose,
bandits multiplied,
magistrates could not restrain them,
cities and towns could not prevent them.
Only then was the shàng dàfū sent, adorned in embroidered robes, to rouse troops against them.
At that time,
the people, the commoners,
could not be assured of their lives,
thus the heroes and worthies east of the mountains
tended to be disloyal at heart.
It was by relying on the former Emperor’s divine sagacity.
The fault lay entirely in desiring to exhaust the Xiōngnú in remote expeditions.
If one calculates for the ruler thus,
can this be called loyalty?”
8.5 "Affairs of the World, Forty-Seventh"
The dàfū said:
“You scholars speak recklessly!
When proposals can be implemented after careful consideration,
do not merely cling to empty talk
that is glib and cannot be followed.
Hàn’s having the Xiōngnú,
is like a tree with borers,
or a man with disease—
if unremedied, it will only deepen.
Therefore, counselors believe in attacking and depriving them to exhaust them.
You scholars speak of moving them with virtue,
but such talk is impracticable.
You neither have anything above to resemble the Three Kings,
nor anything below to be like the recent Qín;
how, then, can you present a policy to officials that can be adopted and put into effect in this age,
to grant peace to the people and settle the borders?”
The wénxué said:
“In the past, Qí Huán Gōng put the people in order within,
and pacified the feudal lords without,
attending both the living and the lost,
and all under heaven followed his lead.
Thereafter,
when virtue waned and conduct declined,
at the meeting at Kuíqiū,
he raised himself proudly,
and nine states defected.
The Spring and Autumn Annals censured him for honoring force over virtue.
Thus, when one relies on virtue,
even powerful Chǔ gives in,
and distant lands come without being summoned;
but when one relies on force,
even those nearby are not close,
and small states do not submit.
These are its effects.
If one truly looks up to the reasons for the Three Kings’ flourishing,
and reflects on the means of Qín’s downfall,
recounts the rise of Qí Huán,
forsakes force for culture,
abandons strength for virtue,
opens the passes and bridges,
removes barriers and fortifications,
and leads by benevolence and righteousness,
then the northern frontiers will have no worry of invaders,
and within China there will be no matter of arms.”
The dàfū said:
“If matters are not debated in advance,
one cannot respond to emergencies.
With no preparations at home,
one cannot resist the enemy.
As the *Shī* says:
‘Instruct your people;
be cautious in your planning;
thus guard against the unexpected.’
Therefore, with civil affairs,
there must be martial preparedness.
In the past, Sòng Xiāng Gōng believed in Chǔ and made no preparations,
and thereby suffered great humiliation:
he was captured, and his state nearly perished.
Thus, though one may have a sincere heart,
if one does not understand flexibility,
it is a path towards peril and ruin.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* would not permit the Yí
and Dí to occupy China,
because they held no trust.
The Xiōngnú are greedy and rapacious,
act as the times permit,
seize upon opportunities,
and attack as swiftly as wind and lightning.
If you wish to use a heart of sincerity and trust,
and treasures of gold and silk,
to place faith in their faithless deceit,
it is as if befriending Zhí
and Jiǎo in supporting a fierce tiger.”
Wénxué said:
“The *Chūnqiū*
says, ‘The king has no enemy.’
This speaks of his benevolence and generosity,
the beauty of his virtue,
that all under Heaven paid him homage,
and none dared oppose him.
The reach of his virtue extended beyond the four quarters,
wherever boats and carriages could reach,
wherever footprints landed,
all without exception received his blessings.
The peoples of Mán and Mò, distant lands,
came by repeated interpretation and translation.
At such a time as this,
the world was harmonious and at peace,
ruler and minister shared the same virtue,
inner and outer trusted each other,
upper and lower were united in concord.
Weapons were set but not wielded,
shields and spears were stored away, unused.
Lǎozǐ said:
‘The rhinoceros has nowhere to use its horn,
venomous insects nowhere to expend their poison.’
Therefore, when the ruler is benevolent, none are not benevolent,
when the ruler is righteous, none are not righteous.
How could the likes of Zhí
or Jiǎo ever be close to such a ruler? ”
The Dàfū said:
“One must lay bare the heart and mind,
present honest intentions,
have inner sincerity that moves others,
and let righteousness be visible in countenance.
When Sòng Huáyuán
and Chǔ Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn met each other,
there was inner harmony and accord,
truly a basis for mutual trust.
But now the Xiōngnú harbor hearts of distrust,
hold hidden and unpredictable deceit,
rush toward benefit,
act opportunistically,
stealthily advance near the marketplace,
to strike those unprepared.
This is as if placing precious treasures by the roadside and not guarding them.
To seek to avoid loss
—how can that be possible?”
Wénxué said:
“If sincerity and trustworthiness are made manifest under Heaven,
and pure virtue flows throughout the four seas,
then those who are near sing songs and rejoice in it,
and those who are distant bring gifts of birds and beast in morning audience.
Thus, to govern the near requires no display of might,
to attract the distant, no use of force;
by cultivating virtue and righteousness and employing worthies and able men.
Thus, when the people set about their tasks,
they shun leisure for toil,
in matters of wealth,
decline plenty and accept lack.
Superiors and inferiors yield to each other,
and travelers on the road walk in the pattern of wild geese.
At such times,
goods are despised but virtue is prized,
righteousness is valued but profit is regarded lightly,
rewards come without theft,
so what need is there to guard treasures!”
8.6 *Peace Through Marriage, Forty-Eighth*
The Dàfū said:
“In the past, Xú Yǎnwáng practiced righteousness and was destroyed,
Lǔ Āigōng loved Rú academics and was diminished.
To know the civil but not the martial,
to know the one and not the other:
Therefore, though the gentleman is steadfast in benevolence,
he must still build walls to defend himself,
set up defenses to prepare himself,
because of the harm caused by those without benevolence.
Thus, in ancient times,
they would hunt and parade the troops, and regularly take stock of the army,
fearing that the people would become complacent and neglect warning of danger.
Therefore, weapons and armor
are a state's utility,
and walls and ramparts
are its support;
to abandon them,
is to remove the outward and expose the inner,
to reveal the heart and mind to the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú act rashly and advance stealthily,
striking at emptiness and vulnerability,
this is like facing the path of arrows and stones without armor,
disaster will surely ensue.
This is why the border fears,
and the officials worry.”
Wénxué said:
“In the past,
passes and bridges were open,
goods and supplies exchanged,
from the Chányú downwards,
all were friendly and attached to Hàn inside the border,
coming and going beneath the Great Wall.
Later,
Wáng Huī erred in plotting at Mǎyì,
and the Xiōngnú severed marriage alliance,
attacking border strongholds,
calamities arose in tangled profusion, never resolving,
war was continuous and unceasing,
frontier people neither removed armor nor slackened crossbows,
for decades,
they farmed in armor,
hoed and weeded while on lookout,
beacons and signal fires were frequently raised,
the able-bodied went out with bows and fought,
the elderly leaped over ditches and took refuge.
To speak of these things brings tears and chills the heart,
so that the benevolent cannot bear it.
The *Shī* says:
‘If one throws peaches to me,
I shall repay with plums.’
Never has it been heard that kindness yields evil in return.
Therefore, the gentleman is reverent and never errs,
respectful and courteous in dealing with others,
within the four seas,
all are siblings.
Thus, if one reflects within and is without shame,
what is there to fear or worry?”
The Dàfū said:
“From the Warring States era, the lords of Zhūxià
convened and formed alliances,
but after three gatherings,
they broke apart and doubted each other,
fighting and warring without end;
the six states formed alliances,
crown hats and sashes intertwined,
but never once was there lasting agreement.
How much more so with a state of beasts and birds!
The *Chūnqiū* records the ruler located in Chǔ,
and the assembly at Gàoyòu,
both deceived the Yí
and Dì.
The Xiōngnú have repeatedly entered alliance by marriage,
but always broke treaties first,
greedy for plunder and thievery,
a nation built on long-standing deceit and schemes.
Betrayal and faithlessness without end,
breaking every pledge,
just as the Zhū
and Xiàng cannot be moved,
and Shāngjūn could not be transformed.
To trust in their preparations for war,
or to win them over with virtue and closeness,
is indeed difficult.”
Wénxué said:
“The King stands impartially and listens to the world,
his virtue extends beyond all quarters,
distant states and alien customs
come to his court,
the phoenix rests among the ceremonial trees,
the qílín dwells in fields and marshes,
all living things,
none fails to receive his blessings.
Not that he walks everywhere to dispense benevolence,
but he extends his benevolence through his kingly virtue,
that is the truth.
Fàn Lǐ departed from Yuè,
Yóu Yú was raised among the Hú,
yet both became great ministers to overlords.
Thus, there are teachings to which the people do not submit,
but in all generations, there are none who cannot be transformed.
The *Shī* says:
‘Dip from the running stream,
scoop from its flowing current.’
Thus for Gōng Liú who lived among the Róng
and Dì, the Róng and Dì were transformed by him.
When Tàiwáng left Bīn,
the people of Bīn followed him.
When Zhōugōng cultivated virtue,
the Yuècháng people came in tribute.
Their embrace of goodness was like an echo.
In government, one must work to draw near by virtue,
what worry is there that they will not change?”
9.1 *Conscription, Forty-Ninth*
The dàfū said:
"A butcher, dividing at the proper joints,
can separate them with his hand;
but when he must extract sinew or bore through bone,
only with metal axe can he sever it.
When a sagely ruler transforms by following nature,
yet there are those who do not comply,
he must also raise troops to subdue them.
Thus Tāng executed Gě Bó,
Wénwáng subdued Quǎn Yí.
In later times, the Róng
and Dí harassed the Huá people,
and the Central States were restless;
Zhōu Xuānwáng
and Zhòng Shānfǔ thus checked and repelled the marauders.
The Book of Poetry states:
'Swiftly attack the Xiǎnyǔn,
reach to Tàiyuán.'
'The war chariots thunder out,
they fortify the northern frontier.'
Since ancient times, enlightened kings could not bring the unrighteous to order without war and conquest,
nor defend against the violent strong without fortresses and ramparts."
The erudite scholar said:
"Shùn wielded shield and halberd to subdue Yǒumiáo,
Wénwáng, by virtue, won the allegiance of the four barbarians.
The Book of Poetry says:
'Hàojīng and Bìyōng,
from west and east,
from south and north,
all submit without exception.'
Under the whole heaven,
all with human faces,
none but craned their necks and returned to rightful order.
Thus, drawing lines upon the land set the borders;
none trespassed them.
The Master said:
'One may face white blades,
but cannot enter the mean.'
Such is called supreme virtue.
Therefore, one skilled in attack does not need strong armor to win;
one skilled in defense does not need moats and bridges to be secure.
When Wǔwáng attacked Yīn,
he wielded the yellow battle-axe,
and swore oath at Mù field;
under heaven, all men wished to offer their service.
When the arms were laid to rest,
with scepter at his belt he governed,
and all people wished to be his ministers.
That which was gained by righteousness,
is guarded by virtue.
Qín conquered by force,
and guarded by law,
grasped neither the root nor the branch,
and thus perished.
The civil is suitable for long use,
but the martial is hard for lasting practice."
The dàfū said:
"The Book of Poetry says:
'The Xiǎnyǔn are most fierce,
therein lies my caution.'
'The warriors radiant and proud,
administer all quarters.'
Thus defense and conquest
have been the way from of old.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, before the Great Róng arrived, they prepared to resist them.
Therefore, when the four limbs are strong, the body is firm;
when the flowers and leaves flourish, the roots are well established.
Thus, securing the four borders brings peace to the Central States;
sending out garrisons and transport boats measures toil and rest.
When the ruler is anxious, the ministers labor;
when danger threatens above, those below die for it.
The late emperor grieved the people's want,
released palace funds,
unyoked the imperial chariot,
cut down music and meals,
to relieve the poor and prepare for border expenses.
Yet there was no sign of gratitude for this;
instead, there was only obstruction of what had already been accomplished.
This is not what I have heard should happen."
The erudite scholar said:
"When the Zhōu way declined,
the traces of kingship faded;
lords strove for strength,
and great and small oppressed each other.
Thus the strong strove to invade,
the weak strove to defend.
Armored men toiled in the ranks,
conscripted for war,
so rulers were troubled and the common people suffered misery.
Now, though the Central States are united as one,
yet within there is no peace;
corvée service is remote, and inside and outside are both wearied.
In antiquity,
there was no corvée that lasted over a year,
nor service beyond its due time.
Now, nearer is several thousand lǐ,
farther exceeds ten thousand lǐ,
spanning two terms.
The eldest son does not return,
parents are sorely worried,
wives and children sing plaintively,
bitterness and resentment stir in the heart,
longing and sorrow ache to the marrow.
This is why 'Duìdù'
and 'Cǎiwēi' were composed in the Book of Poetry."
9.2 "Strongholds and Defenses, Section Fifty"
The dàfū said:
"The tiger and rhinoceros can seize bears and wild beasts
and subdue the herd
because their claws and fangs are sharp for grasping and tearing.
Qín, thus, surpassed the feudal lords,
swallowed the world,
annexed enemy states,
relying on its defensible terrain and evident power.
The tortoise wears its shell,
so that foxes and raccoon dogs cannot capture it;
the viper has its sting,
so men fear and do not take it lightly.
Therefore, with preparedness one controls men;
without preparedness one is controlled by others.
For this reason, Zhòng Shānfǔ filled the gap in the ministerial office;
Lord Méng built the security of the Great Wall,
all for resisting marauders
and repelling threats ten thousand lǐ away.
Now if one does not fortify outwardly
but wishes for inner peace,
it is like a household that keeps no sturdy walls,
where dogs bark and startle in the night,
and thus act blindly and rashly."
The erudite scholar said:
"Qín had Xiáo
and Hán on its left, Lǒng and Dǐ on its right,
Shǔ
and Hàn in front, mountains
and rivers behind, four barriers set as its defenses,
with golden strongholds stretching a thousand lǐ;
fine generals and courageous warriors,
deploying sharp weapons to guard mountain passes,
armaments like Mòzǐ’s cloud ladders for siege.
They thought that even if Tāng,
Wǔ rose again,
Chīyóu returned,
they would not attack lightly.
Yet, in the garrisons, common soldier Chén Shèng without rank as general,
nor the might of an army,
with empty fists broke the army of a million,
without relying on even fences or ditches.
Thus, all is in virtue, not in fortifications.
If one truly uses benevolence and righteousness for defense,
and the Way and virtue for barriers,
the worthy as soldiers,
sages for defense,
then none can enter.
If things are so, then the Central States will have no alarm of barking dogs,
the border no fear of startled deer or watching wolves.
What possibility is there for reckless action then?"
The dàfū said:
"In ancient times,
for statecraft one must examine the land,
the hills and natural obstacles,
the timing of Heaven and the advantage of earth,
and only then could one attain kingship or hegemony.
Thus, lay out city walls,
regulate moats and ramparts,
to defend against marauders and secure the state.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
'In winter they deepened the Zhū River.'
This was to improve the advantage of the land.
The three armies aligned with timely opportunities,
attacking the weak with the strong,
yet were hindered by terrain,
and faced defenses as strong as golden walls.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Sòng in vain,
the Qín forces were defeated at Xiáo and Qīnyín,
so it was.
Therefore it is said:
'The timing of Heaven and the advantage of Earth.'
Qiāng and Hú are strong,
close to the border;
if we do not take them now,
they will be a long-term affliction on the four frontiers.
This is why Jìsūn worried about Zhuān Yú,
why there was the Gōujiàn disturbance,
and why it became a regret to mighty Wú."
Wénxué said:
"Geographical advantage is not as important as harmony among people,
and military force is not as great as civil virtue.
The far-reaching achievements of Zhōu
were not due to geographical advantage,
but to harmony among people.
To last for a hundred generations without being overthrown
comes not from relying on natural barriers,
but from virtue.
Wú had the barriers of the Three Rivers
and Five Lakes,
yet it was annexed by Yuè.
Chǔ had the strongholds of the Rǔ Abyss
and the Twin Halls,
yet it was destroyed by Qín.
Qín possessed Lǒngdì
and Xiáosài,
yet perished at the hands of the feudal lords.
Jìn had the Yellow River,
Huá, and the Nine Rivers,
yet lost power to the six ministers.
Qí had Tāishān
and the Great Sea,
yet was threatened by Tián Cháng.
Jié and Zhòu held all under Heaven,
together with Hào
and Bó. The king of Qín, though possessing all within the Six Directions, was troubled by Chén Shè.
It is not that geographical advantage is not solid,
but without strategy one cannot defend it.
To abandon what is near and worry about the far,
is like Wú failing to first settle its own realm
but instead cutting off the Huái River to the west and contending for supremacy with Qí
and Jìn;
thus Yuè, taking advantage of its exhaustion,
struck at its weakness.
Had the king of Wú heeded Shēn Xū,
cultivated virtue,
and not relied solely on the multitude of his troops,
then Gōu Jiàn would not have escaped being a vassal at the edge of the sea,
how could he have dared to plan otherwise?"
The Dàfū said:
"Chǔ rose from Wūshān to Fāngchéng,
connecting Wū
and Qiánzhōng,
setting up defensive passes to resist Qín.
Qín encompassed Shāng,
Luò, Xiáo,
and Hán, to ward off the feudal lords.
Hán relied on Yíyáng
and Yīquè,
controlled Chénggāo
and Tàiháng,
to secure Zhōu
and Zhèng. Wèi built fortresses along the banks of the Luo River,
shielded by mountains and bordered by rivers,
to safeguard the state of Jìn.
Zhào secured Fēihú,
Gōuzhù,
and Mèngmén,
to preserve Xíng and Dài.
Yān fortified Jiéshí,
severed Xié Valley,
and encircled Liáo.
Qí caressed Ā
and Zhēn, passed through Róng
and Lì, leaned on Tāishān
and backed on the sea
and river. Passes and bridges
are the stability of states;
mountains and rivers
are the treasures of the altars of state.
When the Xú people destroyed Shū,
the *Chūnqiū* called it
'seizing',
condemning their lack of preparedness
and the ease with which they acquired the territory.
Thus, worry comes from invading forces,
and benevolence is harmed by punishments.
When a gentleman governs a state,
he must ensure there are hazards that cannot be breached.
The *Yìjīng* says:
'Barred gates and night patrols
to guard against violent guests.'
This speaks to constant preparation."
Wénxué said:
"To rely on danger is not as good as to rely on righteousness;
in ancient times, Tāng with only seventy lǐ
