governed all under Heaven,
but Shū, with a hundred lǐ,
was lost to enemy states.
This shows what is condemned.
If passes and bridges were sufficient for reliance,
the Six States would not have been annexed by Qín;
if rivers and mountains were secure enough,
Qín would not have perished by the hands of Chǔ
and Hàn. Judging by this:
strategic high ground is not enough to become strong,
high walls are not enough to be secure.
If one does good, one prospers;
if one does evil, one perishes.
The king extends broad love far and wide,
unites inner and outer,
and people from the four seas each come to offer their tribute;
then, why would one need to bar gates and await trouble?
The *Chuán* says:
'That the feudal lords have passes and bridges,
that commoners have rank and emolument,
are not the results of peaceful times,
but began with the Warring States.'"
9.3 *On Courage, Section Fifty-One*
The Dàfū said:
"Jīng Kē nursed his plan for years but did not succeed,
for a dagger of one chi eight cun is not to be relied upon.
King of Qín dreaded the unexpected;
those who cut down Bēn
and Yù
depended on the sharpness of a seven-chi armor.
If Zhuānzhū had fought barehanded,
he could not have avoided capture;
if Yàolí had no water,
he could not have fulfilled his mission.
People say Chǔ was strong and Zhèng formidable,
having armor of rhinoceros and wild ox,
and swords of Tángxī steel.
Within, they relied on golden fortresses;
without, on sharp weapons;
hence their might dominated among the states,
and their strength subdued rival countries.
Thus, when Mèng Bēn raised his arm,
the multitude took him lightly;
when a coward is prepared,
his courage doubles.
How much more, then, the warriors of Wú
and Chǔ,
who wield sharp swords
and shoot powerful crossbows,
to race with the northern tribes in the Central Plain?
One man opposing a hundred
is nothing to boast about!
Even so,
then why did the Hú not defend Gǔ Xī,
nor engage in battle?
Lacking strength to endure the Hàn,
their situation inevitably led to surrender.
Thus, Shāng Jūn fled to Wèi,
and Sūn Bìn defeated Liáng."
Wénxué said:
"The Tángxī and Mòyáng steel of Chǔ
and Zhèng,
are indeed sharp,
and the rhinoceros-hide and wild ox armor
are truly sturdy,
yet despite this, could not ensure survival—
their sharpness is not reliable.
Qín united the forces of the Six States,
held Xiáo
and Hán, and ruled within the empire,
with defenses of metal and stone
and blades of Mòyé steel.
Yet Chén Shè had neither soldiers nor resources,
nor military strength,
using only hoes, mattocks, and thorny sticks
to break through strongholds.
No war drums were sounded;
no banners were raised.
The so-called 'golden fortress'
does not mean merely building walls and raising earth,
nor does it mean digging deep moats.
The so-called 'sharp weapons'
are not just the swords of Wú
and Yuè
or the blade of Gān Jiāng.
It means to take virtue and morality as the wall,
benevolence and righteousness as the outer rampart,
so that none would dare attack,
none would dare enter.
Such was King Wén.
To take virtue and morality as one's armor,
benevolence and righteousness as one's sword,
so that none would dare confront,
none would dare resist—
such were Tāng and Wǔ.
Now if you do not establish an invincible fortress
and invincible weapons,
but hope to depend on the efforts of a lone man
wielding three feet of blade,
this is indeed a trifling matter!"
The dàfū said:
"Jīng Kē, raising his dagger, entered the unfathomably powerful state of Qín;
the King of Qín was so alarmed that he lost his composure,
and all his guards were afraid.
Zhuān Zhū, with sword in hand, pressed upon the imperial chariot,
and stabbed the King of Wú;
Shī Niè stood upright in death,
his tall hat could be seen for a thousand lǐ.
Niè Zhèng, coming from Wèi,
from the court of Hán stabbed his lord;
having accomplished his aim and gained his desire,
he withdrew and punished himself before the court,
exposing his corpse in the marketplace.
Now, if we can indeed gain such heroes,
and ride upon the might of powerful Hàn,
we can overawe the unrighteous Xiōngnú,
controlling their life and death,
holding them accountable for their faults,
just as Cáo Guì pressed Qí Huán Gōng,
accomplishing his aims.
Advancing with sharp weapons to break their power,
disturbing their tents and camps,
those above and below will flee each other,
and then our light troops can swiftly pursue them.
The Xiōngnú will surely cross their arms and not dare to resist."
The scholar said:
"Tang obtained Yī Yǐn,
and with modest Bó as his capital, subjugated all the ministers under heaven;
King Wén obtained Tài Gōng,
and expanded Fēng,
Hào to make the world his own;
Qí Huán Gōng obtained Guǎn Zhòng and became hegemon among the feudal lords;
Duke Mù of Qín obtained Yóu Yú,
and the eight western Rong states submitted.
I have heard that when sages and worthies are obtained, even the Mán
and Mò come to offer tribute;
I have never heard of seizing and killing sovereigns to win over distant peoples.
As the Shī says:
'Bestow benevolence upon the Central States,
to pacify the four quarters.'
Therefore,
'From those Di,
and Qiāng, none dare not come to court.'
It is not out of fear of their power,
but of their virtue that they are in awe.
Thus, the sway of righteousness over the unrighteous
is swifter than a fine horse or a good bow;
virtue's call to the distant
is swifter than couriers or post stations."
9.4 "On Merit, Chapter Fifty-Two"
The dàfū said:
"The Xiōngnú have no walled defenses,
no secure moats or ditches,
no use of long halberds or powerful crossbows,
no abundance in their granaries and storehouses,
above they lack righteous law,
below they lack refined order,
lord and subject act with contempt,
there is no propriety above or below,
they weave willow for shelter,
and use felt for covers.
Their bows are plain and tips are bone,
and their horses do not eat grain.
Internally, their defenses do not merit fear;
externally, their rites deserve no praise.
The Central States are the heart of the world,
where worthy men gather,
where propriety and justice congregate,
where wealth and resources are stored.
To use wisdom to outwit the foolish,
to use justice to attack the unjust,
is like shaking autumn frost to scatter the falling leaves.
The Chūnqiū says:
'When Huán Gōng contended with the Rong
and Dí, he merely drove them away.'
How much more would this be so with the might of all under heaven?"
The scholar said:
"The chariots and implements of the Xiōngnú have no silver, yellow silk, or lacquered decoration;
they are simply made and value strength.
Their silk has no patterns, and their skirts do not follow curving hems;
they are all put together for completeness.
The men have no works of carving or fine craftsmanship,
no achievements in palaces and city walls;
the women do not produce ornate embroidery or sensual crafts,
nor make delicate gauze or fine silk.
Their ways are simple but effective,
easy to accomplish and hard to ruin.
Although they do not have long halberds or powerful crossbows,
warhorses or fine bows;
every household has its preparations,
every person has their use,
and in a time of emergency,
they string their bows, mount their horses, and are ready.
Their supplies are not seen on tables,
yet can sustain them for tens of days.
They use valleys as walls and cities,
and grass and water as granaries and reserves.
Their laws are simple and easily understood,
their wants are few and easily supplied.
Thus, punishments are few and there is no crime,
they merely gesture commands and they are obeyed.
They are careless in ritual but firm in fidelity,
rough in writing but alert in action.
Thus, even though they have no books of propriety and justice,
they carve on bone or roll up wood,
so that all the officials have means to record with each other,
and lord and subject have means to interact.
Whenever officials make plans for the county offices,
all speak of their manageability,
but in fact it is difficult;
thus when Qín tried to drive them off, it was Qín that perished instead.
Weapons are instruments of calamity,
they must not be lightly used.
Taking the strong for weak,
and survival as ruin,
can change in a single day."
The dàfū said:
"Lǔ Lián once said:
'Qín uses power to employ its officers,
Xiōngnú uses captivity to govern its people.'
Therefore, severe government cannot endure.
The Grand Ancestor received Heaven’s mandate to pacify chaos,
and his merit and virtue were lofty,
as great as Heaven itself.
Wén and
Jǐng continued his legacy and embellished it.
When the former emperor campaigned against the unrighteous,
expelling those without virtue,
it was to illuminate the path of benevolence and sagacity,
building the foundation of pure perfect virtue,
accumulated from years of humane rule by the sage-kings.
Now the scholar draws on the failed rule of lost states,
and compares it to our present,
saying, 'The Xiōngnú are hard to pacify,'
and that is as it ought to be!"
The scholar said:
"In the time of the House of Yǒu Yú,
the Sān Miáo were not submissive,
and Yǔ wished to attack them;
but Shùn said:
'It is my virtue that is not yet evident.'
He withdrew and reformed his governance,
and then the Sān Miáo submitted.
For lands that cannot be grazed,
and people who cannot be yoked,
sage kings did not send armies against them,
nor exerted force,
for it was not worth troubling the people and fatiguing the Central States.
Now, the enlightened king continues the legacy of the sages,
spreads virtue and transformation,
but in court there are still those who plot power and counsel conquest,
cherishing the pursuit of merit,
which I firmly find strange.
When ministers leverage the power of the world,
employ the resources of the state,
and enjoy the profits themselves without regard for their ruler,
this is how Wèi Tuó and
Zhāng Hán became kings,
and how Qín lost its government.
Sūnzi said:
'Now the affairs of a state
change a hundred times in a single day,
yet they do not perish,
for they can be adapted.
But once an army is sent forth to the open plains and broad pastures,
drums roar and arrows fly,
even with the wisdom of Yáo and
Shùn,
one cannot undo it.'
To fight and prevail,
then withdraw to repair etiquette and justice,
and continue the legacy of the Three Dynasties,
thus will benevolence and righteousness gather.
But to keep fighting after victory,
so that body dies and the state collapses—
this was the King of Wú."
The Dàfū said:
“To call with a favorable wind is easy to carry the voice,
to act in accord with the times is easy to exert power.
Wén and Wǔ, though possessing surplus strength,
did not plan for their descendants;
therefore, within three generations their virtue declined.
King Zhāo campaigned to the south,
died and did not return.
Fán Bó was imprisoned,
and his envoys were denied passage.
Jìn seized Jiāo,
and Pèi; the royal army was defeated by the Máo Róng.
Now the southwestern yí,
are the progeny of Chǔ Zhuāng.
The king of Cháoxiān is
a fugitive of Yān.
Nányuè’s Wèi Tuó arose from the Central States,
and declared himself king,
his virtue most shallow,
yet all had lost the vastness of the world,
each took himself as head of one province,
unyielding and arrogant,
each calling himself ‘the old man.’
The late emperor planned for all generations,
fearing the troubles of Jìzhōu,
and the dangers of Nánjīng;
therefore he sent the Left General Lóu Chuán to pacify them,
without a drop of blood being shed,
all became counties of the central government.
In the age of the Seven States,
all claimed ten thousand chariots,
sat facing south, calling themselves king,
drawing their swords as rival states for generations,
yet in the end, they could not escape lowering their heads and being bound as captives to Qín.
Now the Xiōngnú do not equal even a commandery of the Hàn,
they have neither the power of the Six States,
nor the counsel of worthy men.
By this, the ease or difficulty is
plainly evident to see.”
The Scholar said:
“Qín destroyed the Six States,
captured seven kings,
possessed abundant surplus strength,
considered itself beyond the harm of Chīyóu
and incapable even for Huáng Dì to expel;
yet in the second generation, was murdered at Wàngyí,
Zǐyīng with neck bound surrendered to Chǔ,
yet could not get those seven kings to lower their heads.
Had the Six States survived together,
Qín would have remained a warring state,
and would not have perished yet.
How is this proven?
From Xiào Gōng to Shǐ Huáng,
each generation was the strongest among the feudal lords,
for more than a hundred years.
But after unifying All Under Heaven,
in but fourteen years it fell.
Why so?
With no threat from enemy states abroad,
inwardly they indulged themselves.
Except for sages,
none, upon gaining power, fail to become arrogant and wanton—
no such one has ever been seen.”
9.5 “On Zōu, Fifty-third”
The Dàfū said:
“Zōu Zǐ disapproved of the scholars and Mohists of later ages,
not understanding the vastness of heaven and earth,
nor the manifest and expansive Way;
seeking to explain nine twists with only a single bend,
guarding one corner and desiring to know the myriad directions,
like wanting to know height and depth with no plumb line,
or round and square with no compass or rule.
He thus derived the movements of the great sage from beginning to end,
to make them understood by kings and lords,
first listing the famous mountains and great valleys of the Central States,
and continuing to those beyond the seas.
What is called the Central States
is but one part in eighty-one of All Under Heaven,
named Chìxiàn Shénzhōu,
and divided into nine provinces.
Separated by impassable mountains and land,
it became a single province,
with the great Yíng Sea encircling its exterior.
This is what is called the Eight Extremities,
where heaven and earth meet.
The ‘Yǔ Gòng’ also marked mountains and rivers, heights and plains,
but did not know the distance of the Great Way.
Therefore Qín wanted to reach the nine provinces and face the Yíng Sea,
to herd the Hu and hold court to the myriad states.
The learned scholars cling to the worries of their own plots of land,
the security of their neighborhood lanes,
unaware of the true meaning of the world.”
The Scholar said:
“Yáo made Yǔ Minister of Works,
to regulate the waters and land,
cutting wood along the mountains,
determining heights and depths and ordering the nine provinces.
Zōu Yǎn was no sage,
invented strange theories and misled,
bewildering the rulers of the Six States,
that they might accept his views.
This is what the ‘Chūnqiū’ called
‘an ordinary man deluding the feudal lords.’
Confucius said:
‘Not yet able to serve men,
how can one serve ghosts and spirits?’
If one cannot comprehend what is near,
how can one know the Yíng Sea?
Therefore, what is of no practical use,
the gentleman does not pursue;
what does not help good governance,
the gentleman does not follow.
The Three Kings entrusted themselves to classical doctrine,
and their virtue shone throughout the Four Seas;
the Warring States believed in fine words,
and were defeated and perished in great heaps.
Formerly, when First Emperor Qín had already swallowed All Under Heaven,
he wished to annex all states,
but lost his thirty-six commanderies;
he wished to reach the Yíng Sea,
and lost his provinces and counties.
To know great principles thus,
is worse than guarding small calculations.”
9.6 “On Zāi, Fifty-fourth”
The Dàfū said:
“Shamans and diviners should not be worshiped together,
nor should the scholars be debated with.
Believing the old, doubting the new,
is not the way for men to determine rightness themselves.
The Way of antiquity is measured by the present,
words about the distant are matched to the near.
The sun and moon are in the sky,
their omens are among men:
the changes of calamities and omens,
the span of life and death,
the transformations of yīn and yáng,
the order of the four seasons,
water, fire, metal, wood,
the responses of portents and blessings,
the spirits of ghosts and gods,
the fortunes from sacrifices,
the courses of sun and moon,
the records of stars and constellations,
the reasons for enigmatic speech—
what is their origin?
If you do not know, be silent;
do not rashly confuse yourself.”
The Wénxué said:
"In the beginning, Dǒng Shēng, Minister of Jiāngdū, expounded upon Yīn and Yáng,
the succession of the four seasons.
The father gives life,
the son nurtures,
the mother completes,
and the son stores.
Thus, spring births,
benevolence; summer grows,
virtue; autumn matures,
righteousness; winter stores,
propriety. This is the order of the four seasons,
which the sage imitates.
Punishment must not be relied upon to accomplish transformation,
thus one broadens the teaching of virtue.
When speaking distantly, it is necessary to examine the nearby,
thus internally practicing empathy,
treating penalties as if they were imposed upon oneself,
and labor as if borne by one's own body.
How then could one bear to kill his infant child,
for a useless cause,
abandoning what he depends on,
and set sail to the distant seas?
The Yuè people esteem snails and clams and neglect the grand sacrifice;
the ignorant delight in harsh sounds and are startled by the melodious Sháo and Huò.
Thus, those unaware of taste
take fragrance for stench;
those unaware of the Way
take fine words for confusion to the ear.
Whether early death or longevity,
each takes his predilections as destiny.
Yì and Áo, through skill and strength, did not meet good ends;
Zhì Bó, through greed and cruelty, destroyed himself.
The proof of Heaven's disasters,
the response of auspicious omens,
is like giving expecting return,
each receiving according to its kind.
Thus, those who delight in doing good,
Heaven assists with blessings,
auspicious signs are thus.
The Yì says:
'Heaven aids one,
there is nothing but good fortune.'
Those who delight in evil deeds,
Heaven repays with calamity,
disasters and anomalies are thus.
The Chūnqiū says:
'If the response is right, Heaven sends disaster.'
Zhōu Wén
and Wǔ honored the worthy and accepted remonstrance,
were reverent and cautious without calamity,
pure virtue at the highest,
the deities conferred blessings together.
The Shī says:
'Blessings descend in abundance,
blessings descend gently.'
The sun is Yáng,
the path of Yáng is clear;
the moon is Yīn,
the path of Yīn is obscure;
the principle of ruler's honor and minister's humility.
Thus, Yáng's brilliance flourishes above,
all Yīn types diminish below;
at the moon's fullness in the sky,
clams and oysters thrive in the depths.
Thus, when ministers fail to be such,
Yīn and Yáng are unbalanced,
and sun and moon change;
if governance is unequal,
then floods and droughts come out of season,
pests arise.
These are the responses of disaster and anomaly.
The times of the four seasons succeed one another,
and humans imitate their achievements;
the stars are arrayed in the sky,
and humans follow their motions.
The fixed stars are like the high ministers,
the multitude of stars like the common people.
When the fixed stars are aligned, the multitude follow;
when the fixed stars are disordered, the multitude fall."
The Dàfū said:
"Wénxué speaks of the types of strength and gentleness,
the five triumphs generating one after another.
The Yì is clear regarding Yīn and Yáng,
the Shū excels in the five elements.
Spring produces, summer grows,
thus fire comes forth from yín wood,
a Yáng type;
autumn is born, winter passes away,
thus water comes forth from shēn metal,
a Yīn thing.
Four seasons and five elements,
rise and fall in turn,
Yīn and Yáng are of different types,
water and fire do not share a vessel.
Metal is completed by earth,
destroyed by fire,
metal is born in sì,
what theory or teaching explains this?"
The Wénxué said:
"Weapons
are tools of misfortune.
Armor is strong and weapons are sharp,
they bring calamity upon the world.
When the mother controls the son,
thus can there be longevity.
The sage models this,
suppressing without being overt.
The Shī says:
'Lay aside shields and spears,
sheath bows and arrows,
I seek admirable virtue,
to practice it in the time of Xià.'
In troubled times it is not so.
Going against Heaven's way to satisfy violent desires,
corpses lie stiff and blood flows,
striving over land and earth.
Rulers who imprison their people,
extinguishers of ancestral sacrifices,
killers of others' sons,
as if severing grass and trees,
punishment blocks the way.
They apply to others what they themselves abhor.
Thus, the state is ruined and destroyed,
and the self suffers calamity,
Qín Wáng is such a one."
The Dàfū said:
"Metal is born in sì,
punishments applied lightly,
thus shepherd's purse and wheat die in summer.
The Yì says:
'Treading on frost,
hard ice will come.'
Autumn first brings frost,
plants wither and fall,
unite to execute punishment in winter,
all things are stored away.
Spring and summer produce and grow,
it is advantageous to practice benevolence.
Autumn and winter slaughter and store,
it is advantageous to administer punishments.
Thus, planting out of season,
though life occurs, nothing comes of it.
Practicing virtue in autumn and winter,
is called going against Heaven's way.
The Yuèlìng says:
'The cool wind arrives,
killing energy stirs;
crickets chirp;
fur garments are completed.
The Son of Heaven applies minor punishments,
begins hunting leopards and tigers,
to comply with Heaven's decree.'
The Wénxué unites with the four seasons,
harmonizes Yīn and Yáng,
esteems virtue and removes punishment.
If it is so,
hawks and falcons do not prey,
fierce beasts do not seize,
in autumn there is no hunting,
in winter no field hunts either."
The Wénxué said:
"The Way of Heaven delights in life, hates killing,
delights in reward, hates punishment.
Thus Yáng resides in substance, proclaiming virtue and bestowing it,
Yīn hidden in emptiness, assisting Yáng.
Yáng is strong, Yīn is gentle,
the last cannot surpass the first.
Heaven thus deprecates winter and esteems spring,
extending Yáng and subduing Yīn.
Thus, the ruler sits facing south to govern the world,
back to the Yīn, facing the Yáng,
placing virtue before punishment.
Frost and snow arriving late,
the five grains still ripen.
If hail and fog fall in summer,
all things are injured.
Observing from this:
Using strict punishment to govern a state
is like relying on autumn and winter to produce grain.
Thus, laws and decrees
are tools to control evil,
but not the custom of attaining great rule.
Therefore, in antiquity,
the enlightened kings flourished in virtue and teaching,
and relaxed in punishments and penalties.
Their nets let pass fish big enough to swallow a boat,
and their punishments were scrutinized beyond literal standards,
yet when the end was reached,
the people did not violate prohibitions."
10.1 "Xíng Dé, Section Fifty-Five"
The dàfū said:
"Edicts are for instructing the people,
laws are for controlling wickedness.
When edicts are strict, the people are cautious;
when laws are established, villainy is contained.
If the nets are loosely woven, beasts escape;
if the laws are loose, crimes are overlooked.
When crimes are overlooked, the people grow reckless and lightly violate prohibitions.
Thus, when prohibitions are not necessary,
the cowardly rely on luck;
but with true punishment,
even Zhí and Jiǎo do not offend.
Therefore, in ancient times, the Five Punishments were created,
branding the skin and flesh, and the people did not overstep the bounds."
The scholar of learning said:
"When the Dao has many paths,
the people do not know which way to take;
when laws and edicts are many,
the people do not know what to avoid.
Therefore, when a king establishes laws,
they should be as clear as the sun and moon,
so the people are not confused;
as broad as the great roads,
so the people are not perplexed.
Even those hidden away in distant places,
when they turn their minds to it,
maidens and young wives
all know what to avoid.
Thus, when laws and edicts are not violated,
the prisons and jails are unnecessary.
In former days, the laws of Qín were more numerous than autumn reeds,
and the nets were finer than congealed fat.
Even so, those above and below evaded each other,
villainy and deceit burgeoned,
and the officials who dealt with them
rushed about as if saving scorched and rotting things,
and could not bring them under control.
It was not that the nets were loose and the crimes escaped;
rather, ritual and righteousness collapsed, and the burden fell on punishments.
Now, the statutes and edicts number over a hundred articles,
the texts are numerous,
the names of crimes are severe;
when the commanderies and kingdoms enforce them,
doubts and confusions, whether shallow or deep, arise.
Even officials familiar with them
do not know how to judge,
how much less the common people!
Laws and edicts gather dust and are eaten by worms in the storerooms;
officials cannot even see them all,
how much less the common people!
This is why the number of legal cases increases
and the people violate prohibitions in growing numbers.
‘Should they go to jail, should they go to prison?
Grasping grain to divine by casting lots,
how can one achieve grain?’
This points to the problem of complicated laws and punishments.
The kinds of kin relationships are very many;
superiors killing inferiors, inferiors killing superiors,
and yet the mourning apparel is no more than five grades.
Of the categories of the Five Punishments, there are three thousand,
from the highest to the lowest,
but the crimes are no more than five categories.
Therefore, the way to govern the people
lies in earnest instruction, and nothing more."
The dàfū said:
"The scholar of learning claims that when a king establishes law,
it should be as broad as a great road.
But now, the imperial way is not narrow,
and yet the people boldly violate it,
because the punishment for the crime is light.
At a height of a thousand rèn,
no one dares to climb lightly;
at a weight of a thousand jūn,
no one dares to lift easily.
Lord Shāng punished those who dumped ashes on the road,
and thus the people of Qín were orderly.
Thus, stealing a horse earned death,
stealing a cow an even greater penalty,
and thereby the roots were valued and the opportunity for petty offenses was cut off.
The names and provisions for military rations
served to support the borders and emphasize the importance of military preparedness.
Hurting and killing were given the same punishment for theft,
so as to press the mind and hold the intention accountable.
Just as Lǔ employed Chǔ’s army to attack Qí,
which the *Chūnqiū* condemned.
Therefore, making the light penalty heavy,
and the shallow deep,
all have their reasons.
The subtleties of law
are, to be sure, not known to the common people."
The scholar of learning said:
"The *Shī* says:
‘The Way of Zhōu is as level as a whetstone,
and as straight as an arrow.’
This speaks to its ease.
‘The gentleman treads upon it,
the petty man observes it.’
This speaks to its clarity.
Thus, when virtue is bright, it is easy to follow;
when the law is simple, it is easy to carry out.
Now, the imperial way traverses all heights and lowlands,
winding throughout the world;
in this way, for the people it becomes a pit miles wide.
The nets are spread and hung over their grain;
pitfalls are set right on their paths;
traps are disguised and placed above them;
how can they not fall into them?
All that they desire is gathered,
all that profits them is opened,
virtue and righteousness decline—
how can they not overstep?
Therefore, by the end,
it leads to attacking cities and entering towns,
depleting the treasury’s gold,
stealing the ancestral temple’s vessels—
is it only the height of a thousand rèn,
or the weight of a thousand jūn!
The *Guǎnzi* says:
‘When the four bonds are not established,
even Gāo Yáo cannot produce worthy men.’
Thus, when moral teaching is discarded, deceit and falsehood thrive;
when ritual and righteousness are destroyed, vice and evil rise,
which means there is no virtue or righteousness.
Benevolence is
the manifestation of love;
righteousness is
the appropriateness of action.
Therefore, the gentleman loves benevolence and extends it to others,
rules the near and thus governs the far.
The *Zhuàn* says:
‘Of all living things,
none is more precious than man;
and of all that is precious to a ruler,
nothing outweighs the people.’
Thus, Heaven gives birth to the myriad things to serve humanity;
the ruler cherishes the people to accord with Heaven.
We have heard of rearing the people with six domestic animals and birds and beasts,
but never of harming people with the very things that nourish them.
When Lǔ’s stables burned,
Kǒngzǐ left his court,
asking after the people but not the horses,
for he valued men above beasts.
Now thieves of horses are executed,
and those who steal cattle are punished more severely;
riding and driving carriages and horses along the imperial way,
the officials prosecute harshly without end,
treating it as theft of horses,
and the penalty is likewise death.
Now if a man wounds another and flees with his sword,
can one also say he has robbed the armory and killed a man?
When a ruler establishes laws and the people violate them,
can this always be considered rebellion and a slight to the ruler’s intent?
To make a light offense punishable by death,
and let a deep one be excused,
is not the principle of prohibition by law.
Law
is established according to human feelings,
not to entrap people by creating crimes.
Therefore, when the *Chūnqiū* adjudicated cases,
it judged intentions to decide guilt.
Those whose intentions were good but who broke the law were excused;
those whose intentions were evil yet accorded with the law were punished.
Now, to wound another and have wrought no harm,
where the mind was not terribly vicious but the act accords with the law,
is it theft and wounding another?
Or is it the fault of the one enforcing the law?
Why does this never sit well with people’s hearts!
In ancient times,
to injure someone and leave a wound was punished,
to steal and have evidence was fined;
to kill someone was death.
Now, to take a weapon and wound a man,
and be punished like a murderer,
is this not far from the original intent?"
The dàfū lowered and raised his head, but did not reply.
Yùshǐ said:
“Those who uphold the law are
the reins and bridle of the state,
and punishments are
the cables and oars of the state.
Therefore, if the reins and bridle are not in order,
even Wáng Liáng could not make the carriage go far;
if the cables and oars are not fitted,
even a skilled craftsman could not cross the waters.
Hánzǐ criticized rulers who cannot make clear their system of laws and authority,
govern their officials and subordinates,
enrich their state and strengthen their troops,
in order to control enemies and guard against difficulties,
but are confused by the ornamental words of foolish scholars,
and doubt the strategies of worthy men,
allowing frivolous and corrupt parasites
to be exalted above actual merit,
yet wish for the governance of the state;
this is like setting aside the steps and wishing to ascend high,
or relying on no bit or rein and trying to drive a spirited horse.
Now, with punishments and laws set up,
still the people violate them;
how much more would they if there were no laws?
Disorder would surely result!”
Wénxué said:
“The reins and bridle
are the implements of steering,
adjusted by a skilled craftsman.
Law and authority
are the implements of governance,
transformed by a worthy person.
If the reins are held by the wrong person,
the horse will run wildly.
If the axle is held by the wrong person,
the boat will capsize and be damaged.
In former times, Wú appointed Zǎi Pǐ to the axle and broke his boat,
Qín appointed Zhào Gāo to the reins and overturned his chariot.
Now, if the way of benevolence and righteousness is discarded,
and reliance is placed only on legalist clerks,
then again the affairs of Wú
and Qín will be repeated.
For a ruler to emulate the Three Kings,
for a minister to emulate Zhōu Gōng,
for practitioners to emulate Kǒngzǐ,
this is the way unchanging for a hundred generations.
Hán Fēi criticized the Former Kings and did not follow them,
set aside just laws and did not abide by them,
and in the end fell into a trap,
was imprisoned,
and died as a guest in Qín.
Not understanding the Great Way but arguing minor points,
this only suffices to harm oneself.”
10.2 “Shēn Hán, Scroll Fifty-Six”
Yùshǐ said:
“If one waits for a Zhōu Gōng to be minister,
then in the world there would be no feudal states.
If one waits for Kǒngzǐ before studying,
then in the world there would be no Rú
nor Mò. When a garment has a small tear,
a patched cloth suffices for repair,
but one insists on waiting for a whole new bolt of silk before changing it;
when government has a small flaw,
laws and decrees can prevent harm,
but one insists on waiting for the “Yǎ”
and “Sòng” before repairing it.
This is like ignoring the doctor nearby
and seeking Yú Fú for a cure;
or discarding the water from the muddy pond
and waiting for the Jiāng
or Hǎi rivers before putting out a fire.
It is circuitous and not direct,
flawed and without intent,
so laws are not followed and governance becomes troubled and chaotic.
As for good rulers,
when something is worn, they patch it;
when there is a leak, they plug it.
Therefore Wúzǐ used law to govern Chǔ
and Wèi; Shēn
and Shāng used law to strengthen Qín
and Hán.”
Wénxué said:
“Those who hold the state select from the multitude and employ the worthy;
those who learn read broadly and pursue the good;
why must it necessarily be Zhōu Gōng
or Kǒngzǐ!
Thus it is said: Just follow the worthy.
Now Shāng Yāng,
went against the way of the sages,
disrupted and changed the customs of Qín,
and afterward his government declined and was in disorder, unable to be governed;
it drifted away and could not be restored.
If a foolish man sets fire in Pèi Zé,
the flames cannot be put out;
if bees or scorpions sting a man,
though he dies, still the poison is not stopped.
The more it is hampered,
the more restless it becomes;
disturbances trouble both high and low,
so disorder only increases.
Therefore, the sage’s teaching and transformation,
above shines with sun and moon,
below flows with heaven and earth,
how could it be said to be mere patching!”
Yùshǐ said:
“If a worn garment is not patched,
it becomes more tattered every day;
if leaks are not plugged,
they worsen daily.
The Great River’s first break at Hùzǐ,
was but a trickle;
by the end,
it flooded and harmed Zhōngguó,
bringing disaster to Liáng
and Chǔ, ruining Cǎo
and Wèi, damaging cities and towns,
driving residents to live on wood platforms,
people living on trees,
with no cottages for a thousand li,
leaving orphans and widows with nowhere to depend,
the old and weak without refuge.
So the former Emperor, grieving for this calamity,
personally inspected the river embankment,
emulated the achievements of Yǔ,
restored the river flow,
so Cǎo and Wèi were at peace.
The people wore his merit upon their heads,
praised his virtue,
singing
‘When Xuānfáng is blocked,
ten thousand blessings come’
—it was just so.
How can one not make even small repairs!”
Wénxué said:
“When the Yellow River bursts as wide as the mouth of a jar,
it still devastates a thousand li;
how much more if the rites are broken?
The harm is indeed great!
Now, lawsuits are counted in the tens of thousands each year,
the number of crimes increases,
and the resulting disaster is not only for Cǎo
and Wèi!
One knows to block Xuānfáng to bring blessing,
but does not know to block the source of chaos for all under heaven to be governed.
In the state of Zhōu they practiced this,
and did not apply only punishments;
the people were thereby harmonious,
the four seasons completed in due order,
and the world was not alone.
The Book of Hymns says:
‘May our longevity be smooth,
and countless blessings come.’
Such is making blessings—
this is not a small matter!
If truly faith and ritual are like Xuānfáng,
achievements will be accomplished,
governing will come simply, without action,
and why would officials need to patch,
and why would laws and orders need to block?”
Yùshǐ said:
“The sharp hoe and spade,
though beneficial for the grains, are also harmful to the weeds.
Clear principles and upright laws,
are hated by the treacherous but are a blessing for the virtuous people.
Therefore a warped piece of wood fears the straight line,
the treacherous hate upright law.
Thus the sage is discerning about right and wrong,
scrutinizes order and disorder,
so sets forth clear laws,
promulgates strict punishments,
to guard against wrong and rectify evil,
just as the square and plumb compound and rectify what is crooked.
Thus, water is
the safeguard against fire,
and law
the prohibition against wickedness.
Without law and authority,
even the worthiest cannot bring order;
without armor and weapons,
even Sūn
and Wú could not defeat the enemy.
Thus, Kǒngzǐ advocated benevolence and righteousness, and the people followed him like the wind;
Bó Yí withdrew to Shǒuyáng and yet the people could not be transformed.”
The Wénxué said:
"The law can punish people but cannot make them honest,
can kill people but cannot make them benevolent.
What is valued in a good physician
lies in his ability to precisely discern conditions and expel evil qi,
not in his skill at inserting needles or stone blades to pierce flesh.
What is valued in a good official
is to eradicate evil before it arises,
to cause men not to do wrong,
not in imprisoning them and punishing or killing them.
Now those who are called 'good officials',
if meticulous, bring disaster to their people through their acumen;
if strong, oppress their inferiors with severity.
They do not rely on the source from which the law arises,
but indulge in their own cruel hearts,
using rhetorical condemnation and false law
to entrap the innocent,
implicating the guiltless;
involving the father through the son,
the brother through the younger or elder;
if one man is guilty,
the whole district is alarmed,
ten families flee.
It is as if ulcers infect one another,
as if illicit desires are linked together,
one segment moves and a hundred branches shake.
The *Shī* says:
'As for those who are guilty,
once they suffer their due penalty,
those who are innocent
need not be dragged down with them.'
How painful it is that the innocent are implicated!
It is not the trouble of hoes and weeders being blunt,
but that they pull up crops while leaving grass.
It is not the lack of correct measures,
but that they straighten cords yet leave the crooked.
Thus, when those close commit a crime and are not punished,
it is like hoes being unused;
when those distant render merit and are not rewarded,
it is like crops being left untended.
Thus, the world does not suffer from lack of law,
but from laws that are not necessarily enforced."
10.3 "Zhōuqín, Section Fifty-Seven"
The Yùshǐ said:
"The *Chūnqiū* omits the names and titles of criminals,
calling them only 'yún dào' (common thieves),
in order to demean the criminals and sever them from human relationships.
Thus, rulers do not have such people as ministers,
officers do not make them friends,
and in the neighborhood they have no place.
Thus the people are ashamed to offend.
Now, these lawless people
break public laws to curry favor among themselves,
abandon their kin,
cannot uphold integrity and die by principle,
run and escape in groups,
bring themselves to crime,
and when they are punished and executed,
is it not as it should be?
Within a single household,
among fathers and elder brothers,
it is like parts of a body joined together:
when one segment moves, it is known in the heart.
Thus, from the Guān nèi hóu downwards,
land is divided into groups of five;
at home, families watch one another,
on going out and coming in, monitor each other;
if a father does not teach his son,
if a brother does not correct his sibling,
then upon whom does the responsibility fall?"
The Wénxué said:
"In ancient times,
they gave priority to ritual and made education clear.
When ritual was thorough and teaching clear,
only those who did not comply were classified for punishment.
Among punishments and penalties,
the people had no resentment.
Thus, Shùn administered four punishments and all under heaven accorded with him,
punishing the unbenevolent.
Heavy or light, all received their proper penalty;
punishment was certainly carried out with no pardon,
except for those in doubt.
If it is this way,
then how would the world produce lawless people for you to punish?
Now, killers live,
robbers and thieves become rich.
So the good people become dispirited within,
cease their toil and grow heartsick.
In ancient times,
men of virtue did not go near criminals;
criminals were not counted as men;
their persons were exiled and they shamed their descendants.
Thus, whether worthy or unworthy,
none failed to feel ashamed.
Now, men without conduct
pursue profit and ruin themselves,
suffer execution and shame, discarding ritual and righteousness,
always seeking to survive however they can.
Why?
One day they are imprisoned,
but their wounds not yet healed,
and they serve as palace guards for the ruler,
coming in and out of palaces,
thereby receiving stipends,
eating at the Grand Kitchen, enjoying gifts,
their own persons become honored,
their wives and children share prosperity.
Thus, some even join the ranks of ministers and counselors,
facing execution without pity,
let alone the multitudes!
What shame can there be!
To abandon moral teaching,
and compel people to observe ritual and righteousness,
is to oppress the people.
The *Chūnqiū zhuàn* says:
'If the son is guilty,
his father is arrested.
If the minister is guilty,
his ruler is arrested.
This is a great error in judgment.'
Yet now, sons are executed for fathers,
brothers for one another,
kin implicated together,
groups of ten and five incriminate one another,
like roots sending trouble to flowers and leaves,
injuring a pinkie finger and thus harming all four limbs.
In this way,
the guilty end up punishing the innocent;
punishing the innocent,
soon there will be very few innocent left under heaven.
When Zāng Wénzhòng governed Lǔ,
he bested the thieves and boasted of it.
Zǐgòng said:
'The people will deceive you—how much more the thieves!'
Therefore, officials are not considered good for many judgments,
nor physicians skillful for many punctures.
Zǐchǎn punished two men,
executed one,
and then goods were no longer abandoned in the road;
the people had no mind to deceive.
Thus, to be parent to the people
is to nurture them as sickly children,
to act with increasingly deep kindness;
that is all.
Ever since the laws of mutual reporting and collective responsibility arose,
the bonds of flesh and blood have been cut,
and punishments have greatly increased.
We have heard that parents, towards their children,
even if guilty, will still conceal them,
simply not wishing them to confess to guilt.
Sons conceal for fathers,
fathers for sons;
we have never heard of fathers and sons implicating one another.
We have heard of brothers delaying pursuit to save from bandits,
never of brothers implicating one another.
We have heard of hating the wicked and stopping with them,
punishing at the start and only the chief offender,
never of groups of ten and five mutually implicating each other.
Lǎozǐ said:
'If those above have no desire, the people will be simple;
if those above do nothing, the people will naturally enrich themselves.'
Let the lord be lord, minister be minister,
father be father, son be son.
Why link households in groups of five,
and what responsibility remains to officials?"
The Yùshǐ said:
"If one bears a thousand-jūn weight,
climbs immeasurable heights,
hangs by precipitous cliffs over deep ravines,
and looks down into unfathomable depths,
then even with the agility of Qìngjì,
the courage of Bēn and Yù,
none would fail to tremble in fear,
knowing that a fall would smash the body and brain on rocks below.
Thus, one who has been burned dares not grasp fire,
for he has seen the burns.
One who has been wounded dares not grasp a blade,
for he has seen the wounds.
If they recognized wrong for what it is,
punishment surely follows;
execution extends to fathers and elder brothers;
they will certainly fear and do good.
Therefore, to establish laws and measures
is like standing over a great chasm,
grasping fire or treading blades;
then people are fearful and cautious,
and none dare violate prohibitions.
A loving mother fosters ruined sons,
because she cannot bear to discipline them.
A strict household has no unruly slaves,
because correction is thorough and urgent.
Now, if a strict household's way of managing inferiors is not established,
but the loving mother's methods are cultivated,
then confusion arises."
Wénxué said:
"Zhòu instituted the punishment of grilling over fire,
and Qín had the law of emptying the treasuries.
Zhào Gāo decided punishments harshly within,
while the officials used severe laws to cut down offenses without.
The dead lay pillowed together,
the punished could see one another;
the people glanced sideways and stepped carefully,
shivering with fear though it was not cold.
The Shī says:
'We say Heaven is so high,
yet dare not stand tall.
We say Earth is so thick,
yet dare not tread its surface with confidence.
Alas for the people of today,
why do they crawl and skulk like vipers and lizards!'
At such a time as this,
was it only a matter of braving fire and treading blades?
Thus fathers turned against sons,
brothers slighted one another,
even to the point of kinsmen harming their own flesh and blood,
superiors and inferiors killing each other.
It was not that the punishments were too light so the penalties were unnecessary,
but rather that the laws were too harsh and kindness and benevolence were not bestowed.
Thus, when government is lenient the people are close to their rulers;
when government is stringent, the people plot against their lord.
Jìn Lì ended in exile,
the Second Emperor met with death;
was the fault to be found in strict laws not being enacted,
or in the house of severity lacking fierce henchmen?
The sages knew this,
and thus strove for harmony, not for intimidation.
Thus Gāo Huángdì moderated the harsh laws of Qín,
to comfort the embittered people,
and foster a spirit of harmony and concord,
ever fearing that harsh punishments would outweigh virtue.
Therefore his benevolence was unending,
and his grace flowed to later generations.
Shāng Yāng
and Wú Qǐ found the laws of Qín
and Chǔ too mild and increased their severity,
imperiling their superiors
and destroying themselves,
was this not indeed like the actions of an overbearing mother!"
10.4 "Decrees of the Sage, Fifty-Eighth"
The Yǔshǐ said:
"The Xiàhòu clan did not violate their word,
the Yīn gave solemn oaths,
the Zhōu made covenants,
yet trust in virtue steadily declined.
Without worthy men like Wén
or Wǔ,
rulers tried to repair their laws;
this was why Yīn
and Zhōu lost their power
and were deprived of it by the feudal lords.
Thus when clothing became threadbare, they changed their cut;
when laws grew obsolete, they reformed their systems.
In the time of Gāo Huángdì,
when All-under-Heaven was first pacified,
he issued edicts of virtue,
enacted stringent decrees,
granting power,
but this was not the common course of restoring order after disorder.
Thereafter,
the laws were gradually violated
and deviated from the right principle.
So, as evil sprouted, the 'Fǔ-Xíng' was composed;
as the kingly way declined, the Shī rebuked shone forth;
as the feudal lords became violent, the Chūnqiū satirized them.
A small-meshed net cannot catch fish,
and the law of only three chapters cannot govern.
Thus decrees inevitably had to be enhanced,
and the laws had inevitably to be multiplied.
Táng and Yú drew distinctions with their dress, not out of partiality;
Tāng and Wǔ marked their skin, not without reason;
as the ages differ,
so do priorities of severity and leniency."
Wénxué said:
"The people look to the law
as fish look to water;
if the water is clear, they are still;
if it is muddy, they are disturbed;
when disturbed, they are uneasy in their dwelling;
when still, they enjoy their callings.
If they enjoy their callings, they prosper;
with prosperity comes benevolence;
when all needs are met, contention ceases.
Thus in the ages of Chéng
and Kāng,
rewards needed not be dispensed,
laws did not need to be imposed.
It was not that crimes went unpunished;
rather, none violated the prohibitions;
it was not that rewards went ungiven;
rather, none failed to practice benevolence.
If it could be thus,
what business would the officials have to attend to in order to govern?
Now, those who govern the people
are like inept charioteers driving a team of horses:
at every step the whip falls,
at every stop the rod is raised.
Their bodies are battered by the lash,
their mouths wounded by the bit,
yet one asks that there be no misstep—
how can that be possible?
In the campaign at Qiánxī, the army collapsed;
the Liáng clan crumbled within;
severe punishments could not prevent it,
nor could harsh laws stop it.
Thus a worn-out horse no longer fears the lash,
and an exhausted people no longer fears punishment.
Though punishments be increased upon them,
what gain is there in their destruction?"
The Yǔshǐ said:
"High walls with triple blades,
but Lóu Jì feared them;
a mountain high and touching the clouds,
yet the herdboy climbs to its peak.
Thus, when strict, Lóu Jì was daunted by the triple blades,
but when the ground was made gentle, the herdboy easily reached the mountain top.
When metal is molten in the furnace,
Zhuāng Qiāo pays it no mind;
coins and knives lie in the road,
and a common woman picks them up;
it is not because the woman is covetous and Zhuāng Qiāo is upright,
but because their value and risk differ,
and the line between profit and harm is obvious.
Therefore, laws and decrees can be looked up to but not overstepped,
can be approached but not entered.
The Shī says:
'Dare not wrestle tigers,
dare not cross rivers.'
Because there is no benefit.
Lǔ loved propriety but had the crises of Jì
and Mèng;
Yān Kuài loved yielding but suffered the turmoil of Zǐzhī.
Propriety and deference are insufficient to check disorder,
while punishments and laws can put a stop to violence.
An enlightened ruler bases his rule on law,
and so can long control his subordinates
and securely keep his state."
Wénxué said:
"In ancient times,
they made clear oaths to benevolence and righteousness,
so that the people would not overstep them;
if they resorted only to punishment
and executed people without teaching,
that was called cruelty.
If punishments cannot be overstepped,
it is not as good as making righteousness the boundary that cannot be crossed.
I have heard of ages where ritual and righteousness prevailed and punishments were moderate,
but never heard of punishments prevailing and filial piety flourishing.
A high wall with a narrow base
cannot stand for long;
severe punishments and harsh laws
cannot endure.
The Second Emperor trusted the plans of Zhào Gāo,
imposed excessive burdens and wielded executions at will;
those punished filled the roads,
the dead accumulated by the day.
To kill many of the people was called loyalty,
to oppress the people utterly was called ability.
The masses endured demands they could not meet,
the common folk endured punishments they could not bear,
and all within the seas suffered together and could not live their lives.
Thus, when the ruler overburdened his ministers,
fathers were estranged from sons;
when the ruler made endless demands,
he lost the loyalty of his ministers.
Knowing that death brings no return,
a cornered rat will bite the cat,
a common man will confront mighty power,
retainers would break their bows,
Chén Shèng
and Wú Guǎng were such men.
At such a time,
all under Heaven rose together,
and attacked Qín from all sides;
before long, the altars and temples became ruins.
How could there be any way to long control subordinates
and securely keep a state?"
The Yǔshǐ was silent and did not reply.
The dàfū said:
"The blind music master, though he does not know black from white, is skilled in discerning words;
the rú scholars, though they do not know how to govern the world, are deft in criticism and discussion.
Those who speak well of Heaven must harmonize their words with the people,
those who speak well of antiquity must examine it by the present.
Why are edicts issued?
Why are laws imposed?
Táng and Wǔ preserved flesh and bone whole and ruled over Yīn
and Zhōu,
Qín used them,
yet the laws failed and were violated.
The standard of two feet four inches
has been the same from ancient to modern times,
sometimes for order,
sometimes for disorder.
The Chūnqiū sets the origin of crimes,
the Fǔxíng establishes punishments.
Now I wish to hear of the root of order and disorder,
and of the reasons for Zhōu and Qín as they are."
The literatus said:
"Spring and summer foster growth,
whereupon the sages patterned edicts accordingly.
Autumn and winter kill and store up,
accordingly, the sages established laws.
Therefore, an edict
is a teaching,
designed to guide the people;
a law
is punishment,
designed to check the violent and strong.
These two
are the instruments for order and disorder,
the measure of survival or extinction,
wielded by those above.
Táng and Wǔ followed rites and righteousness,
clarified likes and dislikes,
used morality to guide their people,
and did not need to impose punishments,
yet the people followed righteousness on their own—
this is how Yīn and Zhōu were governed.
When those above lack virtuous teachings
and those below lack laws,
then entrusting things to punishment must result in executions;
amputation of noses fills baskets,
feet cut off fill carts,
west of the Yellow River
was insufficient to contain the world’s exiles,
and in the end, these brought ruin—
this was King of Qín.
The standard of two feet four inches did not change;
but what was done opposed antiquity and rebelled against the people's hearts."
10.5 "Major Discourse, Chapter Fifty-Nine"
The dàfū said:
"Groaning over yellowed slips,
reciting the words of the dead,
officials today differ from the learned.
The learned know that cases are heard behind the court hall, but do not understand the matter;
they hear of these matters, but do not know the tasks involved.
One who governs the people
is like a great craftsman hewing,
he acts with axe and adze,
and stops when the line is followed.
Dù dàfū
and Wáng zhōngwèi and their ilk,
governed by law,
judged by punishment,
then only did banditry cease and crime was controlled.
Therefore, the archer draws by the mark,
the ruler governs by law.
In Yú and Xià, gentleness was used;
in Yīn and Zhōu, severity;
each age had its own implementation.
Now, to wish to govern a corrupt people
with methods proper to a simple era
is like dawdling to rescue the drowning,
or bowing formally to fight a fire."
The literatus said:
"When King Wén arose, the people loved goodness;
when Yōu and Lì ruled, the people delighted in violence—
not because their nature differed,
but due to customs and habits.
Thus, this is why Shāng
and Zhōu flourished,
and Jié and Zhòu were destroyed.
Táng and Wǔ did not possess the people of Bóyí to achieve good government,
nor did Jié and Zhòu have the people of Zhí
and Jiǎo to bring about disorder.
Therefore, order and disorder do not stem from the people.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'In hearing lawsuits, I am like other men;
but must it not be so that there are no lawsuits at all!'
To have no litigation is difficult;
judging litigation is easy.
To neglect the root but attend to the branch
was what the ancients called 'folly,'
yet now it is called 'wisdom.'
Correcting disorder with baton and staff,
correcting texts with knife and pen,
was what the ancients called 'harm,'
but what is now called 'worthiness.'"
The dàfū said:
"The customs are not of the times of Táng
and Yú,
nor are the people those of Xǔ Yóu's age,
and yet you wish to discard the law and govern—
that would be like refusing compass and axe,
and still wanting to bend the crooked and the straight.
Thus, one who governs does not wait for people already good by nature;
a wheelwright does not look for naturally curved wood.
Of old,
those like Yīng Shǎo and Bó Zhèng ruined Liáng
and Chǔ; Kūn Lú
and Xú Gǔ
stirred up disorder in Qí
and Zhào. The bandits of Shāndōng
and Guān Nèi
guarded the dangerous passes.
At such times,
if one does not employ axe and adze,
but instead severs by gentleness,
and then starts laying out rites and cultivating culture,
it is like a desperate doctor
using short needles to treat an ulcer,
or Kǒng Qiū using rites to persuade Zhí."
The literatus said:
"One who uses chopped, leftover wood to build a house
is not a master craftsman;
one who harms the people yet wants to govern well
is not a worthy official.
Thus, Gōngshū Zǐ used wood as suited its nature,
and the sage did not squander the people's essence.
Therefore, axes and adzes are used sparingly,
punishments are seldom resorted to,
good governance is established and transformation is accomplished.
Biǎn Què treated at the level of the skin and flesh,
cutting off evil qi,
so that ulcers and abscesses could not form.
Sages attend to what is not yet manifest,
so that the origins of disorder never arise.
Thus, acupuncture stones are kept and not used,
law and edict are set out but not applied.
To remedy what has already happened,
to bore down only after eruption
is the business of common folk.
To handle the unformed,
and foresee what has not yet sprouted,
is the task of the gentleman."
The dàfū said:
"The sage lauded by the learned
is Kǒngzǐ,
but his rule in Lǔ did not succeed,
he was sent away from Qí,
unused in Wèi,
entangled at Kuāng,
in distress at Chén
and Cài. To know the times are unready yet still to speak up
is obstinacy;
to know hardship but be unable to stop,
is greed;
to go forth unaware of being deceived,
is folly;
to be disgraced and yet not die,
is shameful.
These four things
are not done by ordinary people,
let alone by a gentleman!
Lord Shāng was received through Jǐng Jiàn,
Lord Yìng advanced through Wáng Jī.
Thus, officers depend on officers,
women on go-betweens;
when their family is illustrious and high,
it is not the work of the intermediary.
That Kǒngzǐ could not gain advancement by referrals
shows he was not a worthy officer or talented woman."
The Wénxué said:
"Kǒngzǐ was born in a turbulent age;
he pondered the way of Yáo
and Shùn.
In all directions,
scorching his head and soaking his feet,
he hoped that the rulers of the world might come to enlightenment.
Yet all was confusion;
the lords were blind,
the great officers jealous—
who would act as a mediator between them?
Thus the homely Mómǔ dressed herself up and boasted proudly,
while Xīzǐ wandered without a home.
It was not that he did not know hardship and disappointment, nor that he was unused;
grieving over the calamities of All Under Heaven,
he was as a loving mother mourning her dead child.
He knew it could not be otherwise,
yet he still despised himself for it.
So he went to Qí;
Jǐng Gōng deceived him;
he went to Wèi;
Líng Gōng laid siege to him;
Yáng Hǔ slandered him;
Huán Tuí sought to harm him.
Those who deceive and injure the sage
are deluded fools;
those who wound and slander the sage
are reckless knaves.
People deluded by cunning
are not truly human.
What shame is there in this!
Mèngzǐ said:
'To observe those close at hand, look to whom they serve;
to observe those at a distance, see what they serve.'
Were the sage to dissemble and seek to go along with others,
making no distinction in conduct nor choosing his friends,
then how could he be Kǒngzǐ!"
The great officer looked dejected and was shamed within,
sat at his four supports and did not speak.
At such a time,
those who rode the wind and courted favor were as thick as woven reeds;
their mouths opened wide and never closed,
their tongues raised and would not be stilled,
dark within, burdened with heavy loads yet receiving reproach.
The great officer said:
"Very well.
The glued carriage, scarce had it met with rain,
let me discuss this with the other students."
10.6 "Assorted Discourses, Sixtieth"
The guest said:
"I have observed the principles of salt
and iron,
and witnessed the arguments of the high ministers,
scholars,
and worthies.
Each intent points in a different direction;
each has its own origin;
some praise virtue and righteousness,
others focus on power and profit."
"Strange indeed is what I have heard.
The Zhōu and Qín were both resplendent;
each ruled All Under Heaven and gazed south from the throne,
yet the tranquility or peril, and the length of their reigns, differed greatly.
It was Zhū Zǐbó of Rǔnán who once said to me:
At such a time,
heroes and talented men advanced together,
and from the four quarters they gathered like spokes converging at the hub.
Over sixty men, such as Táng Shēng of Màolíng among the worthies,
and Wàn Shēng of the state of Lǔ among the scholars and their like, all assembled in the court,
spreading the influence of the Six Arts,
and discussing the sources of Great Peace.
The wise contributed their strategies;
the humane illuminated the practice;
the brave revealed their decisive judgment;
the eloquent presented their cases.
With dignified clarity;
with upright candor;
even if their arguments were not detailed and complete,
from this much could be generally perceived.
Yet, obscured by clouds and mists,
in the end it was abandoned and not implemented—
how lamentable!
The high ministers know that martial power can expand the territory,
yet do not know that broadening virtue can win over distant states;
they know that power and profit can extend usage,
yet do not realize that agriculture can enrich the country.
If those near draw close,
and those far speak well of our virtue,
what could one do that would not succeed,
what seek that would not be gained?
If one does not deviate from this course,
but strives to store up profit and lengthen power,
is this not a great error!
Liú Zǐyōng of Zhōngshān spoke of the Way of Kings;
correcting the customs of his age,
restoring all to the proper,
exerting himself to return to the root.
Upright but not opportunistic;
incisive but not excessively severe;
graceful and brilliant—such a man may be called a broad and magnanimous gentleman.
Zhū Shēng of Jiǔjiāng,
with blazing intention,
carried on the integrity of Shǐ Yú,
expressing indignation,
satirizing the ministers,
upright and unyielding—
he may be called one who does not fear the mighty and oppressive.
Grandee Sāng acted in accordance with current times,
adjusting to circumstances,
carrying forward the way and its techniques,
valuing power and profit,
dismissing minor arguments;
though not following the proper method,
even the most senior scholars grew ashamed,
unable to defend themselves;
he may be called a learned and thorough individual.
Yet occupying the position of minister,
he failed to draw the compass and rule,
and to transform those below through the Way,
letting himself be led by the pursuit of gain,
and not acting as a disciple of the ancient founders.
The Yìjīng states:
'Burns as if to be forsaken.'
When one does not serve in his proper post,
nor act according to the Way,
the result is the loss of his own nature
and the ruin of his lineage.
Chancellor Chē, ranked among Zhōu
and Lǚ,
held the central post at the axis,
yet kept his counsel and did not speak,
maintaining his position and departing quietly—
what of that!
What of that!
As for the chancellors collectively
and the men of the two Censorates,
who could not offer proper counsel to aid the chief minister,
but ran with their kind,
went with the current,
toadying and compromising to please superiors,
all to gain favor above:
petty men with the capacity of a peck or a scoop,
flatterers and sycophants—
what are they worth counting!"
